q: Based on the vapor pressure curves, which liquid has the stronger intermolecular forces?
e: At any temperature, Liquid 1 has the lower vapor pressure, so fewer molecules escape.
Liquid 1 also reaches 760 mmHg (its normal boiling point) at a higher temperature.

q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair with BOTH methyl groups equatorial?
e: On adjacent ring positions, equatorial bonds alternate up/down. Two equatorial groups at 1,4 point to opposite faces: trans.
cis-1,4, cis-1,2 and trans-1,3 always have one axial and one equatorial methyl.
(trans-1,2 and cis-1,3 can also be di-equatorial.)
t: Diequatorial: trans-1,2, cis-1,3, trans-1,4.

q: A molecule has 3 chiral centers and no internal plane of symmetry. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers?
e: Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ, where n = number of chiral centers.
Meso compounds (with an internal mirror plane) would lower this count, but the question rules them out.
t: 2ⁿ is a maximum. If the molecule can have a mirror plane, expect fewer.

q: In a molecule with only ONE chiral center, swapping any two groups on that center produces:
o: A meso form of the same compound
e: Swapping two groups reverses the 3D arrangement around the center, so R ↔ S.
With only one stereocenter, the new molecule is the mirror image: the enantiomer.
t: One swap inverts; two swaps put it back.

q: When assigning E/Z, an alkene is Z when:
o: The two highest-priority groups are on the same side
The two highest-priority groups are on opposite sides
e: Z: 'zame zide'. E: opposite ('entgegen').

q: In a chair conformation of cyclohexane, large substituents prefer:
e: Axial groups clash with other axial hydrogens (1,3-diaxial strain).

q: When assigning R/S, what should you do if the lowest-priority group points toward you?
o: Determine the direction, then reverse it
e: The rule assumes the lowest priority points away. If it points toward you, flip your answer.

q: A pure compound is labeled (R). Without measuring it, what can you say about the sign of its optical rotation?
o: Nothing; R/S does not predict the sign
It is (+) in water but (−) in other solvents
e: R/S is a naming rule based on CIP priorities.
(+)/(−) is an experimental measurement. The two are not linked, so the sign must be measured.
t: R ≠ (+). Many (R) compounds are (−).

q: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that:
o: Are not mirror images of each other
e: For compounds with several stereocenters, diastereomers differ at some, but not all, of them.
Cis/trans (E/Z) alkene isomers are also diastereomers.

q: How can a racemic mixture of a carboxylic acid be separated into its enantiomers?
o: Make diastereomeric salts with one enantiomer of a chiral base, then separate
Make enantiomeric salts with an achiral base, then separate by crystallization
Distill the mixture, since the enantiomers have different boiling points
Run ordinary silica TLC or column chromatography to separate them
e: Diastereomers differ in physical properties, so they can be separated (for example, by crystallization).

q: When a cyclohexane chair flips into the other chair, a substituent that was axial becomes:
o: Equatorial, on the same face of the ring
Axial, on the same face of the ring
Equatorial, on the opposite face of the ring
Axial, on the opposite face of the ring
e: A ring flip swaps every axial position with an equatorial one.
Bonds are not broken, so a group pointing 'up' still points up: it stays on the same face.
t: Ring flip: axial ↔ equatorial, but up stays up.

q: Which carbon in 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃, is a chiral center?
o: None; it has no chiral center
e: C2 is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃: four different groups.
C1 has three H's and C3 has two H's, so neither is chiral.

q: Looking down the C–C bond of ethane, why is the eclipsed conformation higher in energy than the staggered one?
o: Torsional strain from aligned C–H bonds
Angle strain from bonds squeezed below 109.5°
Steric clash between bulky methyl groups
Loss of π overlap between the two carbons
e: In the eclipsed form, the C–H bonds on the front and back carbons line up, and their electron pairs repel.
This is torsional strain (about 12 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethane). Ethane has no methyl groups to clash, and no π bond.

q: Three compounds are run on a silica-gel TLC plate with a nonpolar solvent. Which travels farthest (highest Rf)?
o: The compound with the highest molar mass
e: Silica gel (stationary phase) is very polar.
Polar compounds stick to the silica and move slowly.
The least polar compound spends the most time in the nonpolar solvent, so it moves farthest.
t: 'Like dissolves like' also works for chromatography: compounds travel with the phase they resemble.

q: A mixture of benzoic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.2) and 4-methylphenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.3) in ether is shaken with aqueous NaHCO₃ (pK<sub>a</sub> of H₂CO₃ ≈ 6.4). What happens?
o: Only benzoic acid moves into the aqueous layer
Only 4-methylphenol moves into the aqueous layer
Both move into the aqueous layer as anions
Neither moves; NaHCO₃ is too weak a base for either
e: A base deprotonates an acid when the acid's pK<sub>a</sub> is lower than the pK<sub>a</sub> of the base's conjugate acid.
Benzoic acid (4.2 < 6.4) becomes water-soluble benzoate. 4-Methylphenol (10.3 > 6.4) stays neutral in the ether.
NaOH (conjugate acid H₂O, pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) would extract both.
t: Bicarbonate separates carboxylic acids from phenols; hydroxide pulls out both.

q: Why are boiling chips added to a flask before a distillation?
o: To promote smooth boiling and prevent bumping
To catalyze evaporation of the lower-boiling liquid
To absorb impurities from the boiling liquid
To lower the boiling point of the mixture
e: Liquids can superheat and then boil violently all at once ('bumping').
Porous chips provide sites where small bubbles form, so boiling starts smoothly. They don't change the boiling point.

q: Gas chromatography separates compounds mainly by:
o: Volatility and interaction with the stationary phase
Charge and migration rate in an electric field
Molecular size, with the largest eluting first
Solubility in a polar liquid mobile phase
e: More volatile compounds generally exit the column first.

q: On a silica TLC plate developed in hexane, all the spots stay near the baseline. Which change should move them farther up the plate?
o: Add ethyl acetate to make the eluent more polar
Use pure pentane to make the eluent less polar
Use a longer plate with the same hexane
Spot a larger amount of the sample
e: A more polar mobile phase competes better with the silica for the compounds, so they spend more time moving.
All R<sub>f</sub> values rise. A longer plate does not change R<sub>f</sub>.

q: A mixture contains benzoic acid, aniline and naphthalene in ether. Which aqueous wash removes aniline?
e: HCl protonates the basic amine, pulling it into water.

q: Recrystallization purifies a solid by:
o: Dissolving it in hot solvent and letting pure crystals form on cooling
Dissolving it in cold solvent and letting pure crystals form on heating
Melting it and collecting the pure liquid that distills over
Dissolving it in solvent and then evaporating it quickly to dryness
e: Impurities stay dissolved in the cold solvent.

q: In liquid–liquid extraction, two layers form because the solvents:
e: Example: water and diethyl ether.

q: A developed TLC plate is viewed under a 254 nm UV lamp, and dark spots appear. Which compounds are most easily seen this way?
e: The plate contains a fluorescent indicator that glows green under 254 nm light.
Compounds that absorb UV (aromatic rings, conjugated π systems) block the glow and look dark. Saturated compounds need a stain such as iodine or KMnO₄.

q: An organic amine in an ether layer is shaken with aqueous HCl. Where does the amine go?
o: Into the aqueous layer, as an ammonium salt
It forms a solid at the interface
e: Protonation makes it charged and water-soluble.

q: Why does extracting with three 10 mL portions of solvent remove more solute than one 30 mL extraction?
o: Each fresh portion removes a fixed fraction of what remains
Smaller volumes of solvent have a larger partition coefficient
Three portions add up to more total solvent than 30 mL
Shaking three times heats the mixture and raises solubility
e: At equilibrium, the solute divides between the layers in a fixed ratio (the partition coefficient K).

Each new portion removes a fraction of what is still left, and these fractions multiply. For example, with K = 4 and 100 mL of water, one 30 mL portion leaves 1/(1 + 1.2) ≈ 45% behind, but three 10 mL portions leave (1/1.4)³ ≈ 36%.
The total volume is the same (3 × 10 = 30 mL); only the strategy differs.

q: After an extraction, anhydrous MgSO₄ is swirled into the separated organic layer. What is its purpose?
o: To absorb leftover traces of water
To raise the solvent's boiling point
To make the two layers separate
e: Organic solvents dissolve a little water during an extraction.
Anhydrous MgSO₄ (or Na₂SO₄) binds that water as a hydrate; it is filtered off before the solvent is evaporated.

q: Acid chlorides react with alcohols to form:
e: The alcohol is the nucleophile; Cl⁻ leaves.

q: Nitriles (R–C≡N) can be hydrolyzed with acid and heat to give:
e: The nitrile goes through an amide intermediate.

q: An ester is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
o: A carboxylic acid and an alkane
A carboxylate salt and an alcohol
e: Hydroxide attacks the ester's carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic acyl substitution).
The alkoxide leaves, giving a carboxylic acid that is deprotonated by base.
Products: carboxylate salt + alcohol. This is how soap is made from fats.
t: In base, carboxylic acids show up as carboxylates (−COO⁻). Watch the charge.

q: Local anesthetics are often esters (like procaine) or amides (like lidocaine). Why do amide anesthetics usually last longer in the body?
o: Amides resist hydrolysis by plasma esterases
Amides are excreted unchanged in the urine
Esters resist metabolism by liver enzymes
e: Esters are quickly hydrolyzed in the blood; amides are metabolized more slowly in the liver.

q: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis (saponification) goes essentially to completion, but acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is reversible. Why?
o: The carboxylic acid is deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate
Hydroxide attacks faster, which shifts the equilibrium constant
The alkoxide leaving group is more stable than water in base
The tetrahedral intermediate cannot form under acidic conditions
e: In base, the last step is RCOOH + base → RCOO⁻, a strongly downhill acid–base step (pK<sub>a</sub> about 4–5 vs about 16).
A negatively charged carboxylate repels nucleophiles and has no good leaving group, so the reverse reaction can't occur.
In acid, every step is reversible, so the reaction stops at equilibrium. Rate changes never change K.
t: Saponification uses up a full equivalent of base: it is base-promoted, not truly base-catalyzed.

q: Which product forms when acetic anhydride reacts with ethanol?
e: One acetyl group transfers to ethanol; the other leaves as acetic acid.

q: Ethyl acetate is heated with ammonia. What are the products?
e: NH₃ attacks the ester carbonyl, and ethoxide leaves (aminolysis).
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + CH₃CH₂OH
Ester → amide is downhill because amides are the most stable acid derivatives.

q: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, how does the hybridization of the carbonyl carbon change as the tetrahedral intermediate forms?
e: The carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar (sp²).
After the nucleophile adds, it has four single bonds: tetrahedral, sp³. When the leaving group departs, it returns to sp².
t: Addition–elimination: planar sp² → tetrahedral sp³ → planar sp² again.

q: Acid chlorides must be stored away from moisture because they react with water. What are the products?
e: Water attacks the C=O, and Cl⁻ (a very good leaving group) leaves; the lost H⁺ and Cl⁻ make HCl.
RCOCl + H₂O → RCOOH + HCl. The fumes of HCl are why acid chlorides 'smoke' in moist air.

q: In a tetrahedral intermediate, which group usually leaves?
o: The best leaving group (the weakest base)
The strongest base, being most electron-rich
The most nucleophilic group that is present
The largest group, to relieve steric strain
e: The tetrahedral intermediate collapses by expelling the weakest base (the best leaving group).
This is why acid derivatives are normally converted only to less reactive ones.

q: Which derivative is least reactive?
e: Resonance with the nitrogen lone pair makes amides stable.

q: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is given as an ethyl ester; liver esterases convert it to the active drug, a carboxylic acid. What is the main advantage of giving the ester form?
o: The neutral ester is absorbed across gut membranes better
The ester binds the viral enzyme more tightly than the acid
The ester is more water-soluble than the charged acid
The ester resists all hydrolysis, so it lasts for weeks
e: At intestinal pH, a carboxylic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 4–5) is mostly a charged carboxylate, which crosses lipid membranes poorly.
Masking it as a neutral ester improves absorption; esterases then hydrolyze it to release the active acid. A drug given in an inactive form like this is a prodrug.

q: Which name is correct for CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃?
e: Longest chain: 5 carbons. Methyl groups on C2 and C4.
Combine identical substituents with di-.

q: In anaerobic muscle, lactate dehydrogenase reduces the ketone of pyruvic acid (2-oxopropanoic acid, CH₃COCOOH) to an alcohol, giving lactic acid. What is lactic acid's IUPAC name?
e: Reducing the C=O at C2 gives CH₃CH(OH)COOH; the carboxylic acid is untouched.
The acid is still the principal group (C1), and the –OH on C2 becomes the prefix hydroxy-.

q: The neurotransmitter GABA is γ-aminobutyric acid, H₂NCH₂CH₂CH₂COOH. What is its IUPAC name?
e: Greek letters start at the carbon NEXT to COOH: α = C2, β = C3, γ = C4.
In IUPAC numbering the COOH carbon is C1, so the amino group is on C4.
t: γ is the third Greek letter but the FOURTH carbon. Don't line up α with C1.

q: What is the common name of propan-2-ol?
e: The –OH is on the middle carbon of a 3-carbon chain.

q: CH₃CH₂COCH₃ is named:
e: Four carbons, ketone at C2 → butan-2-one (methyl ethyl ketone).

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃?
e: The chain has 5 carbons with one C=C, so the parent is pentene.
Number from the end nearest the double bond: it starts at C2, giving pent-2-ene (not pent-3-ene).

q: Ethyl butanoate gives pineapples part of their smell. Which formula matches ethyl butanoate?
e: An ester is named alkyl (the group on the single-bonded O) + acid part ending in -oate.
Butanoate = a 4-carbon acyl group counting the C=O carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂CO–. Ethyl = –OCH₂CH₃.
The distractors are butyl ethanoate, propyl propanoate (both isomers) and ethyl pentanoate.
t: Ester names read 'O-side group first', but formulas are usually written acyl side first.

q: CH₃CH₂CONH₂ is named:
e: Amide: replace -oic acid with -amide. Three carbons → propanamide.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂OH?
e: The –OH (suffix) gets the lowest number first: C1.
Counting from C1, the C=C starts at C2: prop-2-en-1-ol (allyl alcohol).
t: The suffix group beats the double bond for low numbers.

q: What is the IUPAC name of OHC–CH₂–CO–CH₃?
e: Aldehyde outranks ketone, so the suffix is -al and the CHO carbon is C1.
The ketone C=O is on C3 and becomes the prefix oxo-: 3-oxobutanal.
t: Only ONE group gets the suffix; the others become prefixes.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CONHCH₃?
e: The acyl part, CH₃C(=O)–, has 2 carbons: ethanamide.
The methyl is on nitrogen, so it gets the locant N: N-methylethanamide.
N-Ethylmethanamide and propanamide are isomers (C₃H₇NO) with the carbons placed differently; N-methylethanamine has no C=O at all.

q: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO is named:
e: Four carbons, aldehyde at C1 → butanal.

q: Which carbocation is most stable?
e: Alkyl groups donate electron density (hyperconjugation and induction), stabilizing the positive charge.

q: How many σ bonds and π bonds does benzene (C₆H₆) contain?
e: σ bonds: 6 C–C + 6 C–H = 12.
π bonds: three (one in each 'double bond' of a Kekulé structure), spread over the ring.
t: Every bond has one σ; only the extra bonds in multiple bonds are π.

q: Which pair are NOT resonance structures of each other?
o: Acetone and its enol form, prop-1-en-2-ol
The two Kekulé structures of benzene
Acetate drawn with − on either oxygen
Allyl cation drawn with + on either end
e: Resonance structures differ only in where electrons are drawn; every atom stays put.
Going from acetone to its enol moves a hydrogen atom, so they are tautomers: two different real compounds.
t: If an atom moves, it's not resonance.

q: In nitromethane, CH₃NO₂, N is bonded to C, double-bonded to one O and single-bonded to the other O. What are the formal charges?
o: N is +1; the single-bonded O is −1
N is 0; both O atoms are 0
N is −1; the double-bonded O is +1
N is +1; the double-bonded O is −1
e: Formal charge = valence e⁻ − lone-pair e⁻ − bonds.
N: 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Single-bonded O: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Double-bonded O: 6 − 4 − 2 = 0.
t: Atoms with 'extra' bonds (N with 4) are +; atoms with 'missing' bonds (O with 1) are −.

q: Lab techs estimate protein concentration from absorbance at 280 nm. Which structural feature is mainly responsible for this absorbance?
o: Conjugated aromatic rings of Trp and Tyr side chains
The C=O π bonds found in every peptide bond
The sp³ C–H bonds of Leu and Val side chains
Hydrogen bonds between backbone N–H and C=O
e: Isolated π bonds (like a peptide C=O) absorb below about 230 nm; sp³ C–H bonds absorb only in the far UV.
The larger conjugated π systems of tryptophan's indole and tyrosine's phenol have smaller HOMO–LUMO gaps and absorb near 280 nm.
t: More conjugation → smaller energy gap → longer wavelength absorbed.

q: Resonance structures differ only in the positions of:
e: The real molecule is a blend of all resonance forms.

q: Histidine's imidazole side chain has two nitrogens. Why is only one of them basic?
o: One N's lone pair is in the aromatic π system; the other's is free
One N is permanently protonated, so only the other can take H⁺
One N is sp³ and the other sp², and sp³ lone pairs aren't basic
The two N atoms share one lone pair, so only one can be protonated
e: The pyridine-like N can be protonated (pKa about 6), making histidine useful in enzyme active sites.

q: Why do molecules with conjugated double bonds absorb longer wavelengths of light than isolated double bonds?
o: Conjugation narrows the HOMO–LUMO energy gap
Conjugation widens the HOMO–LUMO energy gap
Conjugation raises the energy of each absorbed photon
Conjugation localizes the π electrons on each C=C
e: Smaller energy gap → lower-energy (longer wavelength) photons are absorbed.
Highly conjugated molecules like β-carotene absorb visible light and look colored.

q: Which molecule is aromatic by Hückel's rule (planar, cyclic, conjugated, 4n + 2 π electrons)?
e: 4n + 2 = 6 when n = 1.
Cyclobutadiene has 4n π electrons (antiaromatic).

q: What is the hybridization of the nitrogen in an amide (R–CONH₂)?
o: sp², because its lone pair is in resonance with the C=O
sp³, because it has three σ bonds plus one lone pair
sp, because the C–N bond has partial triple-bond character
sp³d, because N expands its octet to form the C–N π bond
e: The N lone pair delocalizes into the C=O, making the amide group planar.
This planarity is why peptide bonds don't rotate freely.

q: Which compound has zero net dipole moment?
e: Each C–Cl bond is polar.
In the trans isomer the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
In the cis and 1,1 isomers they point the same general way and add up; chloroethene has only one C–Cl dipole.

q: Cyclobutadiene is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated, with 4 π electrons. It is:
o: Aromatic, since it is fully conjugated
e: Hückel: 4n + 2 π electrons is aromatic; 4n π electrons in a planar conjugated ring is antiaromatic.
4 = 4n with n = 1, so it is antiaromatic and highly destabilized.

q: Why is OH⁻ a poor leaving group, and how is this usually fixed?
o: It's a strong base; protonating it in acid gives water, a good leaving group
It's a weak base; adding a strong base makes it leave more easily
It's too small; converting it to an alkoxide makes it leave easily
It's a strong nucleophile; simply heating the mixture makes it leave
e: Converting –OH to a tosylate also works.

q: Why do polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO speed up SN2 reactions with anionic nucleophiles?
o: They don't H-bond to the anion, so it stays reactive
They H-bond to the anion, making it more stable
They react with the leaving group to remove it
e: Aprotic solvents have no O–H or N–H, so they can't hydrogen-bond to anions.
They solvate the cation (like Na⁺) but leave the anion 'naked' and highly reactive. SN2 has no carbocation.

q: An oxidation in organic chemistry usually involves:
o: Gaining bonds to oxygen or losing bonds to hydrogen
Gaining bonds to hydrogen or losing bonds to oxygen
Gaining bonds to carbon or losing bonds to halogen
Adding water across a C=C bond with an acid catalyst
e: Example: alcohol → aldehyde is an oxidation.

q: A researcher studies R–Br + Nu⁻ in water. Doubling [R–Br] doubles the rate; doubling [Nu⁻] has no effect; and an optically pure substrate gives mostly racemic product. Which conclusion fits?
o: SN1, with a tertiary (or similarly stabilized) substrate
SN2, with an unhindered primary alkyl substrate
SN2, with a crowded tertiary alkyl substrate
SN1, with a methyl or unhindered primary substrate
e: Rate depends only on [R–Br]: rate = k[R–Br], which is SN1.
Racemization fits a planar carbocation attacked from either face.
SN1 requires a stable carbocation, so the substrate is tertiary (or benzylic/allylic), not methyl or primary.

q: A protecting group is used during synthesis to:
o: Temporarily block a reactive group so a later step doesn't change it
Permanently block a group so the final product is more stable
Activate a group so that it reacts faster in the next step
Make a molecule chiral so that later steps are stereoselective
e: Example: converting an aldehyde to an acetal protects it from a Grignard reagent.

q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br, is a primary halide, yet it reacts extremely slowly by SN2. Why?
o: The bulky tert-butyl group blocks backside attack
Its primary carbocation forms far too slowly
Its C–Br bond is too strong to break easily
Its β-carbon has no hydrogens to remove
e: SN2 needs the nucleophile to approach the carbon from directly behind the C–Br bond.
The tert-butyl group next door crowds that path, so the reaction is very slow even though the carbon is primary.
t: 'Primary' doesn't guarantee fast SN2; check the neighbors too.

q: 2-Methylpropane reacts with Br₂ in light. The main product is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, even though the molecule has 9 primary H's and only 1 tertiary H. Why?
o: Br• selectively removes the H that leaves the most stable (3°) radical
Tertiary C–H bonds are the strongest, so they react last
A tertiary carbocation intermediate forms fastest
Primary radicals rearrange to tertiary radicals first
e: The H-abstraction step by Br• is uphill, so its transition state resembles the radical formed (Hammond).
The tertiary radical is most stable, so that pathway has the lowest barrier, and bromination is highly selective for it.
Radical halogenation goes through radicals, not carbocations.

q: Which is the strongest nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent?
e: In aprotic solvents, nucleophilicity follows basicity: F⁻ is strongest.
In protic solvents, the order flips (I⁻ strongest) because small ions are tightly solvated.
t: Solvent matters! This is a classic MCAT trap.

q: An SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon gives:
e: Backside attack flips the molecule like an umbrella in the wind.

q: An alkyl halide gives a mixture of substitution and elimination products with a strong, unhindered base at high temperature. Which change would favor substitution?
e: Elimination is favored by heat (it increases entropy).
Lower temperatures favor substitution.

q: What is the rate law for an SN2 reaction?
e: Both species are in the single rate-determining step: bimolecular.

q: Glutathione protects liver cells by using the –SH group of its cysteine to attack reactive electrophilic drug metabolites. Why is sulfur especially good at this?
o: Large, polarizable sulfur (as thiolate) is a strong nucleophile
Sulfur is more electronegative than O, so it holds electrons
Thiols are strong bases that pull protons off toxins
Sulfur forms strong π bonds that add across C=C bonds
e: Sulfur's outer electrons are far from its nucleus and easily distorted (polarizable), and they are weakly solvated in water.
That makes thiolates (RS⁻) excellent nucleophiles even though they are weaker bases than alkoxides.
The S attacks the electrophile, forming a conjugate that can be excreted.

q: A student wants to oxidize a primary alcohol to an aldehyde without over-oxidizing. Which reagent is best?
o: NaBH₄ in methanol, then acid workup
e: PCC works without water, so the aldehyde can't form a hydrate that gets oxidized further.

q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated HBr and forms bromoethane. By which mechanism does this mainly occur?
o: SN2 attack by Br⁻ on the protonated alcohol
E2 elimination followed by addition of Br₂
e: H⁺ first protonates –OH to –OH₂⁺, so water can leave.
A primary carbocation is too unstable, so Br⁻ attacks the carbon directly as water leaves (SN2).

q: Dehydration of an alcohol with concentrated H₂SO₄ and heat gives:
e: Water is eliminated (E1 for 2° and 3° alcohols).

q: Oxidizing propan-2-ol with chromic acid gives:
e: A secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone.

q: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol gives:
e: Secondary alcohols have one H on the carbinol carbon to remove.

q: A chemist needs to convert (R)-butan-2-ol into (S)-butan-2-ol with high stereochemical purity. Which sequence works best?
o: H₂SO₄ and heat, then H₂O and H⁺
e: Tosylation does not break the C–O bond, so the tosylate keeps the (R) configuration.
SN2 attack by OH⁻ then inverts the carbon once, giving (S).

HBr then NaOH gives at best a double inversion back to (R), with partial racemization because a 2° alcohol reacts partly by SN1 with HBr. PCC/NaBH₄ and the alkene route pass through flat intermediates and give racemic product.
t: Tosylation = retention; SN2 = inversion. Count the inversions.

q: Three alcohols are each shaken with HCl and ZnCl₂. Which one turns cloudy (forms an insoluble alkyl chloride) fastest?
e: ZnCl₂ helps the –OH leave, and the reaction proceeds by SN1 for 2° and 3° alcohols.
SN1 rate depends on carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°.
So the tertiary alcohol reacts almost instantly.
t: This is the Lucas test: 3° fast, 2° slow, 1° essentially no reaction at room temperature.

q: An alcohol's –OH group is on a carbon that is bonded to exactly two other carbon atoms. How is the alcohol classified?
e: Classify by counting the carbons attached to the carbinol carbon (the C bearing –OH).
Two attached carbons = secondary, e.g. propan-2-ol.

q: An alcohol reacts with sodium metal. What forms?
e: 2 ROH + 2 Na → 2 RONa + H₂

q: Why don't tertiary alcohols oxidize with PCC or chromic acid?
o: The carbinol carbon has no hydrogen to remove
The O–H is too weakly acidic to form a chromate ester
Tertiary alcohols are reduced rather than oxidized
The O–H hydrogen is too hindered to be removed
e: Oxidation requires removing an H from the carbon bearing the –OH.

q: Which reagent converts an alcohol into an alkyl chloride, releasing SO₂ and HCl as by-products?
e: SOCl₂ turns –OH into a good leaving group (a chlorosulfite), and Cl⁻ then replaces it.
The gaseous by-products SO₂ and HCl bubble away, driving the reaction.

q: Converting an alcohol to a tosylate (OTs) makes it:
e: Tosylate is a resonance-stabilized weak base, so it leaves easily.

q: Acetone reacts with hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) under mildly acidic conditions. What type of product forms?
e: The nitrogen of NH₂OH adds to the C=O carbon, then water is lost.
The result, (CH₃)₂C=N–OH, has a C=N bond like an imine: an oxime.

q: Which compound forms a hydrate (gem-diol) most readily in water?
e: Formaldehyde's carbonyl is the least hindered and most electrophilic.

q: Glucose cyclizes when its C5 –OH attacks its C1 aldehyde. What functional group forms?
e: One –OH and one –OR on the same carbon: a hemiacetal.

q: NaBH₄ reductions are often run in methanol, but Grignard reactions cannot be. What explains the difference?
o: A Grignard carbon is far more basic and is protonated
NaBH₄ is a much stronger base than a Grignard
Methanol reacts with ketones faster than Grignards
Methanol oxidizes the Grignard to an alcohol
e: A Grignard's carbanion carbon (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) grabs H⁺ from methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) instantly.
NaBH₄ reacts only slowly with methanol, so it survives long enough to reduce the carbonyl.

q: A Grignard reagent (RMgBr) is added to formaldehyde (H₂C=O), followed by acidic workup. What type of product forms?
e: R⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving R–CH₂–O⁻.
Acid workup gives R–CH₂OH, a primary alcohol with one more carbon than R.
t: Formaldehyde → 1°, other aldehydes → 2°, ketones → 3°.

q: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B₆) forms an imine with amino acids during transamination. Which functional group on PLP makes this possible?
e: The aldehyde reacts with the amino acid's amine to form a Schiff base.

q: When a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl carbon, the hybridization and shape of that carbon change from:
e: The C=O carbon has three groups: sp², about 120°.
After addition it has four groups (the new nucleophile, O⁻ and the two old groups): sp³, about 109.5°.

q: NaBH₄ reduces butan-2-one to butan-2-ol, which has a stereocenter. What stereochemical outcome is expected?
o: A racemic mixture, since H⁻ adds to either face
Only (R), since H⁻ adds to the less hindered face
Only (S), since the product is more stable
A meso compound, since the product has symmetry
e: The C=O carbon is flat (trigonal planar), so hydride can approach from the top or bottom face.
Neither face is favored in an achiral reaction, giving 50:50 (R) and (S).

q: In the body, the amino acid lysine forms an imine with retinal in rhodopsin. What type of bond links them?
e: The aldehyde of retinal reacts with lysine's side-chain amine.

q: An aldehyde is converted to an alkene using a phosphorus ylide. This reaction is the:
e: The C=O becomes a C=C.

q: Which reagent reduces an aldehyde to a primary alcohol?
e: Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon.

q: During acetal formation, chemists often remove water as it forms (for example, with a Dean–Stark trap). Why?
o: The reaction is reversible; removing water drives it forward
Water permanently poisons the acid catalyst it needs
Water oxidizes the acetal into an ester
Removing water makes the reaction exothermic
e: Carbonyl + 2 ROH ⇌ acetal + H₂O is an equilibrium.
Removing a product shifts the equilibrium to the right (Le Châtelier's principle).
Adding water does the reverse, which is how acetals are hydrolyzed.

q: Propanal and butanal are mixed with NaOH. Ignoring stereoisomers, how many different aldol addition products can form?
e: Both aldehydes have α-hydrogens, so each can form an enolate (2 nucleophiles).
Each enolate can attack either aldehyde (2 electrophiles).
2 × 2 = 4 products: two self-aldols and two crossed aldols.
t: Crossed aldols are only clean when one partner can't form an enolate (like benzaldehyde).

q: LDA at −78 °C removes the α-hydrogen from the less hindered side of a ketone, forming the:
e: Kinetic: fast, less substituted, bulky base, low temperature.

q: The α-carbon is the carbon:
o: Directly next to a carbonyl carbon
Two carbons away from the carbonyl
e: α-hydrogens are on this carbon.

q: Why can a ketone's stereocenter at the α-carbon be lost over time in a basic drug formulation?
o: Enolate formation lets the α-stereocenter racemize
Base hydrolyzes the ketone into a carboxylate salt
Hydroxide attacks the α-carbon by SN2, inverting it
Base reduces the ketone to an achiral alcohol
e: Formulations may be buffered to slow this process.

q: In an acid-catalyzed aldol reaction, what species acts as the nucleophile?
e: In acid there is almost no enolate; the neutral enol forms instead.
The enol's electron-rich C=C attacks a protonated carbonyl of another molecule.
t: Base → enolate nucleophile. Acid → enol nucleophile.

q: Propanal is treated with dilute NaOH at low temperature (no dehydration). What is the aldol addition product?
e: The enolate forms at C2 of propanal (the CH₂ next to C=O).
C2 attacks C1 of a second propanal: CH₃CH₂–CH(OH)–CH(CH₃)–CHO.
Longest chain with CHO: 5 carbons, OH on C3, methyl on C2.
t: The α-carbon becomes the branch point, so self-aldols of aldehydes other than acetaldehyde always give a branch at C2.

q: Racemization at an α-carbon stereocenter can happen in acid or base. Why?
o: Forming the planar enol or enolate erases the stereochemistry
Forming a planar carbocation at the α-carbon erases it
Repeated SN2 attack by water inverts the α-carbon
Reduction of the carbonyl makes the α-carbon achiral
e: Re-protonation can occur on either face.

q: Which compound gives a positive iodoform test (yellow CHI₃ precipitate with I₂ and NaOH)?
e: The iodoform test detects a methyl ketone, CH₃–CO–R (or an alcohol that oxidizes to one).
Pentan-2-one is CH₃–CO–CH₂CH₂CH₃: its CH₃ group is triiodinated and then cleaved off as CHI₃.
Pentan-3-one has ethyl groups on both sides; pentanal and cyclopentanone have no CH₃–C=O.

q: Optically pure (S)-2-methylcyclohexanone is dissolved in basic D₂O. Researchers find that the sample loses optical activity at the same rate that deuterium is incorporated at C2. What best explains this?
o: Both happen through the same planar enolate
D⁺ adds to the carbonyl carbon and inverts C2
Racemization happens by SN2 attack at C2
The keto form is planar at C2, so it can't be chiral
e: Removing the C2 hydrogen gives a flat enolate, which erases C2's configuration.
Adding D⁺ to either face gives (R) or (S), each now carrying D.
One enolate event causes both deuteration and loss of configuration, so the rates match.

q: A Claisen condensation needs a full equivalent of base, not just a catalytic amount. Why?
o: Deprotonating the product drives the equilibrium
The base is consumed by the alcohol solvent
Each step of the mechanism uses up a base
The ester must be fully converted to a carboxylate
e: The addition–elimination steps are reversible and slightly uphill overall.
The product's CH₂ between two C=O groups (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 11) is much more acidic than ethanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16), so ethoxide removes it.
This final, favorable deprotonation pulls the equilibrium forward; acid workup then gives the neutral β-keto ester.

q: In a crossed aldol between benzaldehyde (no α-hydrogens) and acetone with NaOH, which compound forms the enolate?
e: Only acetone has α-hydrogens.
Using a partner without α-H prevents a messy mixture.

q: In base, halogenation of a methyl ketone keeps going until all three α-H on the methyl are replaced. In acid, it usually stops after one. Why does base keep going?
o: Each added halogen makes the remaining α-H more acidic
Each added halogen makes the C=O oxygen more basic
Base turns the halogen into a better leaving group
In base, the halogen adds to the carbonyl carbon first
e: The electron-withdrawing halogen stabilizes the next enolate, so the second and third deprotonations are faster than the first.
In acid, the rate depends on enol formation, which needs protonation of the C=O; a halogen makes the oxygen less basic, slowing further reaction.

q: Benzoic acid is treated with SOCl₂, and the product is then added to excess NH₃. What is the final product?
e: SOCl₂ converts –COOH into the very reactive acid chloride, C₆H₅COCl.
NH₃ attacks the acid chloride C=O and Cl⁻ leaves, giving the amide (extra NH₃ absorbs the HCl).
Mixing benzoic acid with NH₃ directly would only give the ammonium salt.

q: A carboxylic acid has pK<sub>a</sub> = 4.0. What percentage is ionized (as RCOO⁻) at pH 6.0?
e: Henderson–Hasselbalch: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10<sup>(pH − pK<sub>a</sub>)</sup> = 10² = 100.
Fraction ionized = 100/(100 + 1) ≈ 0.99, or 99%.
t: Each pH unit above the pK<sub>a</sub> multiplies the A⁻:HA ratio by 10.

q: Butanedioic (succinic) acid is heated strongly. What forms?
e: The two –COOH groups are positioned to close a five-membered ring.
One –OH attacks the other C=O, and water is lost, giving succinic anhydride.
Easy decarboxylation needs a β-carbonyl; succinic acid's carbonyls are 1,4, so CO₂ is not lost.

q: Benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH) reacts with aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
e: This is a simple acid–base reaction: OH⁻ removes the acidic H from –COOH.
The products are a carboxylate salt (sodium benzoate) and water.
H₂ forms only with active metals (like Na) or hydrides.

q: Why can't NaBH₄ reduce carboxylic acids?
o: It's too mild a reducing agent
e: Use LiAlH₄ for carboxylic acids and esters.

q: How can the yield of a Fischer esterification be increased?
o: Use excess alcohol or remove water as it forms
Add NaOH to speed up the reaction
Add extra water to dissolve the acid
Use less acid catalyst to avoid side reactions
e: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O is an equilibrium with K near 1.
Adding a reactant or removing a product shifts it toward the ester (Le Châtelier).
NaOH would convert the acid to an unreactive carboxylate; water pushes the reaction backward.

q: Why are carboxylic acids poor substrates for nucleophilic attack under basic conditions?
o: Base converts them to carboxylates, which repel nucleophiles
Base makes their carbonyl carbon much more electrophilic
Base reduces their carbonyl group to an alcohol first
Their –OH becomes an excellent leaving group in base
e: The negatively charged carboxylate is unreactive toward nucleophiles.

q: A dicarboxylic acid like malonic acid loses CO₂ when heated because:
o: It's a β-carbonyl acid that decarboxylates via a cyclic transition state
It has no α-hydrogens, so CO₂ is lost by homolytic radical cleavage
Its carboxylate is aromatic, and that aromaticity drives CO₂ loss
Its two carboxyl groups are oxidized by air to CO₂ and water
e: Malonic acid → acetic acid + CO₂.

q: How does distance affect the acid-strengthening effect of a chlorine substituent?
o: The closer the Cl is to the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The farther the Cl is from the carboxyl group, the stronger the effect
The effect is the same at every position along the carbon chain
A nearby Cl weakens the acid, while a distant Cl strengthens it
e: The inductive effect falls off quickly with distance.

q: When LiAlH₄ reduces a carboxylic acid, bubbles of H₂ appear right away, and extra hydride is needed. Why?
o: The first hydride removes the acidic O–H proton
The carboxylic acid is oxidized to CO₂ and H₂
The alcohol product is reduced to an alkane
e: H⁻ is a strong base: RCOOH + H⁻ → RCOO⁻ + H₂(g).
Only then do further hydrides reduce the carboxylate (via an aldehyde) to the primary alcohol.
So more hydride is used than the reduction alone would require.

q: Lactic acid (pKa ≈ 3.9) builds up in muscles during intense exercise. At body pH, what form mainly exists?
o: Lactate (the deprotonated anion), plus released H⁺
A roughly 50:50 mix of lactic acid and lactate
Lactic acid dimers held together by H-bonds
e: pH 7.4 is far above the pKa, so the acid is almost fully ionized; the released H⁺ lowers pH.

q: The pKa of a typical carboxylic acid is about:
e: Acetic acid pKa ≈ 4.76.

q: Why are amides not basic, unlike amines?
o: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl
The nitrogen lone pair is held in a compact sp orbital
Hydrogen bonding to water ties up the nitrogen lone pair
The amide nitrogen is sp³ and too hindered to protonate
e: This resonance also makes amides planar.

q: Phosphorylation of a serine residue by a kinase adds which group to the protein?
e: The serine –OH is esterified with phosphate.

q: A drug that is a weak base (pKa 8.5) is taken orally. Where in the GI tract is it MOST in its neutral, absorbable form?
e: Higher pH means more of the base is unprotonated (neutral).

q: A tripeptide is formed from three amino acids. How many peptide bonds does it have?
e: n amino acids form n − 1 peptide bonds.

q: Which group is the phosphate unit commonly connected to in biological nucleotides?
e: Phosphate groups form phosphoester linkages to sugar hydroxyl groups.

q: Acetylating aniline gives acetanilide, C₆H₅NHCOCH₃. How does the basicity of its nitrogen compare with that of aniline?
o: Much less basic, since the lone pair is also shared with C=O
Much more basic, since the acetyl group donates electrons
About the same, since the N still has a lone pair
More basic, since the N now has only one H attached
e: In acetanilide, the N lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl (amide resonance) as well as the ring.
Amide nitrogens are essentially non-basic, so acetylation is a way to 'tame' a reactive amine.

q: Quaternary ammonium ions (R₄N⁺) differ from other amines because they:
o: Have no lone pair and stay positively charged at any pH
Have a lone pair and are protonated only at low pH
Have no lone pair and are neutral at physiological pH
Lose a proton at high pH to give a neutral amine
e: Choline and many drugs contain them.

q: Phosphorus can bond to five atoms (as in PCl₅), but nitrogen in the same group never does. What is the best explanation?
o: Phosphorus is larger and can hold more than eight valence electrons
Phosphorus is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it bonds more
Nitrogen has no lone pair left over to use in bonding
Phosphorus has more valence electrons than nitrogen does
e: N and P are both in group 15, with 5 valence electrons each.
N is in period 2 and limited to an octet (at most four bonds, as in NH₄⁺).
P is a larger, period-3 atom that can accommodate more electron groups around it, as in PCl₅ and in the expanded structures drawn for phosphates.

q: A drug's amine group has a conjugate-acid pK<sub>a</sub> of 8.4. At pH 7.4, what is the approximate ratio of protonated (R–NH₃⁺) to neutral (R–NH₂) forms?
e: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pK<sub>a</sub> + log([R–NH₂]/[R–NH₃⁺]).
7.4 = 8.4 + log(ratio), so log([R–NH₂]/[R–NH₃⁺]) = −1.
t: pH below pK<sub>a</sub> → the protonated form wins, by a factor of 10 for each pH unit.

q: Which amine is the strongest base in water?
e: Alkyl groups donate electrons, increasing basicity.
In water, secondary amines are often slightly stronger than tertiary amines because of solvation.

q: At pH 7.4, a typical primary amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) exists mainly as:
o: A roughly 50:50 mix of R–NH₂ and R–NH₃⁺
e: pH below pKa → protonated.

q: N-Ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine has three different groups and a lone pair on nitrogen, yet it can't be separated into stable enantiomers. Why?
o: The nitrogen rapidly inverts, interconverting the two enantiomers
A lone pair cannot count as one of four different groups
The molecule has an internal mirror plane passing through N
Amines are planar, so their N cannot be a stereocenter
e: The lone pair acts as the fourth 'group', so the N is a stereocenter at any instant.
But the N flips through a planar transition state (like an umbrella turning inside out) with a low energy barrier, so the two enantiomers interconvert very rapidly at room temperature.
Quaternary ammonium ions (four groups, no lone pair) can't invert, and they can be resolved.

q: An isopropyl group, (CH₃)₂CH–, attached to an atom with no hydrogens gives which ¹H NMR pattern?
o: A 6 H doublet and a 1 H septet
A 6 H septet and a 1 H doublet
A 6 H triplet and a 1 H quartet
A 6 H singlet and a 1 H singlet
e: The 6 equivalent CH₃ hydrogens have 1 neighbor (the CH): 1 + 1 = 2 → doublet.
The CH has 6 neighbors: 6 + 1 = 7 → septet.
t: Ethyl = triplet (3 H) + quartet (2 H); isopropyl = doublet (6 H) + septet (1 H).

q: IR spectroscopy mainly identifies:
o: Functional groups, by their bond vibrations
e: Different bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers.

q: A hospital lab uses pulse oximetry and UV–vis spectroscopy in blood tests. Why does hemoglobin absorb visible light strongly?
o: Its heme group contains a highly conjugated ring
Its many peptide C=O groups absorb visible light
Its iron atom emits light when it binds oxygen
Its aromatic amino acids absorb strongly at 280 nm
e: The extended conjugation gives hemoglobin its red color.

q: A mass spectrum shows a pair of molecular ion peaks (M and M + 2) in about a 3:1 ratio. Which element is present?
e: ³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl ≈ 3 : 1.
Bromine gives about a 1:1 pair.

q: In ¹H NMR, the number of signals tells you:
o: The number of different hydrogen environments
The number of hydrogens on neighboring carbons
The total number of hydrogens in the molecule
The number of different carbon environments
e: Equivalent hydrogens give a single signal.

q: In ethyl acetate's ¹H NMR, the O–CH₂ signal is split by the neighboring CH₃ into a:
e: 3 neighbors + 1 = 4 peaks.

q: A sharp, strong IR peak near 3300 cm⁻¹ together with a weak peak near 2120 cm⁻¹ indicates:
e: ≡C–H stretch: sharp, about 3300 cm⁻¹. (An alcohol O–H is broad; a primary amine shows two weaker N–H peaks.)
C≡C stretch: weak, about 2100–2260 cm⁻¹. A nitrile absorbs near 2250 cm⁻¹ but has no ≡C–H peak.

q: Why does the CH₃ signal of chloromethane (δ ≈ 3.0) appear downfield of the CH₃ signal of ethane (δ ≈ 0.9)?
o: Electronegative Cl pulls electron density away, deshielding the H
Cl adds more neighboring H, which increases the splitting
Cl's lone pairs shield the H, pulling the signal upfield
Chloromethane has a larger molar mass than ethane does
e: Less electron density around a proton means less shielding from the magnet's field, so the signal appears at higher δ (downfield).
Chlorine withdraws electron density from the C–H bonds, moving CH₃Cl's signal to about 3.0 ppm.

q: In ¹H NMR, the integration (area) of a signal tells you:
o: The relative number of hydrogens producing it
The number of hydrogens on neighboring carbons
How strongly deshielded those hydrogens are
The number of distinct hydrogen environments
e: Example: a CH₃ signal is three times larger than a CH signal.

q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has a fruity odor on the breath. GC–MS of a breath sample shows a compound with M⁺ at m/z 58 and a base peak at m/z 43. Which compound fits?
e: Acetone, C₃H₆O: 3(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 58 ✓ (ethanol = 46, acetic acid = 60, acetaldehyde = 44).
Losing ·CH₃ (15) gives the stable acylium ion CH₃C≡O⁺ at m/z 43.
Acetone forms when the ketone body acetoacetate loses CO₂.

q: A neutral organic compound that contains only C, H, O and possibly N has its molecular ion at m/z 87. What can you conclude?
o: It contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms
It contains no nitrogen atoms at all
It contains an even number of nitrogens
It has an odd number of oxygen atoms
e: Nitrogen rule: compounds of only C, H and O always have even molecular masses.
Each N (mass 14, three bonds) makes the H count odd, so an odd M⁺ means an odd number of N atoms.
Example: morpholine, C₄H₉NO = 48 + 9 + 14 + 16 = 87.

q: How many signals appear in the proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum of butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
e: No carbon is equivalent to another: the CH₃ on the C=O, the C=O, the CH₂ and the ethyl CH₃.
So there are 4 signals: the C=O near 209 ppm and the other three below 40 ppm.

q: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in CO₂?
e: Lewis structure: O=C=O. Carbon has 2 electron groups and no lone pairs.
2 electron groups → linear geometry, 180°.
2 groups → sp hybridization.
t: Count electron groups: 2 = sp, 3 = sp², 4 = sp³. Double bonds count as ONE group.

q: An IR spectrum shows a strong peak at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad peak above 3000 cm⁻¹. Which compound is most likely?
e: C=O present, O–H absent.

q: What is the configuration of the chiral center in the 2-bromobutane molecule shown? (The H is on a wedge.)
o: It can't be assigned from this drawing
e: Priorities: Br (1) > CH₂CH₃ (2) > CH₃ (3) > H (4).
In the drawing, Br and the ethyl point in opposite directions, so follow the rest of the circle: 2 → 3 → 1 (ethyl → methyl → Br) runs counterclockwise, which looks like S.
But the lowest-priority H points TOWARD you (wedge), so reverse it: R.
t: H on a wedge? Read the direction, then flip the answer.

q: Which combination gives 2-phenylpropan-2-ol (shown) after acidic workup?
e: The target is a tertiary alcohol, so a ketone is needed.
The carbinol carbon bears C₆H₅, CH₃ and CH₃: adding C₆H₅⁻ to (CH₃)₂C=O gives exactly that.
The aldehyde routes give secondary (or primary) alcohols.
t: Work backward: break one C–C bond to the carbinol carbon; that piece is the Grignard, the rest is the carbonyl.

q: How many chiral centers does menthol (shown) have?
e: Check each ring carbon with a branch: the C–OH, the C bearing the isopropyl group and the C bearing the methyl are each bonded to four different groups.
The isopropyl CH has two identical CH₃ groups, and the CH₂ ring carbons have two H's, so they are not chiral.
Total: 3 chiral centers (2³ = 8 possible stereoisomers).

q: 4-Hydroxypentanal (shown) exists in water mainly as a cyclic form. What is it?
e: The C4 –OH attacks the C1 aldehyde carbon.
The ring contains O, C1, C2, C3 and C4: five atoms.
C1 then carries one –OH and one ring –O–, which is a hemiacetal (not an acetal).
t: Five- and six-membered rings form easily; this is why sugars exist mainly as rings.
