q: A ball is kicked at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. What is the initial vertical velocity?
e: v_y = v sin θ = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m s⁻¹

q: An object falls from rest for 3.0 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). How far does it fall?
A bowling ball and a tennis ball are dropped together from the same height in a vacuum. Which lands first?
o: They land at the same time
It depends on the height of the drop
e: Gravity gives every object the same acceleration, g, when air resistance is absent.
Heavier objects feel more force but have proportionally more inertia, so a = F/m = g for both.

q: A patient's forearm holds a 10 N weight 0.30 m from the elbow joint. The biceps attaches 0.030 m from the elbow and pulls straight up. What biceps force keeps the forearm in rotational equilibrium? (Ignore the forearm's own weight.)
e: Rotational equilibrium: clockwise torque = counterclockwise torque.
t: Muscles have short lever arms, so they pull with forces much larger than the load. Expect a big number.

q: A car drives 60 km north in 1.0 h, then 20 km south in 1.0 h. What is its average velocity for the whole trip?
e: Displacement = 60 km north − 20 km south = 40 km north.
Average velocity = 40 km ÷ 2.0 h = 20 km h⁻¹ north.
(40 km h⁻¹ is the average SPEED: 80 km ÷ 2.0 h.)
t: Velocity uses displacement; speed uses total distance.

q: A ball is launched with an initial vertical velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). How long until it reaches its peak?
e: At the peak, v_y = 0: t = v_y/g = 10/10 = 1.0 s

q: A lab centrifuge spins samples at a radius of 0.10 m and 100 revolutions per second. About how many times g is the centripetal acceleration? (Use π² ≈ 10.)
e: a = v²/r = 4π²rf², with v = 2πrf.
Divide by g = 10 m s⁻²: about 4000 g.
t: 40,000 is the answer in m s⁻²; the question asks for multiples of g.

q: A car accelerates from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 4.0 s. What is its average acceleration?
In which situation is a box in translational equilibrium?
o: It slides at constant velocity across a floor
It speeds up steadily as it slides down a ramp
It is momentarily at rest at the top of a toss
It moves at constant speed around a circular path
e: Equilibrium means zero net force, so zero acceleration.

q: Newton's third law says that when you push on a wall, the wall:
o: Pushes back on you with an equal and opposite force
Pushes back with a smaller force, since it doesn't move
Pushes back with an equal force in the same direction
Pushes back on you only if it starts to move away
e: Action–reaction pairs act on different objects.

q: A mechanic pulls with 40 N on the end of a 0.25 m wrench, at 30° to the wrench handle. What torque does she apply to the bolt? (sin 30° = 0.50)
e: τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wrench and the force.
10 N·m would be correct only for a perpendicular pull.

q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. Which statement is true?
o: It is accelerating toward the center
e: The direction of velocity changes, so there's centripetal acceleration.

q: When friction does work on a sliding block, the mechanical energy:
e: Total energy is conserved, but mechanical energy isn't.

q: The body converts food energy into work with about 25% efficiency. If a person does 300 J of mechanical work, about how much food energy is used?
e: Efficiency = useful work ÷ energy input
Input = 300/0.25 = 1200 J (the rest becomes heat).

q: A ramp lets a worker push a 100 kg crate up 1.0 m in height over a 5.0 m ramp (frictionless). What force is needed along the ramp? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
e: Work = mgh = 1000 J

q: A frictionless roller coaster car passes a point 20 m high at 10 m s⁻¹. What is its speed when it reaches a point 5.0 m high?
e: Energy per kg: ½v₁² + gh₁ = ½v₂² + gh₂
v₂² = 400, so v₂ = 20 m s⁻¹
t: 17 m s⁻¹ forgets the starting kinetic energy.

q: A 2 kg cart at 3 m s⁻¹ hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. What fraction of the kinetic energy is lost?
e: KE before = ½(2)(9) = 9 J. After = ½(3)(4) = 6 J.

q: A motor does 600 J of work in 3.0 s. What is its power?
A 2 kg cart at 3 m s⁻¹ hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. What is their speed afterward?
e: Momentum: 2 × 3 = 3 × v, so v = 2 m s⁻¹.

q: A person carries a box horizontally at constant velocity. How much work does the person's upward force do on the box?
e: The force is vertical; the motion is horizontal (θ = 90°).

q: Kinetic energy depends on:
e: KE = ½mv².

q: A child pulls a sled 10 m along level snow with a rope that makes 60° with the ground. The rope tension is 50 N. How much work does the rope do? (cos 60° = 0.50)
e: W = Fd cos θ
Only the horizontal component of the pull does work on a horizontal displacement.

q: Mechanical advantage of a simple machine means:
o: Less force is needed, over a longer distance
e: Machines don't reduce work (ignoring friction): W = Fd stays the same.

q: A 60 kg person climbs 3.0 m of stairs in 6.0 s. What is their average power output? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
A wooden raft has a volume of 0.50 m³ and a density of 400 kg m⁻³. What is the largest extra mass it can carry in fresh water (1000 kg m⁻³) without sinking below the surface?
e: Fully submerged, the raft displaces 0.50 m³ of water = 500 kg, so it can support 500 kg total.
The raft itself is 0.50 × 400 = 200 kg.
Extra load = 500 − 200 = 300 kg

q: Atherosclerosis narrows a coronary artery by 50% in radius. According to Poiseuille's law, how much more pressure difference is needed to keep the same flow?
e: Q ∝ r⁴ΔP. To keep Q constant when r halves, ΔP must increase by 2⁴ = 16.

q: Blood flow becomes turbulent more easily in which situation?
o: High speed through a wide vessel
Slow flow in a narrow vessel
e: Turbulence rises with Reynolds number: ρvD/η.
Turbulent flow causes heart murmurs and bruits.

q: A block with specific gravity 0.60 floats in oil of density 800 kg m⁻³. What fraction of the block's volume is submerged?
e: Block density = 0.60 × 1000 = 600 kg m⁻³.
Fraction submerged = ρ<sub>block</sub>/ρ<sub>fluid</sub> = 600 ÷ 800 = 0.75
t: 0.60 is the answer only if the fluid were water.

q: A hydraulic lift has a 0.01 m² input piston and a 0.50 m² output piston. What force on the input lifts a 10,000 N car?
At depth h in a stationary liquid, the gauge pressure is proportional to:
e: Hydrostatic gauge pressure is ΔP = ρgh.

q: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid:
o: Is transmitted equally throughout the fluid
Decreases with distance from where it is applied
Acts only in the direction it was applied
Is transmitted only to the bottom of the container
e: This is how hydraulic lifts work.

q: A 3.0 kg object with a volume of 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is fully submerged in water (1000 kg m⁻³) and hangs from a spring scale. What does the scale read?
e: Buoyant force = ρVg = 1000 × 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 10 = 10 N.
Scale reading (apparent weight) = 30 − 10 = 20 N

q: A tall water tank has small holes at several depths. Water spurts fastest from which hole?
o: The deepest hole, farthest below the surface
The highest hole, nearest to the surface
The middle hole, halfway down the tank
All holes give the same speed of water
e: Torricelli's result: v = √(2gh), where h is the depth below the water surface.
Greater depth means greater pressure and a faster jet.

q: A solid object with density 800 kg m⁻³ floats in water (1000 kg m⁻³). What fraction of its volume is below the waterline?
e: For a floating object, weight = buoyant force.
ρ(object) V g = ρ(water) V(submerged) g
t: Fraction submerged = (object density) ÷ (fluid density). Quick and calculator-free.

q: In a standing adult, the feet are about 1.3 m below the heart. About how much higher is the blood pressure in the foot arteries than at heart level? (ρ<sub>blood</sub> ≈ 1000 kg m⁻³; 1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa)
e: Extra hydrostatic pressure ΔP = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 1.3 = 1.3 × 10⁴ Pa
1.3 × 10⁴ Pa ÷ 133 Pa per mmHg ≈ 100 mmHg
t: That's why blood pressure is measured on the upper arm, level with the heart.

q: An ice cube floats in a full glass of water. When the ice completely melts, the water level:
e: Floating ice displaces a mass of water equal to its own mass.
When it melts, it becomes exactly that much water, filling the volume it displaced.

q: A 4 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. A 24 V battery drives the circuit. What current leaves the battery?
e: Total R = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω.
t: 1.1 A comes from adding all three resistors (22 Ω) as if they were in series.

q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on conservation of:
e: Current into a junction = current out.

q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What current flows?
A 10 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a battery. Which resistor dissipates more power?
o: It depends on the battery voltage
e: In parallel both resistors have the same voltage V.
P = V²/R, so the smaller resistance gets more power (twice as much here).
t: Same V → use P = V²/R. Same I (series) → use P = I²R.

q: Resistors in parallel share the same:
e: Each branch connects across the same two points.

q: Three bulbs are wired in series to a battery. One bulb burns out (its filament breaks). What happens to the other two?
o: They stay lit at the same brightness
One stays lit and the other goes out
e: In series there is only one path for current.
A broken filament opens the circuit, so the current everywhere drops to zero.
In a parallel circuit, the other bulbs would stay lit.

q: What is the equivalent capacitance of a 3.0 µF capacitor in series with a 6.0 µF capacitor?
A 60 W bulb runs on 120 V. What current does it draw?
A 100 kΩ resistor and a 10 µF capacitor are connected in series to a battery, starting with the capacitor uncharged. About what fraction of its final charge does the capacitor hold after 1.0 s?
e: After one time constant, Q = Q<sub>max</sub>(1 − e⁻¹) ≈ 0.63 Q<sub>max</sub>.
t: 37% is what remains after one τ when a capacitor DISCHARGES.

q: A defibrillator charges a capacitor to a high voltage, then discharges it through the chest. What property of a capacitor makes this possible?
o: It stores energy and releases it quickly
It produces a steady current for hours
e: U = ½CV².

q: Two copper wires have the same length. Wire B has twice the diameter of wire A. How does B's resistance compare with A's?
e: R = ρL/A, and area A = πr², so A ∝ d².
Doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times larger, so R becomes 1/4.

q: A lamp with a resistance of 240 Ω is plugged into a 120 V outlet. What power does it use?
Sound travels fastest in:
e: Sound can't travel in a vacuum.

q: The frequency of a wave is:
o: The number of cycles per second
e: Measured in hertz (Hz).

q: A small speaker radiates 0.12 W of sound uniformly in all directions. What is the sound level 1.0 m away? (Use π ≈ 3 and I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻².)
t: 110 dB comes from skipping the 4πr² and using I = 0.12 W m⁻².

q: The Doppler effect explains why an ambulance siren:
o: Sounds higher in pitch as it approaches and lower as it moves away
Sounds lower in pitch as it approaches and higher as it moves away
Sounds louder as it approaches but keeps exactly the same pitch
Sounds higher in pitch only after it has passed by the listener
e: Relative motion changes the observed frequency.

q: Long exposure to sounds above about 85 dB can cause hearing loss. A 115 dB rock concert is how many times more intense than an 85 dB sound?
e: 30 dB difference = 10³ in intensity.

q: What is the period of a simple pendulum 1.0 m long on Earth? (g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻², π² ≈ g)
e: ≈ 2.0 s (the period does not depend on the bob's mass).

q: A string's fundamental frequency is 200 Hz. What is its second harmonic?
e: Harmonics of a string fixed at both ends: f_n = n × f₁.

q: Ultrasound for imaging a thyroid gland uses 5.0 MHz waves in soft tissue, where sound travels at about 1500 m s⁻¹. What is the wavelength, which limits the smallest detail that can be resolved?
e: Higher frequencies give finer detail but are absorbed faster, so they are used for shallow organs like the thyroid.

q: In a standing wave, what is the distance between two neighboring nodes?
e: Nodes are spaced λ/2 apart, with an antinode halfway between them.
So a node to the next antinode is λ/4.

q: A pipe that is closed at one end and open at the other can produce which harmonics?
o: Only the fundamental, and no higher harmonics
e: A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode.
Only odd multiples of λ/4 fit: L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 …, so f = n v/(4L) with n odd.

q: Resonance occurs when:
o: A system driven at its natural frequency reaches large amplitude
A system is driven at twice its natural frequency, doubling amplitude
Two waves of equal frequency meet and cancel each other out
A wave is fully absorbed, so the system stops oscillating
e: Example: a singer shattering a glass.

q: A sound's intensity increases from 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² to 10⁻⁵ W m⁻². By how many decibels does the sound level increase?
e: Intensity increases by 10³.
Δβ = 10 log(10³) = 30 dB

q: As people age, their lens becomes stiffer and they struggle to read close up (presbyopia). Which glasses help?
e: Converging lenses add focusing power for near objects.

q: In a double-slit experiment, the two slits are moved farther apart while everything else stays the same. What happens to the bright fringes on the screen?
o: They stay in the same places
They all merge into one bright band
e: Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d.
Increasing the slit separation d makes Δy smaller, so the fringes crowd together.

q: Which type of electromagnetic radiation carries the most energy per photon?
e: E = hf = hc/λ
Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energy per photon.
Order of increasing energy: IR < red < UV < X-ray.
t: This is why X-rays and UV can damage DNA but IR mostly just warms you.

q: Light that is already polarized vertically passes through a polarizing filter whose axis is 60° from vertical. What fraction of the intensity gets through? (cos 60° = 0.50)
e: Malus's law: I = I₀ cos²θ.

q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is its focal length?
e: For a spherical mirror, f = R/2.
f = 40/2 = 20 cm (positive, since a concave mirror converges light).

q: Using the standard sign convention, a real image formed by a concave mirror is located:
o: On the same side as the object, with a positive image distance
Behind the mirror, with a positive image distance
On the same side as the object, with a negative image distance
Behind the mirror, with a negative image distance
e: A mirror reflects light back toward the object, so real images form in front of the mirror.
Real images have positive i. (For a lens, real images form on the far side.)
t: Real is where the light actually goes: in front of a mirror, behind a lens.

q: An object 30 cm from a converging lens forms a real image 15 cm on the other side. What is the magnification?
The law of reflection says:
o: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of reflection equals the angle of refraction
Light bends toward the normal when it is reflected
n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ at the reflecting surface
e: Both angles are measured from the normal.

q: A converging lens is:
o: Thicker in the middle than at the edges
Thinner in the middle than at the edges
Flat on one side and thinner in the middle
Uniform in thickness from middle to edge
e: Converging lenses have positive focal lengths.

q: A farsighted patient's near point is 100 cm, but she wants to read a book held 25 cm from her eyes. What power reading lens does she need? (Ignore the lens-to-eye distance.)
e: The lens must make a book at o = 25 cm appear at her near point: a virtual image at i = −100 cm.
P = 1/f = 1/0.33 m = +3.0 D (converging).
t: Diopters need f in meters: f = 0.33 m gives P = +3.0 D, not 0.33 D.

q: A lens has a focal length of 0.25 m. What is its power?
e: P = 1/f (in meters) = 1/0.25 = 4 D

q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels:
o: From a higher-n medium to a lower-n medium, beyond the critical angle
From a lower-n medium to a higher-n medium, beyond the critical angle
From a higher-n medium to a lower-n medium, below the critical angle
From a lower-n medium to a higher-n medium, at any angle of incidence
e: This lets fiber optics and endoscopes carry light.

q: Light of frequency f ejects electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of 1.0 eV from a metal whose work function is 2.0 eV. If the frequency is doubled to 2f, what is the new maximum kinetic energy?
e: Photon energy at f: hf = KE + W = 1.0 + 2.0 = 3.0 eV.
At 2f, the photon energy is 6.0 eV.
KE<sub>max</sub> = 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 eV (more than double, because W is subtracted only once).

q: A fluorescent dye absorbs ultraviolet light and then glows blue. Why is the emitted light at a longer wavelength than the absorbed light?
o: Some absorbed energy is lost as heat before the photon is emitted
The dye adds energy to each photon before it is emitted
Blue photons carry more energy than ultraviolet photons
Wavelength always increases whenever light is reflected
e: The molecule absorbs a UV photon, then loses some energy to vibrations (heat) as it relaxes within the excited state.
The emitted photon has less energy, and since E = hc/λ, lower energy means longer wavelength.

q: An alpha particle consists of:
e: It's a helium-4 nucleus.

q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction remains after 24 days?
e: 24/8 = 3 half-lives: (½)³ = 1/8.

q: An excited nucleus emits a gamma ray. How do its atomic number (Z) and mass number (A) change?
o: Z drops by 2 and A drops by 4
Z rises by 1 and A stays the same
Z stays the same and A drops by 1
e: A gamma ray is a photon: it has no charge and no mass number.
The nucleus simply drops to a lower energy state of the same isotope (for example, Tc-99m → Tc-99).

q: Stable heavy nuclei, such as lead-208 (82 protons, 126 neutrons), have many more neutrons than protons. Why?
o: Extra neutrons add strong-force binding without adding repulsion
Neutrons carry a slight negative charge that cancels protons
Electrons inside the nucleus need neutrons to pair with
Neutrons are lighter than protons, keeping the nucleus small
e: Every proton repels every other proton (long-range Coulomb force), and this grows quickly as Z increases.
Neutrons feel the short-range strong attraction but no electric repulsion, so extra neutrons stabilize large nuclei.
Neutrons are neutral and slightly heavier than protons.

q: About how much energy is equivalent to 1 atomic mass unit (1 u) of mass?
e: From E = mc², 1 u (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) corresponds to about 931.5 MeV.
0.511 MeV is the rest energy of an electron; 13.6 eV is hydrogen's ionization energy; 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J is 1 eV.
t: Mass defect in u × 931 = binding energy in MeV.

q: A sample of 80 g decays to 10 g in 15 days. What is its half-life?
e: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 is 3 half-lives.
15 days ÷ 3 = 5 days

q: Why are alpha emitters dangerous mostly when swallowed or inhaled, not outside the body?
o: They can't penetrate skin, but inside they deposit energy in a small area
They penetrate deeply, spreading their energy over a large area
They are uncharged, so they only interact once inside the tissue
They turn into gamma rays inside the body, which then ionize cells
e: Alpha particles are highly ionizing over a short range.

q: Radiation therapy damages cancer cells more than many normal cells. Which property of cancer cells is mainly responsible?
o: They divide rapidly, so DNA damage is more harmful to them
They contain more DNA, so they absorb more of the radiation
They are larger, so they absorb more radiation per cell
They are less oxygenated, which makes them more radiosensitive
e: Fractionated doses give normal tissue time to repair between treatments.

q: A Geiger counter reads 3200 counts per minute from a sample. Exactly 2.5 hours later it reads 100 counts per minute (background is negligible). What is the half-life?
A mass defect of 0.0010 kg is completely converted into energy. How much energy is released? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

A hospital starts a hand-hygiene campaign in January. By April, its rate of hospital-acquired infections has fallen 30%. Officials credit the campaign, but flu season also ended in March. Which design change best supports a causal claim?
o: Track a similar hospital without the campaign
Survey nurses about the campaign's value
Double the number of hand-hygiene posters
e: A seasonal event (history) coincided with the campaign, so the drop could be seasonal.
A comparison hospital over the same months experiences the same season. A larger drop at the campaign hospital points to the campaign.
t: Before-and-after studies without a comparison group can't separate an intervention from whatever else changed over time.

q: A drug trial finds patients who knew they got the drug improved more than those who didn't know. How should the trial be redesigned?
o: Make it double-blind with a placebo control
e: Blinding removes expectation effects.

q: A survey of patient satisfaction gets responses mostly from very happy and very unhappy patients. Which problem is this?
e: People with strong feelings are more likely to respond.

q: Which is NOT a core principle of research ethics (from the Belmont Report)?
e: Informed consent comes from respect for persons.

q: A survey finds that people with arthritis exercise less than people without it. A news report concludes that inactivity causes arthritis. What is the strongest alternative explanation?
o: Arthritis pain may cause people to exercise less
The sample was too large to show causation
Exercise and arthritis cannot be measured reliably
The study needed a larger effect size to count
e: In a correlational study, the direction of causation is unclear.
Reverse causation: the outcome (arthritis) may be producing the 'exposure' (less exercise).

q: Researchers want each treatment arm to contain equal numbers of smokers and nonsmokers. They first sort participants by smoking status, then randomly assign treatments within each group. This is called:
e: Stratified randomization guarantees balance on a key variable (smoking) while keeping random assignment.
Sampling methods (simple random, convenience) describe how people are recruited, not how they are assigned.

q: A researcher tests the vocabulary of the same 500 children every year from age 5 to age 15. Which study design is this?
e: The same individuals are measured repeatedly over a long period, so it is longitudinal.
A cross-sectional design would test different children of each age at one time point.

q: A cohort study:
o: Follows a group over time to see who develops an outcome
Starts with people who already have the disease and looks back
e: Cohort studies can be prospective or retrospective.

q: A new anxiety questionnaire is given to the same people twice, two weeks apart. Their anxiety is stable, but their scores differ greatly between the two sessions. What does this show?
e: Reliability means consistency. A stable trait should give similar scores each time.
Large changes between sessions show low test–retest reliability. (An unreliable test also cannot be fully valid.)

q: Researchers testing a new antibacterial compound treat one set of culture plates with ampicillin, an antibiotic known to kill the bacteria. What is the role of the ampicillin plates?
e: A positive control receives a treatment known to produce the effect, confirming the assay can detect it.
A negative control (for example, plates with no compound) should show no effect.

q: A study finds that regular exercise reduces depressive symptoms, and that it does so because exercise improves sleep quality, which in turn lifts mood. In this model, sleep quality is a:
e: A mediator lies on the causal path: exercise → better sleep → less depression. It explains HOW the effect happens.
A moderator changes the strength of an effect (for example, if exercise helped only older adults).

q: Surgeons compare recovery times at Hospital A, which uses a new rehab protocol, with Hospital B, which uses the old one. Patients at Hospital A are on average 15 years younger. What is the main weakness of this comparison?
o: Age could explain the faster recovery
Recovery time is not a measurable outcome
The sample includes two hospitals, not one
The study has no dependent variable at all
e: Younger patients generally recover faster, and age differs between the groups.
So age is a confounding variable: it is linked to both the protocol (hospital) and the outcome.
Randomizing patients to protocols would balance age.

q: A vacuum flask keeps coffee hot for hours. How does the vacuum gap between its double walls help?
o: It blocks heat flow by conduction and convection
It blocks heat flow by radiation only
It absorbs heat and stores it as latent heat
It reflects heat back toward the hot coffee
e: Conduction and convection both need matter to carry energy; a vacuum has almost none.
Radiation can cross a vacuum, which is why the walls are also silvered to reflect it.

q: A refrigerator moves heat from its cold interior to the warm room. Why doesn't this violate the second law?
o: It uses work (electricity), and total entropy still increases
Heat naturally flows from cold to hot inside a closed box
It uses work, so the total entropy decreases slightly
The second law limits heat engines, not refrigerators
e: Heat moves 'uphill' only with work input.

q: What is the maximum (Carnot) efficiency of an engine operating between 600 K and 300 K?
An inventor claims an engine running between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K has an efficiency of 50%. What should you conclude?
o: Impossible: the maximum possible efficiency is 40%
Possible: it is below the 60% maximum efficiency
Possible: any efficiency under 100% is allowed
Impossible: the maximum possible efficiency is 20%
e: Carnot limit: e<sub>max</sub> = 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub> = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40.
No real engine can beat the Carnot efficiency, so 50% violates the second law.

q: Why does sweating cool the body?
o: Evaporation absorbs latent heat from the skin
Sweat leaves the body cooler than the skin is
Sweat reflects radiant heat away from the skin
Liquid sweat insulates the skin from warm air
e: Each gram of water evaporated removes about 2.4 kJ.

q: Heat conducts from a person's core through a 2.0 cm layer of fat (k = 0.20 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) of area 1.5 m², with a 2.0 K temperature difference across it. What is the rate of heat flow?
e: Q/t = kAΔT/L, with L = 0.020 m.
t: Convert cm to m first; 0.30 W comes from using L = 2.0.

q: The second law of thermodynamics says that the total entropy of an isolated system:
e: Spontaneous processes increase total entropy.

q: Absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which:
o: Particles have their minimum possible energy
Water freezes at standard atmospheric pressure
Gas pressure reaches its maximum possible value
The entropy of a perfect crystal is maximum

q: A metal dental filling and the surrounding tooth expand at different rates when heated. Why might this matter?
o: Unequal expansion with hot and cold foods can cause gaps or cracks
Expansion tightens the filling, making its seal stronger
Teeth stay at body temperature, so foods have no effect
The mismatch only matters during the drilling procedure
e: Filling materials are chosen to match the tooth's thermal expansion.

q: In an adiabatic process:
o: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings
The temperature of the gas stays constant
The volume of the gas stays constant
The internal energy of the gas stays constant
e: ΔU = −W.

q: The absolute temperature of a radiating object is doubled. By what factor does the power it radiates increase?
e: Stefan–Boltzmann law: P = εσAT⁴.
Doubling T multiplies P by 2⁴ = 16.
t: Radiation goes as T to the FOURTH power, and T must be in kelvins.

q: A 2.0 L sample of a liquid with volume expansion coefficient β = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ is warmed by 20 K. By how much does its volume increase?
An MRI scanner uses a 1.5 T magnetic field. Why must patients remove metal objects?
o: Ferromagnetic objects are strongly pulled and can become projectiles
Metal objects block the X-rays the scanner uses for imaging
The strong field makes metal objects emit ionizing radiation
Aluminum and titanium objects are pulled hardest by the field
e: Iron-containing objects experience large forces.

q: Equipotential lines are always:
e: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.

q: A charged particle moves in a circle perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, what happens to the radius and the period of its orbit?
o: Radius doubles; period stays the same
Radius stays the same; period halves
e: r = mv/(qB), so r is proportional to v: doubling v doubles r.
T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB), which contains no v, so the period is unchanged.

q: An electron is released from rest in a uniform electric field. Which way does it move, and what happens to its electric potential energy?
o: Toward higher potential; its PE decreases
Toward lower potential; its PE decreases
Toward higher potential; its PE increases
Along the field direction; its PE increases
e: A negative charge feels a force opposite to E, which points toward higher potential.
ΔU = qΔV: with q < 0 and ΔV > 0, ΔU is negative, so PE turns into KE.
t: Released from rest, every charge moves to LOWER potential energy, whatever its sign.

q: What is the SI unit of magnetic field?
e: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹; 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ T.

q: A balloon is rubbed on dry hair and picks up −5 nC of charge. If no charge escapes, what is the charge on the hair?
e: Charge is conserved: rubbing only moves electrons from one object to the other.
The balloon gained electrons (−5 nC), so the hair lost them and is left at +5 nC.

q: A proton (m ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.10 T magnetic field. What is the radius of its circular path?
e: Magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB).

q: A charge of +q and a charge of +4q are fixed 0.30 m apart. Where on the line between them is the net electric field zero?
e: Let x be the distance from +q. Set the field magnitudes equal: kq/x² = k(4q)/(0.30 − x)².
Taking square roots: 0.30 − x = 2x, so x = 0.10 m.
The zero point lies closer to the smaller charge.

q: How does the electric force between two charges change if the distance between them triples?
What is the electric field 0.10 m from a +1.0 µC charge? (k = 9 × 10⁹)
A proton (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. What magnetic force acts on it?
How does the magnetic field inside a long solenoid change if the number of turns per meter is doubled at the same current?
e: Inside a long solenoid, B = μ₀nI, where n is turns per meter.
B is directly proportional to n, so doubling n doubles B.

q: A drug dose is 5 mg/kg. How much should a 70 kg patient receive?
What is 15% of 80?
For electric force, F ∝ q₁q₂ ÷ r². If both charges are doubled and the distance between them is also doubled, what happens to F?
e: Numerator: 2 × 2 = 4 times larger.
Denominator: 2² = 4 times larger.
4 ÷ 4 = 1, so F is unchanged.
t: Handle each factor separately, then multiply the factors together.

q: Whole blood has a density of about 1.06 g cm⁻³. What is this in kg m⁻³?
e: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.
t: Water is 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³; use that as a sanity check.

q: A student adds two measured masses, 12.11 g and 0.3 g. How should the total be reported?
e: For addition, round to the fewest decimal places among the values.
0.3 g has one decimal place, so 12.41 g rounds to 12.4 g.
t: Add/subtract: count decimal places. Multiply/divide: count significant figures.

q: An object's kinetic energy is ½mv². If its mass is halved and its speed is tripled, by what factor does its kinetic energy change?
e: Mass factor: ½. Speed factor squared: 3² = 9.

q: A graph of log(y) versus x is a straight line. The relationship between y and x is:
e: y = A × 10<sup>(kx)</sup> gives log y = log A + kx.

q: A resting adult's cardiac output is about 5 L per minute. About how many liters of blood does the heart pump in one day?
e: 1 day = 24 h × 60 min = 1440 min.
5 L min⁻¹ × 1440 min = 7200 L

q: A protein in a lab sample denatures at 335 K. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius?
t: Adding 273 instead of subtracting gives an impossible 608 °C for a protein denaturing in a lab.

q: Estimate √(2 × 10⁻⁵).
e: Rewrite with an even exponent: 2 × 10⁻⁵ = 20 × 10⁻⁶.
√20 ≈ 4.5 and √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³, so the answer is ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻³.
t: Make the exponent even before taking a square root.

q: How many significant figures are in 0.004050?
e: Leading zeros aren't significant; the trailing zero after the decimal is.

q: Newborn birth weights at a hospital are approximately normal, with a mean of 3.4 kg and a standard deviation of 0.5 kg. About what percentage of newborns weigh between 2.9 kg and 4.4 kg?
e: 2.9 kg is 1 SD below the mean; 4.4 kg is 2 SD above (3.4 + 2 × 0.5).
Mean − 1 SD to mean: 34%. Mean to mean + 2 SD: 47.5%.
t: Split asymmetric ranges at the mean and add the halves of the 68–95–99.7 rule.

q: Increasing sample size usually:
e: Larger samples detect smaller effects.

q: A researcher wants to display the distribution of ages among 500 clinic patients. Which graph is most appropriate?
e: A histogram groups a single continuous variable into bins and shows how many values fall in each.
A scatter plot needs two variables; a pie chart suits a few categories, not a continuous scale.

q: Researchers want to make the 95% confidence interval for a mean half as wide as in their pilot study. Assuming the SD stays the same, how should they change the sample size?
e: CI width ∝ SE = SD ÷ √n.
To halve the width, √n must double, so n must increase by 2² = 4.

q: A Type I error is:
o: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive)
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
e: Its probability equals α (often 0.05).

q: A research team tests 20 different supplements against placebo, each at α = 0.05. In truth, none of the supplements has any effect. About how many 'significant' results should they expect by chance?
e: Each test has a 5% chance of a false positive when the null is true.
Expected false positives = 20 × 0.05 = 1.
This multiple-comparisons problem is why corrections (such as Bonferroni) are used.

q: A correlation coefficient of r = −0.9 indicates:
e: As one variable goes up, the other goes down.

q: A lab lowers the cutoff value at which a blood test is called 'positive' for a disease. What is the most likely effect?
e: A lower cutoff calls more people positive, catching more true cases (fewer false negatives → higher sensitivity).
It also labels more healthy people positive (more false positives → lower specificity).
Prevalence is a property of the population, not of the test.

q: A case–control study has 100 cases and 100 controls. Among cases, 40 were exposed; among controls, 20 were exposed. What is the odds ratio?
e: Odds of exposure in cases = 40 ÷ 60. In controls = 20 ÷ 80.
2.0 is the ratio of exposure proportions (0.40 ÷ 0.20), not the odds ratio.

q: A histogram of age at diagnosis for a disease shows two separate peaks, one in the 20s and one in the 60s. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The distribution is bimodal, so the mean alone misleads
The distribution is normal with a large SD
The distribution is skewed right with one mode
The mean age is the most typical age at diagnosis
e: Two peaks means two modes: a bimodal distribution, possibly two patient subgroups.
The mean is likely to fall between the peaks, at ages when few people are actually diagnosed.

q: The mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7 is:
e: The most frequent value.

q: The range of 5, 9, 12 and 20 is:
e: Range = max − min = 20 − 5.

q: An object is 30 cm from a converging lens with a 10 cm focal length. Where is the image?
e: 1/d_i = 2/30, so d_i = 15 cm (positive = real).

q: The standing wave shown is on a string fixed at both ends. Which harmonic is it?
e: There are 3 loops (antinodes) between the fixed ends: n = 3.

q: Light passes from medium 1 into medium 2 as shown, bending toward the normal. Which statement is correct?
o: Medium 2 has a higher index of refraction than medium 1
Medium 2 has a lower index of refraction
The frequency of the light decreases in medium 2
e: Bending toward the normal means the light slows down: n₂ > n₁.
Frequency doesn't change at a boundary.

q: A seesaw: a 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from the pivot. Where must a 40 kg child sit on the other side to balance?
e: Torques balance: 30 × 2.0 = 40 × d
