q: Binding data for a multisubunit enzyme give a Hill coefficient of 2.8. What does this indicate?
o: Positive cooperativity among several binding sites
Negative cooperativity between two binding sites
One binding site with no cooperativity
Exactly 2.8 substrate molecules bind to each enzyme
e: A Hill coefficient > 1 means binding at one site raises affinity at the others (positive cooperativity).
It is not a literal count of sites; it is at most the number of sites, so this enzyme has at least 3.
t: n<sub>H</sub> > 1 cooperative, = 1 independent, < 1 negative cooperativity.

q: Trypsinogen is cleaved by enteropeptidase to form active trypsin. Trypsinogen is an example of a:
e: Zymogens are inactive precursors activated by cleavage.
Making digestive proteases as zymogens keeps them from digesting the pancreas.

q: In a serine protease, the catalytic serine is mutated to alanine. Substrate still binds about as well as before, but catalysis nearly stops. How do the kinetic constants change?
o: k<sub>cat</sub> drops sharply; K<sub>m</sub> changes little
K<sub>m</sub> rises sharply; k<sub>cat</sub> changes little
k<sub>cat</sub> and K<sub>m</sub> both stay the same
k<sub>cat</sub> rises, because alanine is smaller
e: Binding unchanged means K<sub>m</sub> (roughly the dissociation constant here) stays similar.
Without the serine –OH nucleophile, the chemical step is very slow, so k<sub>cat</sub> (turnover) falls dramatically.
t: Binding problems show up in K<sub>m</sub>; chemistry problems show up in k<sub>cat</sub>.

q: A Lineweaver–Burk plot crosses the x-axis at −0.50 mM⁻¹. What is Km?
e: x-intercept = −1/Km
−1/Km = −0.50 mM⁻¹, so Km = 2.0 mM

q: An enzyme sample has Vmax = 10 µM s⁻¹ and total enzyme [E]T = 0.010 µM. What is kcat (the turnover number)?
e: kcat = Vmax ÷ [E]T
Each enzyme converts 1000 substrate molecules per second.

q: What does an enzyme’s Km represent in Michaelis–Menten kinetics?
e: At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2 for Michaelis–Menten behavior.

q: A drug forms a permanent covalent bond with an active-site residue, inactivating each enzyme molecule it hits. How does this change the measured kinetics of the sample?
o: V<sub>max</sub> falls; K<sub>m</sub> of remaining enzyme is unchanged
K<sub>m</sub> rises; V<sub>max</sub> is unchanged, as if it were competitive
V<sub>max</sub> rises, because fewer enzymes compete
Both fall, exactly as in uncompetitive inhibition
e: Irreversibly inhibited enzymes are effectively removed, lowering [E]<sub>T</sub> and therefore V<sub>max</sub>.
The enzyme molecules that escape work normally, so K<sub>m</sub> is unchanged. Adding more substrate cannot reverse it.
t: Irreversible inhibition looks like noncompetitive on a plot: less enzyme, same K<sub>m</sub>.

q: At 37 °C (where 2.303RT ≈ 5.9 kJ mol⁻¹), an enzyme lowers a reaction's activation energy by about 18 kJ mol⁻¹. Assuming the Arrhenius pre-factor is unchanged, by roughly what factor does the rate increase?
e: k ∝ 10<sup>−E<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>, so the rate ratio is 10<sup>ΔE<sub>a</sub>/(2.303RT)</sup>.
18/5.9 ≈ 3, so the rate increases by about 10³ = 1000-fold.
t: Each ~6 kJ mol⁻¹ off E<sub>a</sub> at body temperature ≈ 10× faster.

q: An enzyme has V<sub>max</sub> = 50 µM s⁻¹. What is the initial rate when [S] = K<sub>m</sub>/4?
e: v = V<sub>max</sub>[S]/(K<sub>m</sub> + [S]) = 50 × (0.25K<sub>m</sub>)/(1.25K<sub>m</sub>).

q: A drug binds an enzyme's active site and competes with the substrate. How does it affect Km and Vmax?
e: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site.
More substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax, so the apparent Km increases.
At very high [S], substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so Vmax is unchanged.
t: Competitive = 'can be outcompeted' = same Vmax. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the lines cross on the y-axis.

q: In a pathway A → B → C → D, product D inhibits the enzyme that converts A to B. This is called:
e: The end product shuts down the first committed step.
This keeps the cell from wasting resources once there is enough D.

q: An enzyme's protein portion, without the cofactor it needs for activity, is called the:
e: Apoenzyme (inactive protein) + cofactor = holoenzyme (active).
A zymogen is an inactive precursor activated by cleavage, a different idea.
t: Apo = 'apart' from its cofactor; holo = 'whole'.

q: In a β-pleated sheet, where do the side chains of consecutive residues along one strand point?
o: Alternately above and below the plane of the sheet
All toward the neighboring strand to form H-bonds
All outward from a central axis, as in a helix
All into the sheet's plane, between the strands
e: The backbone N–H and C=O groups make the H-bonds between strands, within the plane.
Side chains alternate up and down, so one face of a sheet can be nonpolar and the other polar.
t: Helix: side chains point out like bristles; sheet: they alternate up and down.

q: An aspartate side chain and a lysine side chain lie next to each other on a protein's surface at pH 7. Which interaction most likely forms between them?
e: At pH 7, Asp is –COO⁻ and Lys is –NH₃⁺.
Opposite charges attract, forming a salt bridge (an ionic interaction) that helps hold tertiary structure.

q: In collagen, every third residue is glycine. Replacing one of these glycines (as in some forms of brittle bone disease) weakens the triple helix. Why?
o: Only glycine's tiny side chain fits in the crowded helix center
Glycine forms the disulfides that link the three chains
Glycine is the residue that vitamin C–dependent enzymes hydroxylate
Glycine's charged side chain repels water from the helix
e: In the triple helix, every third residue faces the packed center where the three chains meet.
Only glycine (side chain = H) fits there; any larger side chain pushes the strands apart.

q: A cysteine thiol in a peptide has pK<sub>a</sub> = 8.3. At pH 7.3, what is the approximate ratio of thiolate (–S⁻) to thiol (–SH)?
e: [–S⁻]/[–SH] = 10⁻¹, so the ratio is 1 : 10; most cysteines are still –SH.
t: pH below pK<sub>a</sub> → protonated form wins; each pH unit = factor of 10.

q: Protein folding in water is favorable even though the folded chain is more ordered than the unfolded one. What mainly drives nonpolar side chains to the interior?
o: Ordered water around them is released, gaining entropy
Nonpolar side chains form covalent bonds in the core
Nonpolar groups hydrogen-bond strongly to each other
Burial lowers the entropy of the surrounding water
e: Water forms ordered 'cages' around exposed nonpolar groups.
Burying those groups frees the water, raising its entropy (ΔS > 0), which makes ΔG for folding negative. This is the hydrophobic effect.
t: The hydrophobic effect is about water's entropy, not attraction between oily groups.

q: Which point substitution in a protein's buried hydrophobic core is LEAST likely to disrupt folding?
e: Leu and Ile are both nonpolar with the same formula; this is a conservative substitution.
The others place a charged side chain inside the core, where it cannot be hydrated, destabilizing the fold.
t: 'Conservative' = same chemical class (nonpolar for nonpolar, acidic for acidic).

q: A synthetic 20-residue peptide with two cysteines is stirred in air at pH 8. Mass spectrometry then shows the main species is 2 Da lighter than the starting peptide, and it is still a single chain. What happened?
o: An intramolecular disulfide formed, losing two H atoms
Two peptides joined by a disulfide, losing water
A peptide bond was hydrolyzed, losing a hydrogen
Both cysteine thiols were oxidized to sulfonic acids
e: 2 R–SH → R–S–S–R + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻: forming a disulfide removes two H atoms (≈ 2 Da).
A single chain means the S–S bond is within one peptide. Hydrolysis would add 18 Da; a dimer would double the mass; sulfonic acids add O atoms.

q: The tripeptide Lys–Lys–Gly is placed in an electric field at pH 7. Which way does it move?
o: Toward the cathode (negative electrode), because it is positively charged
Toward the anode (positive electrode), because it is negatively charged
It doesn't move, because it is neutral
Toward the anode, because peptides are always negative
e: At pH 7: N-terminus +1, two Lys side chains +2, C-terminus −1.
Net charge = +2, so the peptide moves toward the negative electrode.

q: In a neurodegenerative disease, a normal brain protein and its disease form have the identical amino acid sequence. The disease form resists proteases, is insoluble, and forms stacked fibrils held by H-bonds between backbone strands. What best describes the change?
o: α-Helical regions refolded into stacked β-sheets
A point mutation changed the protein's sequence
Peptide bonds were replaced with disulfide bonds
β-Sheets unfolded into a soluble random coil
e: Same sequence means primary structure is unchanged; the difference is in folding (secondary/tertiary structure).
Backbone H-bonds between stacked strands describe β-sheets; these amyloid fibrils are insoluble and protease-resistant, as in prion diseases.

q: A researcher unfolds an enzyme with urea and β-mercaptoethanol, then slowly removes both. The enzyme refolds and becomes fully active again. What does this show?
o: The primary sequence contains all the information needed for folding
Chaperones must be present for the protein to refold correctly
Disulfide bonds, not the sequence, dictate the folded structure
Urea and β-mercaptoethanol never fully denatured the enzyme
e: Removing the denaturants let the chain refold on its own into its active shape.
So the primary sequence alone determines the 3D structure (Anfinsen's classic experiment).
t: Real cells use chaperones to prevent misfolding and aggregation, but the folding information is in the sequence.

q: What is the approximate net charge of the tripeptide Asp–Lys–Arg at pH 7?
e: Ends: N-terminal –NH₃⁺ (+1) and C-terminal –COO⁻ (−1).
Side chains: Asp (−1), Lys (+1), Arg (+1).

q: Which amino acid has an imidazole ring in its side chain?
e: Histidine's imidazole ring has a pKa near 6, so it can gain or lose H⁺ near physiological pH.
That makes histidine a common acid–base catalyst in enzyme active sites.

q: In PCR, why is a heat-stable DNA polymerase (like Taq polymerase) used?
o: The reaction is heated to about 95 °C in each cycle to separate the strands
It can extend new DNA without needing primers bound to the template
It copies RNA into DNA, so no separate reverse transcriptase is needed
It has proofreading activity that heat-sensitive polymerases lack
e: Each cycle: denature (~95 °C), anneal primers (~55–65 °C), extend (~72 °C).
A normal polymerase would be destroyed during the first heating step.

q: A 10-base-pair DNA segment contains 4 G–C pairs and 6 A–T pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
e: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds; A–T pairs have 2.
4 × 3 + 6 × 2 = 12 + 12 = 24 hydrogen bonds.

q: Heterochromatin is:
o: Tightly packed and mostly transcriptionally silent
e: Heterochromatin is condensed (dark-staining).
Euchromatin is loosely packed and accessible for transcription.

q: A bacterial chromosome has one origin of replication, but a human chromosome has many. Why do human chromosomes need many origins?
o: Its DNA is too long for one origin to finish copying within S phase
Human DNA polymerase can copy only one strand starting from each origin
Each origin copies only the genes of one chromosome arm
Many origins are needed because human DNA is single-stranded
e: A human chromosome holds roughly 50–250 million bp, and eukaryotic forks move fairly slowly.
Thousands of origins firing across the genome let replication finish in a few hours.

q: Which bases are purines?
e: Purines have two fused rings: adenine and guanine ('Pure As Gold').
Pyrimidines have one ring: cytosine, thymine and uracil.

q: When a DNA solution is slowly heated, its absorbance at 260 nm rises sharply near the melting temperature. Why?
o: Separated strands have unstacked bases, which absorb more UV light
Heat breaks the phosphodiester backbone into free nucleotides
Heat converts thymine into uracil, which absorbs more strongly
The DNA strands aggregate and scatter more light
e: Stacked bases in double-stranded DNA absorb less UV than unstacked ones.
When the strands separate, absorbance at 260 nm rises (the hyperchromic effect), so A₂₆₀ can track melting.

q: Histones bind DNA tightly mainly because they:
o: Are rich in positive lysine and arginine, which attract DNA's negative backbone
Are rich in negative aspartate and glutamate, which bind DNA's nitrogenous bases
Form covalent bonds between their lysine side chains and DNA's bases
Are rich in hydrophobic residues that insert between DNA's stacked bases
e: DNA's phosphate backbone is negatively charged.
Positive histone tails attract it; acetylating those lysines loosens the grip and promotes transcription.

q: A 6.0 kb circular plasmid has one EcoRI site and one BamHI site, 1.5 kb apart. What fragments appear on a gel after cutting with both enzymes?
e: Two cuts in a circle give two linear pieces.
One piece is the 1.5 kb between the sites; the other is the rest: 6.0 − 1.5 = 4.5 kb.
t: n cuts in a circular plasmid give n fragments; n cuts in a linear DNA give n + 1.

q: A reactive oxygen species converts one guanine into 8-oxoguanine without distorting the helix. Which repair pathway most directly removes this damaged base?
e: Base excision repair starts with a DNA glycosylase that removes a single damaged base; the gap is then filled and sealed.
Nucleotide excision repair handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as thymine dimers; mismatch repair fixes replication errors; NHEJ joins double-strand breaks.
t: One bad base → BER. Bulky bump in the helix → NER. Wrong partner after copying → MMR.

q: Which technique detects a specific DNA sequence?
e: Southern = DNA; Northern = RNA; Western = protein. ELISA uses antibodies to detect proteins or antigens.

q: Which DNA molecule would have the highest melting temperature (Tm)?
e: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly.
More G–C content means more energy is needed to separate the strands.

q: In quantitative PCR, sample A reaches the detection threshold (Ct) at cycle 22 and sample B at cycle 25. Assuming perfect doubling, how did their starting amounts of target compare?
o: A had about 8 times as much as B
A had about 3 times as much as B
B had about 8 times as much as A
B had about 3 times as much as A
e: More starting template reaches the threshold in fewer cycles, so A had more.
Each cycle doubles the product: 25 − 22 = 3 cycles → 2³ = 8-fold difference.
t: Lower Ct = more template. Each cycle of difference = 2×.

q: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) usually reduce a gene's expression by:
o: Base-pairing with its mRNA to block translation or trigger degradation
Binding its promoter DNA to stop RNA polymerase from starting transcription
Cutting out its introns before the mRNA can leave the nucleus
Adding methyl groups to cytosines in the gene's own promoter DNA
e: A mature miRNA is loaded into the RISC complex.
It pairs (often partly) with sequences in target mRNAs, usually in the 3′ UTR, which represses translation or leads to mRNA breakdown.

q: In eukaryotes, which RNA polymerase transcribes the genes for tRNAs?
e: Pol I makes most rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S), Pol II makes mRNA, and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
t: Order by product: I – rRNA, II – mRNA, III – tRNA ('R-M-T').

q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 300 nucleotides long. How many amino acids are in the protein?
e: 300 nucleotides ÷ 3 = 100 codons.
The last codon is a stop codon, which doesn't code for an amino acid.
100 − 1 = 99 amino acids (counting the initial Met).

q: Which RNA type brings amino acids to the ribosome?
e: Transfer RNA uses an anticodon to match codons and carries amino acids.

q: One nucleotide is inserted near the start of a gene's coding region. What is the most likely result?
o: A frameshift altering all downstream codons, usually yielding a nonfunctional protein
A single amino acid substitution, with the rest of the protein unchanged
No change in the protein, because the genetic code is degenerate
One extra amino acid is added, but the rest of the protein is normal
e: Codons are read in groups of 3 from a fixed starting point.
Adding 1 base shifts every following codon and often creates an early stop codon.

q: A mutation changes the codon UCU to UCC. Both code for serine. This is a:
e: The amino acid doesn't change, thanks to the code's degeneracy.

q: The genetic code is called degenerate (redundant) because:
o: Most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon
Most codons encode more than one amino acid
Codons overlap so one base is read twice
e: 64 codons encode only 20 amino acids plus stop signals, so most amino acids have 2–6 codons.
The code is still unambiguous: each codon means only one thing.

q: Tetracycline binds the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA from entering the A site. Why does it harm bacteria more than human cells?
o: Bacterial 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S) differ from human cytosolic 80S ribosomes
Human cytosolic 80S ribosomes have no A site for aminoacyl-tRNA to enter
Human ribosomes sit inside the nucleus, which tetracycline cannot enter
Bacterial ribosomes lack a 50S subunit, leaving the 30S subunit exposed
e: Antibiotics can be selective by targeting structures found in bacteria but not human cytosol.
Human mitochondria have bacteria-like ribosomes, which helps explain some side effects.

q: When a stop codon reaches the ribosome's A site, what normally binds there?
o: A protein release factor, which frees the finished chain
A tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the stop codon
A snRNP, which splices the mRNA
e: No normal tRNA reads UAA, UAG or UGA.
A release factor binds instead and triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA.

q: In many eukaryotic promoters, the TATA box about 25–30 bp upstream of the start site is first bound by:
o: RNA polymerase II acting by itself
e: TBP (in TFIID) binds the TATA box and bends the DNA.
Other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II then assemble on the promoter.

q: Researchers charge a tRNA<sup>Cys</sup> with cysteine, then chemically convert the attached cysteine into alanine. When used in translation, where does this alanine end up in the protein?
o: At positions coded by cysteine codons
At positions coded by alanine codons
At random positions throughout the protein
Nowhere, because the ribosome rejects it
e: The ribosome checks only codon–anticodon pairing, not the attached amino acid.
This tRNA still carries the Cys anticodon, so alanine is placed at Cys codons. Translation accuracy depends on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charging tRNAs correctly.

q: An E. coli strain has a lacI mutation that makes a nonfunctional repressor. When grown with no lactose and no glucose, its lac genes are:
o: Transcribed at a high level anyway
Silent, because no inducer is present
Transcribed only after lactose is added
e: With no working repressor, nothing blocks the operator, so expression no longer requires lactose (constitutive).
With glucose absent, cAMP–CAP is bound, so transcription is high.
t: Broken repressor (lacI⁻) = always on. CAP still needs low glucose for high-level transcription.

q: Arsenate (AsO₄³⁻) can replace Pi in the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction. The product, 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate, hydrolyzes spontaneously to 3-phosphoglycerate. What is glycolysis's net ATP yield per glucose?
e: The phosphoglycerate kinase step is skipped, so the 2 ATP it normally makes per glucose are lost.
Gross ATP: 4 − 2 = 2 (from pyruvate kinase only). Invested: 2 (hexokinase, PFK-1).
Net = 2 − 2 = 0 ATP, although NADH is still produced.

q: Glycogen phosphorylase breaks down glycogen by:
o: Cleaving α(1→4) bonds with phosphate to release glucose-1-phosphate
Hydrolyzing α(1→6) branches into free glucose only
e: Phosphorolysis (using Pi, not water) releases glucose-1-phosphate, which is converted to G6P.
A separate debranching enzyme handles the α(1→6) branch points.

q: Glycogen is stored mainly in:
e: Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose; muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself.

q: A 20-year-old gets painful muscle cramps during intense exercise. In an exercise test, blood ammonia rises normally but blood lactate barely rises. Fasting glucose is normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
e: Intense exercise normally breaks down muscle glycogen to make lactate; no lactate rise means muscle can't use its glycogen.
The normal ammonia rise shows the muscle was working hard (AMP deamination).
Normal fasting glucose shows liver glycogen and gluconeogenesis are fine, so the defect is muscle-specific (McArdle disease).

q: In the Cori cycle, lactate from exercising muscle is:
o: Carried to the liver and converted back to glucose
Burned directly by the muscle for ATP
Converted into fatty acids in muscle
e: Muscle makes lactate during intense exercise.
The liver uses it for gluconeogenesis and sends glucose back to the muscle.

q: Why can't humans make net glucose from even-chain fatty acids?
o: Their product, acetyl-CoA, can't be converted to pyruvate or net oxaloacetate
Their β-oxidation occurs in the cytosol, away from gluconeogenic enzymes
The liver lacks the enzymes needed to oxidize fatty acids to acetyl-CoA
Their acetyl-CoA is entirely consumed making ketone bodies in the liver
e: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible.
For each acetyl-CoA (2 C) that enters the citric acid cycle, 2 carbons leave as CO₂, so there's no net gain of oxaloacetate.
(Glycerol and odd-chain fatty acids CAN contribute to glucose.)

q: Gluconeogenesis spans several cell compartments. Which enzyme–location pairing is correct?
e: Pyruvate carboxylase is in the mitochondrial matrix.
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase is cytosolic, and glucose-6-phosphatase faces the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum.
PEPCK occurs in the matrix and/or cytosol depending on species, never only in the ER.
t: Gluconeogenesis tours the cell: mitochondria → cytosol → ER.

q: Which enzyme catalyzes the main rate-limiting (committed) step of glycolysis?
e: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
This irreversible step is the main control point.

q: During fasting, liver pyruvate kinase is phosphorylated by protein kinase A and inhibited. What is the main benefit?
o: PEP made by gluconeogenesis isn't turned straight back into pyruvate
More ATP is produced from each PEP molecule in the fasting liver cell
Pyruvate builds up and activates pyruvate dehydrogenase in liver
Glucose-6-phosphate builds up and activates liver glycogen synthase
e: Gluconeogenesis spends ATP and GTP to make PEP from pyruvate.
If pyruvate kinase stayed active, PEP would go right back to pyruvate, wasting energy in a futile cycle.
Turning pyruvate kinase off sends PEP up toward glucose.

q: In the glucose–alanine cycle, muscle sends alanine to the liver. What does the liver do first with the alanine?
o: Transaminates it to pyruvate, sending its nitrogen toward urea
Decarboxylates it directly to acetyl-CoA for ketone body synthesis
Joins it to UDP-glucose and stores it as liver glycogen
Oxidizes it to lactate using lactate dehydrogenase
e: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) moves alanine's amino group to α-ketoglutarate, giving pyruvate and glutamate.
Pyruvate goes into gluconeogenesis; the nitrogen is released from glutamate and enters the urea cycle.
The new glucose returns to muscle.

q: In gluconeogenesis, which enzyme converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, using GTP?
e: Oxaloacetate + GTP → phosphoenolpyruvate + CO₂ + GDP.
Together, pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) and PEPCK bypass the irreversible pyruvate kinase step of glycolysis.

q: Liver cells making fatty acids need much NADPH but little ribose-5-phosphate. What happens to the extra ribose-5-phosphate from the pentose phosphate pathway?
o: Transketolase and transaldolase recycle it to glycolytic sugars
G6PD oxidizes it to CO₂, making still more NADPH for the cell
It is exported into the blood for other tissues to use
It is converted to deoxyribose and stored as DNA in the nucleus
e: The non-oxidative branch (transketolase, transaldolase) is reversible and reshuffles sugar carbons.
Ribose-5-phosphate becomes the glycolytic intermediates fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
These can re-form glucose-6-phosphate for more NADPH or continue through glycolysis. G6PD acts on glucose-6-phosphate, not ribose-5-phosphate.

q: Using about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH₂, about how much ATP comes from oxidizing one acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle and ETC?
e: 1 GTP = 1. Total ≈ 10 ATP

q: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) is stimulated by high NADH and acetyl-CoA. What does PDK do?
e: PDK adds a phosphate to the E1 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, switching it off.
PDH phosphatase removes it, switching PDH back on (insulin and Ca²⁺ stimulate the phosphatase).
So when products are high, PDH is shut down both allosterically and covalently.
t: Kinase = OFF for PDH (and for glycogen synthase); phosphatase = ON.

q: No citric acid cycle reaction uses O₂, yet the cycle stops within seconds when O₂ runs out. Why?
o: Without O₂, NADH isn't reoxidized, so NAD⁺ and FAD run out
O₂ is a required allosteric activator of citrate synthase
Without O₂, acetyl-CoA is converted straight into lactate
O₂ is needed to regenerate oxaloacetate directly from malate
e: Four cycle dehydrogenases need NAD⁺ or FAD as electron acceptors.
Only the electron transport chain, ending at O₂, turns NADH and FADH₂ back into NAD⁺ and FAD.
No O₂ → carriers stay reduced → the dehydrogenases stall → the cycle stops.

q: A person with chronic alcoholism and thiamine (vitamin B₁) deficiency develops lactic acidosis. Why?
o: Pyruvate dehydrogenase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate
Pyruvate carboxylase can't work, so pyruvate is converted to lactate
Lactate dehydrogenase needs thiamine, so lactate can't be reoxidized
Complex IV needs thiamine, so cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis
e: PDH requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP).
Without it, pyruvate can't become acetyl-CoA and builds up, and lactate dehydrogenase converts it to lactate.

q: Cyanide and carbon monoxide both block the electron transport chain at:
e: Both bind complex IV, which passes electrons to O₂.
With no final transfer to O₂, the whole chain backs up.

q: What is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
e: Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass down the chain of complexes.
At complex IV, electrons are passed to O₂.
O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ → 2 H₂O
t: Cyanide blocks complex IV, which is why it stops aerobic respiration so quickly.

q: Arsenite binds tightly to the two thiol groups of reduced lipoic acid. Which pair of metabolites would most likely build up?
e: Lipoic acid is a cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
Blocking both enzymes makes their substrates, pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate, accumulate (and pyruvate spills over into lactate).

q: The mammalian ATP synthase c-ring has 8 c subunits. Each full rotation moves 8 H⁺ through F₀ and makes 3 ATP in F₁. About how many H⁺ pass through the synthase per ATP made?
e: Each c subunit carries one H⁺ per turn: 8 H⁺ per rotation.
F₁ has three catalytic β subunits: 3 ATP per rotation.
8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.7 H⁺ per ATP; adding about 1 H⁺ for importing Pi and exchanging ADP/ATP gives the ~4 H⁺ per ATP used for P/O ratios.

q: A patient rescued from a house fire has severe lactic acidosis, and blood drawn from a vein is bright red with an unusually high O₂ content. Cyanide poisoning is suspected. Why is venous O₂ high?
o: Complex IV is blocked, so tissues extract little O₂ from the blood
Cyanide binds hemoglobin directly and greatly raises its O₂ affinity
Cyanide uncouples the chain, so O₂ is pumped back into blood
Lactic acidosis shifts the curve left, trapping O₂ on hemoglobin
e: Cyanide binds the Fe³⁺ of cytochrome a₃ in Complex IV, so cells can't use O₂.
O₂ stays in the blood, making venous blood look 'arterial.'
Cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid. (Acidosis shifts the curve right, not left.)

q: Which set of cofactors does the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex use?
o: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺
Biotin, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NADPH
Pyridoxal phosphate, biotin, CoA, FMN and NAD⁺
Thiamine pyrophosphate, biotin, CoA, FMN and NADP⁺
e: PDH needs TPP (from B₁), lipoic acid, CoA (from B₅), FAD (from B₂) and NAD⁺ (from B₃).
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses the same set.

q: Why does FADH₂ from succinate yield fewer ATP (about 1.5) than NADH (about 2.5)?
o: Its electrons enter at CoQ, skipping Complex I's proton pumping
FADH₂ carries only one electron instead of the usual two
Its electrons skip Complex IV, so O₂ is never reduced by them
FADH₂ must first be carried out of the matrix by a shuttle
e: NADH's electrons pass through Complexes I, III and IV, all of which pump protons.
FADH₂ in Complex II hands electrons straight to CoQ, so only III and IV pump. Fewer H⁺ pumped → fewer ATP.

q: When citric acid cycle intermediates are drawn off for biosynthesis, which reaction most directly refills oxaloacetate?
o: Citrate lyase: citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA in cytosol
e: Reactions that replenish cycle intermediates are called anaplerotic.
Pyruvate carboxylase adds CO₂ to pyruvate in the matrix, making new oxaloacetate.
Acetyl-CoA only cycles through; it can't add net carbon to the pool.
t: Anaplerotic = 'filling up.' Acetyl-CoA keeps the cycle turning but never refills it.

q: About how much net ATP does complete oxidation of palmitate yield? (2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, 10 per acetyl-CoA; activation costs 2 ATP equivalents)
e: 7 rounds: 7 NADH (17.5) + 7 FADH₂ (10.5) = 28 ATP.
8 acetyl-CoA × 10 = 80 ATP.
108 − 2 for activation = 106 ATP
t: Older textbooks (3 and 2 ATP per NADH and FADH₂) give 129. Use whatever ratio the question gives you.

q: How many rounds of β-oxidation are needed to break palmitic acid (16:0) completely into acetyl-CoA?
e: 16 carbons ÷ 2 = 8 acetyl-CoA.
The last round splits a 4-carbon unit into two acetyl-CoA, so only 7 rounds are needed (n/2 − 1).

q: Which lipoprotein carries dietary triglycerides from the intestine to tissues?
e: Chylomicrons: dietary fat from the intestine. VLDL: fat made by the liver. LDL: cholesterol delivery. HDL: cholesterol return to the liver.

q: Chronic heavy drinking often causes fatty liver. Ethanol oxidation raises the liver's NADH:NAD⁺ ratio. How does this promote triglyceride buildup?
o: β-Oxidation slows, and more DHAP is reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate
β-Oxidation speeds up, flooding the liver cells with free fatty acids
NADH directly activates lipoprotein lipase on liver cells
Ethanol molecules are linked straight into triglycerides
e: β-Oxidation needs NAD⁺; when NADH is high, fatty acids aren't burned and are re-esterified.
High NADH also drives DHAP → glycerol-3-phosphate, supplying the backbone for triglycerides.
Fatty acids + glycerol-3-phosphate → triglycerides that accumulate in liver cells.

q: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the ___ and uses ___ as its reducing agent.
e: Synthesis: cytosol, uses NADPH (largely from the pentose phosphate pathway).
Breakdown (β-oxidation): mitochondria, makes NADH and FADH₂.

q: Muscle and brain release much of their excess nitrogen into the blood as glutamine rather than free NH₄⁺. Why?
o: It moves two N atoms in a nontoxic form to liver and kidney
Free NH₄⁺ cannot dissolve in blood plasma at any pH
Glutamine is converted directly to urea by arginase in muscle
Glutamine synthetase makes ATP while it traps ammonia
e: Glutamine synthetase adds NH₄⁺ to glutamate (using ATP), giving glutamine with an amine and an amide N.
In liver and kidney, glutaminase releases the NH₄⁺ for urea synthesis or urinary excretion.
Free ammonia is toxic, especially to the brain.

q: Fatty acid synthesis needs acetyl-CoA in the cytosol, but acetyl-CoA is made in mitochondria. How does it get out?
o: It joins oxaloacetate to form citrate, which is exported and cleaved in the cytosol
It diffuses directly through the inner mitochondrial membrane into the cytosol
It is converted to malonyl-CoA, which is then exported to the cytosol
It is converted back to pyruvate, which is exported and then reconverted
e: The inner membrane is impermeable to acetyl-CoA.
Citrate leaves, and ATP-citrate lyase regenerates acetyl-CoA in the cytosol (the citrate shuttle).

q: A toddler becomes very drowsy after a long fast during a stomach virus. Blood glucose is low, urine ketones are nearly absent, and blood medium-chain acylcarnitines are high. Which explanation fits best?
o: A β-oxidation defect leaves the liver unable to make ketones or support gluconeogenesis
A urea cycle defect is preventing amino acids in muscle from being used to make glucose
Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency is blocking all glucose release from glycogen
Ketone bodies are being made normally but are lost too quickly in the urine
e: High medium-chain acylcarnitines point to a blocked step in medium-chain fatty acid oxidation (e.g., MCAD deficiency).
Without β-oxidation, the fasting liver lacks acetyl-CoA for ketones and the ATP and acetyl-CoA (pyruvate carboxylase activator) that support gluconeogenesis.
The result is 'hypoketotic hypoglycemia'; treatment centers on avoiding long fasts.

q: Lipoprotein lipase, found on capillary walls in muscle and adipose tissue, has which function?
o: Hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL
Hydrolyzes triglycerides stored inside fat cells
Transfers cholesterol esters from HDL particles to LDL
e: Lipoprotein lipase (activated by apoC-II) frees fatty acids from circulating lipoproteins so tissues can take them up.
Stored fat inside adipocytes is broken down by a different enzyme, hormone-sensitive lipase.

q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies build up even though blood glucose is high. What best explains this?
o: Low insulin allows lipolysis, and low malonyl-CoA frees CPT-I
High glucose is converted directly into ketone bodies by the liver
High insulin activates HMG-CoA lyase in the liver mitochondria
Muscle can't release glucose, so it makes ketones in its place
e: Without insulin, hormone-sensitive lipase is active and adipose releases huge amounts of fatty acids.
With low insulin and high glucagon, acetyl-CoA carboxylase is off, so malonyl-CoA is low and CPT-I is not inhibited.
The liver oxidizes the fatty acids and turns the excess acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies; cells sense 'starvation' despite high blood glucose.

q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis?
e: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA (using biotin and ATP).
Insulin and citrate activate it; glucagon inhibits it.

q: In prolonged fasting, much of the liver's acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation becomes ketone bodies instead of entering the citric acid cycle. Why?
o: Oxaloacetate is drawn off for gluconeogenesis, so little citrate can form
The fasting liver stops making the enzyme citrate synthase entirely
Ketone bodies yield more ATP in the liver than the citric acid cycle would
Acetyl-CoA can't enter the mitochondrial matrix of liver cells
e: Acetyl-CoA enters the cycle by combining with oxaloacetate.
In fasting, the liver uses oxaloacetate to make glucose, so acetyl-CoA builds up.
Extra acetyl-CoA is converted to acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate and exported for other tissues.

q: A membrane transport protein moves about 10⁷ ions per second, and its rate keeps rising in proportion to ion concentration over the range tested. It is most likely:
e: Channels form open pores, so ions flow at rates of roughly 10⁶–10⁸ per second.
Carriers and pumps change shape for every cycle, so they move only about 10²–10⁴ molecules per second and saturate sooner.

q: Which molecule crosses a lipid bilayer by simple diffusion most easily?
e: Small, nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂, N₂) dissolve through the hydrophobic core.
Ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.

q: Which movement most directly requires ATP hydrolysis by a membrane pump?
e: Primary active transport couples solute movement directly to ATP hydrolysis.

q: A drug opens more K⁺ channels in a resting neuron. What happens to the membrane potential?
e: More K⁺ permeability pulls the membrane potential toward K⁺'s equilibrium potential (about −90 mV).
That is more negative than −70 mV, so the cell hyperpolarizes.

q: Why is a neuron's resting membrane potential (about −70 mV) much closer to the K⁺ equilibrium potential than to the Na⁺ equilibrium potential?
o: At rest, the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺
There is more Na⁺ than K⁺ inside the cell
Na⁺ cannot cross membranes at all
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump makes all of the voltage
e: The Goldman equation weights each ion by its permeability.
Many K⁺ leak channels are open at rest, so K⁺ dominates the resting potential.

q: Desmosomes give tissues such as skin mechanical strength by linking neighboring cells through cadherins anchored to:
o: Actin filaments of the contractile ring
Collagen fibers in the basement membrane
e: Desmosome cadherins bind each other between cells and attach inside to intermediate filaments (keratin in epithelia).
Hemidesmosomes, by contrast, anchor cells to the basement membrane.

q: After a meal, insulin rapidly increases glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells. What is the main mechanism?
o: GLUT4 transporters move from intracellular vesicles into the plasma membrane
Glucose starts diffusing directly through the lipid bilayer of the membrane
SGLT1 transporters are activated to cotransport glucose with Na⁺ in muscle
GLUT2 transporters move from intracellular vesicles into the plasma membrane
e: GLUT4 is stored in vesicles inside the cell.
Insulin signaling triggers those vesicles to fuse with the membrane, adding transporters within minutes.

q: Each cycle of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. How does this pump directly affect the membrane potential?
o: It removes one net positive charge per cycle, making the inside slightly more negative
It adds one net positive charge per cycle, so the inside becomes slightly more positive
It moves equal charges each way, so it has no direct effect
It sets the entire −70 mV resting potential by itself
e: Charge out = 3 (+), charge in = 2 (+), net = 1 positive charge out per cycle, so the pump is electrogenic.
This contributes only a few millivolts; most of the resting potential comes from K⁺ leaking down the gradient the pump creates.

q: The carbohydrate chains of plasma membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids face:
o: The extracellular side of the cell
The cytosolic side of the cell
The hydrophobic core of the bilayer
Both sides of the bilayer equally
e: Sugars are added in the ER and Golgi lumen, which becomes the outside of the cell after vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane.
These sugars form the glycocalyx, used in cell recognition (e.g., ABO blood antigens).

q: A small fluorescent dye (about 400 Da) injected into one liver cell quickly spreads into its neighbors, but a 10 kDa labeled protein stays in the injected cell. Which structures connect these cells?
e: Gap junctions are connexon channels that link the cytoplasm of adjacent cells.
They pass ions and small molecules (below roughly 1 kDa) but not proteins. The other junctions seal or anchor cells and do not join cytoplasm.

q: Most integral membrane proteins can be removed from a membrane only with detergents. Why?
o: Their nonpolar surfaces interact with the fatty acid tails of the bilayer
They are covalently bonded to the phosphate head groups of the membrane lipids
They are held by ionic bonds to the extracellular matrix
They are too large to fit through the membrane's pores
e: Integral proteins have hydrophobic regions buried among the lipid tails.
Only an amphipathic detergent can replace the lipids around those regions and carry the protein into solution.

q: A patient with high blood potassium (hyperkalemia) is at risk for heart rhythm problems. How does raising extracellular [K⁺] affect a cardiac cell's resting membrane potential?
o: It becomes less negative (depolarizes), because the K⁺ gradient is smaller
It doesn't change, because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump compensates instantly
e: The resting potential is close to K⁺'s equilibrium potential, E = 61.5 log([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in).
Raising [K⁺]out makes that log less negative.
A partly depolarized cell has fewer recoverable Na⁺ channels, which disrupts normal heart rhythm.

q: Myoglobin's O₂-binding curve is hyperbolic, while hemoglobin's is sigmoidal. What explains the difference?
o: Hemoglobin has four subunits that bind O₂ cooperatively; myoglobin has one
Myoglobin lacks a heme group, so it binds O₂ by a different mechanism
Hemoglobin binds O₂ more tightly than myoglobin at every partial pressure
Myoglobin has four subunits that bind O₂ independently; hemoglobin has one
e: When one hemoglobin subunit binds O₂, the others shift toward the high-affinity (R) state.
This cooperativity gives the S-shaped curve, letting hemoglobin load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues.
Myoglobin, a single chain, can't be cooperative.

q: Edman degradation determines a protein's sequence by:
o: Removing and identifying amino acids one at a time from the N-terminus
Cleaving after lysine and arginine and sorting the fragments by mass
Hydrolyzing the whole protein and measuring its amino acid composition
Removing and identifying amino acids one at a time from the C-terminus
e: Phenyl isothiocyanate labels the N-terminal residue, which is then cleaved off and identified.
It works well for short peptides (up to about 50 residues).

q: Epinephrine binds a Gs-coupled receptor on a liver cell. Which second messenger increases?
e: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP.
cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which drives glycogen breakdown.
Gq-coupled receptors use IP₃, DAG and Ca²⁺ instead.

q: Affinity chromatography separates proteins based on:
o: Specific binding to a ligand attached to the column
Size, as proteins pass through porous beads
Net charge interacting with a charged resin
Hydrophobicity interacting with a nonpolar resin
e: The column carries a molecule that the target protein binds specifically (for example, an antibody or a His-tag binding Ni²⁺).
Everything else washes through.

q: SDS-PAGE separates denatured proteins mainly by:
e: SDS unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge, so they all move toward the + electrode.
Smaller proteins slip through the gel faster.

q: Which technique measures a specific protein in a sample by capturing it with antibodies in plastic wells and detecting it with an enzyme-linked antibody that produces a color change?
e: ELISA = enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
The amount of colored product is proportional to the amount of antigen captured.

q: Proteins marked for destruction by the proteasome are usually first tagged with chains of which small protein?
e: Enzymes attach chains of ubiquitin to lysine side chains of the target.
The 26S proteasome recognizes polyubiquitin, unfolds the protein, and cuts it into short peptides.

q: Which method determines a protein's three-dimensional atomic structure from the pattern a crystal makes when it scatters a beam?
e: Protein crystals diffract X-rays; the diffraction pattern is used to calculate an electron-density map and atomic positions.
NMR works in solution, not crystals.

q: A ligand-gated ion channel opens when:
o: A specific signaling molecule binds to it
ATP is hydrolyzed by the channel
e: Example: acetylcholine binding the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction.
Voltage-gated channels respond to voltage; mechanically gated ones respond to stretch.

q: A hormone binds a Gq-coupled receptor. Which sequence of events follows?
o: Phospholipase C makes IP₃ and DAG; IP₃ releases ER Ca²⁺
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, which opens Ca²⁺ channels
The receptor dimerizes and phosphorylates its tyrosines
Gq opens an ion channel that is part of the receptor
e: Active Gαq stimulates phospholipase C, which splits the membrane lipid PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG.
IP₃ opens Ca²⁺ channels on the ER; DAG and Ca²⁺ activate protein kinase C.

q: An activating mutation in Ras prevents it from hydrolyzing its bound GTP. Why does this promote uncontrolled cell growth?
o: Ras stays 'on', signaling for growth without any input
Ras can no longer bind to growth factors at the membrane
Ras is quickly degraded, releasing its growth signal
Ras becomes a kinase that adds phosphates to DNA
e: Ras is active when GTP is bound and turns itself off by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP.
If hydrolysis fails, Ras stays active and keeps the MAP kinase pathway signaling cell division even with no growth factor.
t: Ras is a GTPase switch: GTP = on, GDP = off. Lose the GTPase, lose the off switch.

q: Cells are treated with a Gs-coupled receptor agonist that raises cAMP. A second drug then activates a Gi-coupled receptor on the same cells. What happens?
o: cAMP falls because Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase
cAMP rises further because Gαi also activates PKA
Ca²⁺ rises because Gαi stimulates phospholipase C
Nothing changes, because Gi needs a receptor tyrosine kinase
e: Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; Gαi inhibits it.
With both active, cyclase activity drops, so cAMP and PKA activity decrease.

q: Which D-aldohexose gives an optically inactive (meso) alditol when its aldehyde is reduced to –CH₂OH?
e: Reduction makes both ends –CH₂OH, so the alditol is meso if its top and bottom halves mirror each other.

In D-galactose the Fischer –OH groups at C2–C5 point right, left, left, right: the pattern is symmetric, so galactitol is meso. Glucitol, mannitol and talitol lack this symmetry, so they remain chiral.

q: Pure α-D-glucose dissolved in water slowly becomes a mix of α and β forms. This is called:
e: The ring opens to the straight-chain aldehyde and recloses.
It can close into either anomer, so an equilibrium mixture forms (about 36% α, 64% β).

q: Which disaccharide is NOT a reducing sugar?
e: A reducing sugar needs a free anomeric carbon that can open into an aldehyde.
In sucrose, both anomeric carbons (glucose C1 and fructose C2) are tied up in the glycosidic bond.

q: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucopyranose, the –OH on the anomeric carbon is:
o: Trans to the CH₂OH group (pointing down)
Cis to the CH₂OH group (pointing up)
e: α: anomeric –OH on the opposite side from CH₂OH (down in a standard D-sugar Haworth).
β: same side as CH₂OH (up).
t: 'Alpha = axial = down' works for D-glucose drawn in the standard orientation.

q: Which bond connects the anomeric carbon of one monosaccharide to another sugar?
e: Glycosidic bonds join carbohydrate units.

q: Chitin, the structural polysaccharide of insect exoskeletons and fungal cell walls, is built mainly from which monomer?
e: Chitin is β(1→4)-linked N-acetylglucosamine, like cellulose but with –NHCOCH₃ at C2.
The β linkages and many H-bonds make it a tough, insoluble polymer.

q: When D-glucose cyclizes to its six-membered (pyranose) ring, which oxygen atom becomes the ring oxygen?
o: The oxygen of the C5 –OH group
The oxygen of the C1 aldehyde group
The oxygen of the C6 –OH group
The oxygen of the C4 –OH group
e: The C5 –OH oxygen attacks the C1 carbonyl carbon, so that oxygen bridges C5 and C1 and becomes the ring O (five carbons + one O = pyranose).
The former C=O oxygen becomes the new anomeric –OH on C1; C6 stays outside the ring as –CH₂OH.

q: What is the simplest aldose, a three-carbon sugar with one chiral carbon?
e: Glyceraldehyde (HOCH₂–CHOH–CHO) is an aldotriose with one chiral carbon at C2.
Dihydroxyacetone is the simplest ketose and has no chiral carbon; glycerol is not a sugar.
t: D and L sugars are named by comparison with D- and L-glyceraldehyde.

q: How many chiral carbons does open-chain D-fructose (a 2-ketohexose) have?
e: Fructose: C1 is –CH₂OH, C2 is the C=O, C3–C5 each carry H, OH and two different carbon groups, and C6 is –CH₂OH.
So C3, C4 and C5 are chiral: 3 centers (2³ = 8 ketohexose stereoisomers).

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for an aldohexose (which has 4 chiral carbons in its open-chain form)?
e: Maximum stereoisomers = 2ⁿ
2⁴ = 16 (8 D-sugars and 8 L-sugars).

q: Complete hydrolysis of a linear amylose chain containing 500 glucose units requires how many water molecules?
e: A linear chain of 500 units has 500 − 1 = 499 glycosidic bonds.
Each hydrolysis uses one H₂O, so 499 waters are needed.

q: Reducing D-glucose with NaBH₄ gives one alditol, but reducing D-fructose gives two. Why?
o: Reducing fructose's C2 ketone creates a new chiral center
Fructose's ring opens two ways, giving two ketones
NaBH₄ also removes fructose's C1 –OH as water
Fructose first isomerizes to glucose and galactose
e: Glucose's C1 aldehyde becomes –CH₂OH, which is not chiral: one product (sorbitol).
Fructose's C2 becomes –CHOH– bonded to two different carbons, a new chiral center; hydride adds to either face, giving sorbitol and mannitol.

q: Aspirin and ibuprofen reduce pain, fever and inflammation mainly by:
o: Inhibiting cyclooxygenase, which turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandins
Inhibiting lipoxygenase, which turns arachidonic acid into prostaglandins
Blocking the steroid hormone receptors that respond to prostaglandin signals
Activating phospholipase A₂ to remove arachidonic acid from the body
e: Cyclooxygenase (COX) catalyzes the first committed step from arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes.
NSAIDs block COX, so fewer prostaglandins are made. Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes, not prostaglandins.

q: Prostaglandins are signaling lipids made from:
e: Arachidonic acid (20:4) is converted by COX enzymes into prostaglandins (eicosanoids).
NSAIDs like ibuprofen block COX, reducing inflammation and pain.

q: Sphingolipids are built on a backbone of:
e: Sphingolipids (like sphingomyelin in myelin) use the amino alcohol sphingosine instead of glycerol.

q: An omega-3 fatty acid has its first double bond:
o: At carbon 3, counting from the carboxyl end
e: The omega (ω) carbon is the last one, at the methyl end.
Omega-3s (like EPA and DHA) have their first C=C between carbons 3 and 4 counting from that end.

q: A patient with fat malabsorption bruises easily and bleeds longer than normal. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
e: Vitamin K is needed to carboxylate (activate) several clotting factors.
Fat malabsorption reduces uptake of fat-soluble vitamins.

q: Unlike phospholipids, triacylglycerols do not form bilayers in water. Why?
o: They have no charged or strongly polar head group
They are too water-soluble to stay together
Their three fatty acids are always fully saturated
They are too small to span half a bilayer
e: Bilayers need amphipathic molecules: a polar head facing water and nonpolar tails facing each other.
All three glycerol –OH groups of a TAG are esterified, leaving it almost entirely nonpolar, so it coalesces into oil droplets instead.

q: Phospholipase C cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂. Which statement correctly describes the two products?
o: IP₃ diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; DAG stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
DAG diffuses to the ER to release Ca²⁺; IP₃ stays in the membrane to activate protein kinase C
IP₃ and DAG both leave the cell and bind receptors on neighboring cells
IP₃ activates adenylyl cyclase, and DAG is stored in fat droplets
e: PIP₂ has a hydrophobic diacylglycerol part and a charged inositol trisphosphate head.
The soluble head (IP₃) moves through the cytosol to open ER Ca²⁺ channels; the hydrophobic DAG stays in the membrane, where it (with Ca²⁺) activates PKC.
t: Think solubility: the charged piece (IP₃) travels; the greasy piece (DAG) stays put.

q: At pH 7.4, which membrane phospholipid carries a net negative charge?
e: Phosphatidylserine: phosphate (−1) + serine carboxylate (−1) + serine amine (+1) = net −1.
Phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine and sphingomyelin each pair a −1 phosphate with a +1 head group, giving net 0.
t: PS = Phosphatidyl-Serine = the Sour (negative) one; it has the extra carboxylate.

q: Some snake venoms contain phospholipase A₂, which removes the fatty acid from carbon 2 of membrane glycerophospholipids. Exposed red blood cells burst. What is the most direct reason?
o: The single-tailed lysophospholipids made act like detergents and disrupt the bilayer
The released fatty acids are converted to cholesterol, which makes the bilayer rigid
Removing one tail turns phospholipids into triacylglycerols that leave the membrane
The enzyme hydrolyzes the cells' membrane proteins, opening large pores
e: PLA₂ converts a two-tailed phospholipid into a lysophospholipid (one tail) plus a free fatty acid.
Cone-shaped, single-tailed lysophospholipids favor micelles, so they solubilize the bilayer like a detergent and the cell lyses.
t: One tail = cone = micelle (detergent-like). Two tails = cylinder = bilayer.

q: A wax is an ester of:
o: A long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol
Glycerol and three long-chain fatty acids
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate
Sphingosine and a long-chain fatty acid
e: Waxes are very hydrophobic and solid at room temperature.
They waterproof leaves, feathers and skin.

q: A food maker partially hydrogenates a liquid vegetable oil. Compared with the starting oil, the product:
o: Is more solid at room temperature and may contain trans fats
Is more liquid at room temperature and contains more cis bonds
Has shorter fatty acid chains and a lower melting point
Has more double bonds and spoils by oxidation more quickly
e: Adding H₂ across C=C bonds lowers unsaturation, so chains pack better and the melting point rises (oil → margarine-like solid).
During partial hydrogenation, some remaining cis double bonds isomerize to trans.

q: Arachidonic acid is 20:4 with cis double bonds at Δ5, Δ8, Δ11 and Δ14 (counted from the carboxyl carbon). It is an omega-what fatty acid?
e: The ω number counts from the methyl end: ω = (chain length) − (position of the last double bond).
ω = 20 − 14 = 6, so arachidonic acid is an ω-6 fatty acid.
t: Δ counts from the COOH end; ω counts from the CH₃ end. Subtract the last Δ from the chain length.

q: Which compound has a more negative standard free energy of phosphate hydrolysis than ATP, allowing it to phosphorylate ADP directly?
e: ΔG°′ of hydrolysis: PEP ≈ −62, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate ≈ −49, phosphocreatine ≈ −43, ATP ≈ −30.5, glucose-6-phosphate ≈ −14 kJ mol⁻¹.
Phosphate flows 'downhill' from compounds above ATP to ADP, and from ATP to compounds below it.

q: Which way of controlling a metabolic pathway usually takes the longest to change its flux?
o: Changing how much enzyme is synthesized
e: Allosteric effects and substrate changes act in seconds or less; phosphorylation cascades act in seconds to minutes.
Changing gene expression (enzyme induction or repression) takes hours to days, as during adaptation to a long fast.

q: Complete oxidation of glucose has ΔG°′ ≈ −2870 kJ mol⁻¹. If it yields 32 ATP (ΔG°′ = +30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ each), about what fraction of the energy is captured as ATP under standard conditions?
e: Energy stored = 32 × 30.5 ≈ 976 kJ.
Efficiency = 976 ÷ 2870 ≈ 0.34, or about 34%; the rest is released as heat.
t: Under real cell conditions ATP's ΔG is larger, so true efficiency is higher than this estimate.

q: Cortisol released during long-term stress promotes:
o: Gluconeogenesis and breakdown of muscle protein
Glucose uptake by muscle and protein synthesis
Ketone body breakdown and lower blood glucose
Insulin release and storage of liver glycogen only
e: Cortisol provides amino acids (from muscle) as fuel for liver gluconeogenesis, raising blood glucose.

q: The well-fed (absorptive) state is mainly:
o: Anabolic, building glycogen, fat and protein
Catabolic, breaking down glycogen, fat and protein
Catabolic, driven mainly by glucagon and cortisol
Neither, since synthesis and breakdown are balanced
e: After a meal, high insulin promotes storage.
Fasting is catabolic, dominated by glucagon.

q: How do cells drive an unfavorable reaction (ΔG > 0)?
o: They couple it to a favorable reaction such as ATP hydrolysis, so net ΔG < 0
They use an enzyme to lower the reaction's ΔG until it becomes negative
They raise the temperature until the reaction's ΔG becomes negative
They couple it to another unfavorable reaction so the ΔG values cancel
e: ΔG values for coupled reactions add together.
If the total ΔG is negative, the combined process is spontaneous.

q: In a patient with insulin resistance, a brisk 30-minute walk lowers blood glucose even though insulin signaling in muscle is impaired. What best explains this?
o: Rising AMP activates AMPK, which moves GLUT4 to the membrane without insulin
Exercise raises glucagon, which makes skeletal muscle take up glucose
Exercise releases insulin that is stored inside the muscle fibers
Contraction makes the liver convert blood glucose into glycogen
e: Contracting muscle uses ATP, so AMP rises and activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
AMPK (along with Ca²⁺ signals) moves GLUT4 to the muscle surface through a pathway independent of the insulin receptor.
This is one reason exercise helps control blood glucose in type 2 diabetes.

q: Which carrier mainly supplies electrons for biosynthetic (reductive) reactions such as fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis?
e: Cells keep NADPH/NADP⁺ high, ready to donate electrons for building molecules.
NADH/NAD⁺ is kept mostly oxidized for catabolism, sending electrons to the ETC. ATP carries energy, not electrons.
t: P for 'production' (biosynthesis): NADPH builds, NADH burns.

q: Metabolic pathways are usually regulated at enzymes whose reactions are far from equilibrium. Why?
o: Their large negative ΔG means changing their activity changes pathway flux
Near-equilibrium enzymes are too slow to affect pathway flux at all
Far-from-equilibrium steps are easily reversed by mass action
Enzymes near equilibrium can't bind allosteric effectors
e: A near-equilibrium step runs both ways quickly; its net direction simply follows substrate and product levels.
A far-from-equilibrium step (ΔG ≪ 0) is effectively one-way and often slow, so it limits flux; speeding it up or slowing it down controls the whole pathway.
Examples: hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase, isocitrate dehydrogenase.

q: Muscle biopsies from a patient show GLUT4 transporters stuck in intracellular vesicles even after insulin is given. Which process is most impaired?
o: Glucose uptake by neurons in the brain
Glucose release from liver glycogen into blood
Glucose absorption from the small intestine
e: Insulin signaling normally moves GLUT4 vesicles to the plasma membrane of muscle and fat cells.
If GLUT4 can't reach the surface, those tissues take up little glucose after a meal, and blood glucose stays high.
Brain (GLUT1/3), liver (GLUT2) and intestine (SGLT1, GLUT2) don't depend on GLUT4.

q: A person uses about 8,000 kJ of free energy as ATP each day. If each mole of ATP hydrolyzed in cells releases about 50 kJ and ATP's molar mass is about 500 g mol⁻¹, about how much ATP is recycled per day?
e: Moles of ATP = 8000 kJ ÷ 50 kJ mol⁻¹ = 160 mol.
Mass = 160 mol × 0.5 kg mol⁻¹ = 80 kg.
The body holds only a small ATP pool at any moment, so each ATP is regenerated hundreds of times a day.

q: A snack contains 10 g fat, 20 g carbohydrate and 10 g protein. Using 9, 4 and 4 kcal g⁻¹, about how much energy does it provide?
e: Fat: 10 × 9 = 90 kcal. Carbohydrate: 20 × 4 = 80 kcal. Protein: 10 × 4 = 40 kcal.

q: Which digestive enzyme is most likely Enzyme 1 in the graph?
o: Pepsin, which works in the stomach
Trypsin, which works in the small intestine
e: Enzyme 1 peaks near pH 2, matching the acidic stomach.
Trypsin (Enzyme 2-like) peaks near pH 8.

q: Cholesterol (shown) sits in membranes with its single polar group near the phospholipid heads. Which part is that polar group?
o: The hydroxyl group on ring carbon 3
The double bond between C5 and C6
e: Cholesterol's only polar atom is the O of its 3-OH group, which hydrogen-bonds near the phospholipid head groups.
The fused rings and side chain are nonpolar and lie among the fatty acid tails.

o: The enzyme begins to denature, losing its active-site shape
The enzyme becomes a competitive inhibitor
e: Heat breaks the noncovalent interactions that hold the folded structure.

Malate dehydrogenase then oxidizes malate to oxaloacetate, completing the cycle.

q: Which shorthand describes the fatty acid shown?
e: Count carbons: 16 in total, with one C=C double bond.
Numbering from the carboxyl carbon (C1), the double bond starts at C9, so Δ⁹.
Both chain segments are on the same side of the double bond, so it is cis (this is palmitoleic acid, an ω-7).

q: Four amino acids are shown. Which has a positively charged side chain at pH 7.4?
e: A is lysine: its side-chain –NH₂ (pKa ≈ 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4.
D (aspartate) is negative; B (leucine) is nonpolar; C (serine) is polar and neutral.

q: Cytosine in DNA slowly deaminates on its own to form uracil. How does using thymine (5-methyluracil) rather than uracil in DNA help repair?
o: Any uracil found in DNA can be recognized as damage and removed
Thymine cannot be deaminated, so it never needs repair
Thymine pairs with guanine, so the mistake is corrected automatically
Uracil forms three hydrogen bonds, making mismatches too stable
e: If uracil were a normal DNA base, a U made from deaminated C could not be told apart from a real one.
Because DNA normally uses T, uracil-DNA glycosylase removes every U, and base excision repair restores the C.

q: Long-chain fatty acyl groups cross the inner mitochondrial membrane while attached to compound X (shown). What is compound X?
e: Carnitine acyltransferase I moves the acyl group from CoA to carnitine on the outer side.
A translocase carries acyl-carnitine across; carnitine acyltransferase II puts the acyl group back on CoA in the matrix.
t: Choline also has a trimethylammonium group but no carboxylate; don't confuse the two.
