q: Only about 80% of people who carry a disease-causing genotype ever show the disease. This describes:
e: Penetrance = the fraction of people with a genotype who show the phenotype at all.
Variable expressivity means affected people show the trait with different severity.
t: Penetrance: whether it shows. Expressivity: how strongly it shows.

q: Two genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is:
e: Close genes are rarely separated by crossing over, so they don't assort independently.

q: A gene's sequence differs by 30 substitutions between species A and B, and by 90 substitutions between species A and C. If A and B shared a common ancestor 5 million years ago and substitutions build up at a constant rate, about when did A and C share a common ancestor?
e: Rate = 30 differences ÷ 5 million years = 6 differences per million years.
A and C: 90 ÷ 6 = 15 million years.
t: This 'molecular clock' only works if the rate really is constant.

q: Two genes are 10 map units apart. About what percentage of offspring are recombinant?
e: 1 map unit (centimorgan) = 1% recombination frequency.

q: A river changes course and splits a population of beetles into two groups that can no longer meet. Over many generations they become separate species. This is:
e: Allopatric ('other homeland') speciation follows a physical barrier that stops gene flow.
Sympatric speciation happens without geographic separation.

q: A woman who is a carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder has children with an unaffected man. What is the probability that a son will be affected?
e: Mother: XᴬXᵃ. Father: XᴬY.
A son always gets Y from dad and one X from mom.
Mom passes Xᵃ half the time, so P(affected son) = ½.
t: Read carefully: 'probability a son is affected' (½) differs from 'probability a child is an affected son' (¼).

q: A sample of 100 plants contains 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa individuals. How does the number of heterozygotes compare with the Hardy–Weinberg expectation?
o: Far fewer than expected, as with inbreeding
Far more than expected, as with heterozygote advantage
About the same as expected, so the population is in equilibrium
It can't be compared without knowing the mutation rate
e: Expected heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 (48 plants), but only 20 are observed.
A heterozygote shortage suggests inbreeding (for example, self-pollination) or population subdivision.

q: A child has type O blood, and the mother has type A blood. Which man could NOT be the biological father?
o: A man with type AB blood
A man with type O blood
A man with type A blood
A man with type B blood
e: Type O means the child is ii, so each parent must have given an i allele (the mother must be Iᴬi).
Men with type A (Iᴬi) or type B (Iᴮi) can carry i, and type O men are ii; a type AB man (IᴬIᴮ) has no i to pass on.
t: Blood typing can exclude a possible father but can never prove that a man is the father.

q: A hurricane kills most of an island's lizards at random, and the few survivors carry only a small fraction of the original alleles. This is an example of:
e: A bottleneck is a sharp drop in population size that randomly removes alleles.
The founder effect is similar, but happens when a small group leaves to start a new population.

q: Structures that look different but share a common evolutionary origin, like a human arm and a bat wing, are:
e: Analogous structures (like bird and insect wings) have similar function but different origins.

q: Genetic drift has the biggest effect in:
e: Random chance changes allele frequencies more in small groups.

q: For two unlinked genes, a cross is made between AaBb and aabb. What fraction of the offspring are aabb?
e: Each gene separately: Aa × aa gives ½ aa, and Bb × bb gives ½ bb.
Unlinked genes assort independently: ½ × ½ = ¼

q: Which cell type would you expect to have the most rough ER?
o: Pancreatic acinar cell secreting digestive enzymes
Mature red blood cell carrying oxygen
Adrenal cortex cell synthesizing steroid hormones
e: Rough ER makes proteins for secretion.
Pancreatic acinar cells secrete large amounts of enzyme protein.

q: A bacterial culture in steady log-phase growth rises from 1.0 × 10³ to 8.0 × 10³ cells in 90 minutes. What is its doubling time?
e: 8.0 × 10³ ÷ 1.0 × 10³ = 8 = 2³, so the population doubled 3 times.
Doubling time = 90 min ÷ 3 = 30 minutes.
t: 11 minutes comes from dividing by 8; count doublings, not the fold-increase.

q: Which eukaryotic organelle is most directly responsible for oxidative ATP synthesis?
e: The inner mitochondrial membrane houses oxidative phosphorylation complexes.

q: A virus that inserts its genome into the host chromosome and stays dormant is in which cycle?
e: In the lysogenic cycle, the viral DNA (prophage) is copied along with the host's DNA.
Stress can switch it to the lytic cycle, which kills the cell.

q: Which statement is true of prokaryotic cells?
o: Their DNA is in a nucleoid region
e: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, including a nucleus.
Their circular chromosome sits in the nucleoid region.
They have 70S ribosomes (eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes are 80S).
t: Many antibiotics target 70S ribosomes, which is why they can kill bacteria without killing you.

q: In a eukaryotic cell, the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with which organelle?
o: The cis face of the Golgi apparatus
e: The outer nuclear membrane folds directly into the ER membrane, so the space between the two nuclear membranes connects to the ER lumen.
Like rough ER, the outer nuclear membrane is studded with ribosomes.

q: HIV is a retrovirus. What does its reverse transcriptase do?
e: A retrovirus carries an RNA genome.
Reverse transcriptase uses that RNA as a template to make DNA.
The DNA is then integrated into the host genome by integrase.
t: 'Reverse' because it runs the central dogma backward: RNA → DNA.

q: A mutation deletes the nuclear localization signal from a large transcription factor made on free cytosolic ribosomes. Where will most of the protein end up?
e: Large proteins enter the nucleus through nuclear pores only if they carry a nuclear localization signal.
The protein has no ER signal sequence either (it is made on free ribosomes), so it stays in the cytosol, where it cannot reach its target genes.

q: Where are ribosomal subunits assembled in a eukaryotic cell?
e: The nucleolus makes rRNA and assembles it with proteins into ribosomal subunits, which then leave through nuclear pores.

q: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S-like ribosomes. These features support which idea?
o: Cell theory's claim that all cells have nuclei
e: Mitochondria resemble bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell.
Chloroplasts share the same features.

q: Bacteria transfer DNA through a sex pilus in which process?
e: Conjugation: direct transfer through a pilus (often of a plasmid).
Transformation: uptake of free DNA. Transduction: transfer by a virus.

q: Under the microscope, a bacterium appears as a short rod. Which term describes its shape?
e: Cocci are spheres, bacilli are rods, and spirilla and spirochetes are spirals.
t: Bacillus sounds like 'baton', a rod.

q: After ovulation, the corpus luteum mainly secretes:
e: Progesterone keeps the uterine lining ready for implantation.
If no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down and menstruation follows.

q: Which checkpoint ensures that every chromosome is attached to the spindle before anaphase starts?
e: Unattached kinetochores block the start of anaphase.
This prevents chromosome loss or gain in daughter cells.

q: In males, luteinizing hormone (LH) acts mainly on which cells, and with what effect?
e: LH binds Leydig (interstitial) cells between the seminiferous tubules and stimulates testosterone production.
FSH is the hormone that acts on Sertoli cells, which support sperm development and secrete inhibin.
t: L for L: LH → Leydig. S for S: FSH → Sertoli.

q: In males, where are sperm produced?
e: Sperm form in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis.

q: A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes. How many does a human gamete have?
e: Gametes are haploid (n = 23).
Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).

q: Which event happens in meiosis I but not in mitosis?
o: Homologous chromosomes pair up and separate
e: Synapsis (pairing of homologs) and crossing over happen in prophase I.
In anaphase I, homologs (not sister chromatids) separate.

q: In pregnancy, what keeps the corpus luteum from breaking down in the first trimester?
e: hCG acts like LH to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone.
Pregnancy tests detect hCG.

q: A cell's chromosomes fail to attach to spindle fibers. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
o: A microtubule inhibitor, like some chemotherapy drugs
An actin polymerization inhibitor, like cytochalasin
A DNA polymerase inhibitor, like some antivirals
A ribosome inhibitor, like some antibiotics
e: Drugs such as vinca alkaloids block microtubule assembly, and taxanes block disassembly.
Both stop dividing cancer cells in mitosis.

q: Why can men produce sperm for decades, while women are born with a limited supply of oocytes that is not renewed?
o: Spermatogonia keep dividing by mitosis as stem cells
Primary spermatocytes skip meiosis I entirely
Mature sperm divide by mitosis to make new sperm
Oocytes are destroyed by sperm after puberty
e: In the testes, spermatogonial stem cells divide by mitosis throughout adult life, renewing themselves while supplying cells that enter meiosis.
In females, oogonia stop dividing before birth, leaving a fixed pool of primary oocytes.

q: Combined oral contraceptives provide steady levels of estrogen and progestin. How do they mainly prevent pregnancy?
o: Negative feedback suppresses the mid-cycle LH surge
They raise FSH so that many follicles ovulate
They destroy the oocytes stored in the ovaries
They make the corpus luteum form much earlier
e: Steady estrogen and progestin feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH.
Without an LH surge, ovulation does not occur.

q: At the conclusion of mitosis and cytokinesis, a typical diploid somatic cell produces:
e: Mitosis normally yields two daughter cells that retain the parental chromosome number.

q: Mutation of a proto-oncogene into an oncogene typically causes:
o: A gain of function that drives division even without signals
A recessive loss of function needing both alleles mutated
Faster DNA repair that lowers the mutation rate
Increased apoptosis that eliminates the mutant cells
e: Oncogenes act like a stuck accelerator; one mutated copy can be enough.
Tumor suppressors act like brakes; usually both copies must be lost.

q: Scientists turn adult skin cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). Why are these useful in medicine?
o: They can become many cell types and match the patient's own genome
They are totipotent, so they can also form placental tissue
They never form tumors, since they come from adult cells
They can become only skin cells, which simplifies grafting
e: iPSCs are reprogrammed with a few transcription factors.
Because they come from the patient, transplants may avoid immune rejection.

q: Fertilization took place 3 days ago, yet a sensitive hCG pregnancy test is negative. What is the best explanation?
o: hCG is made only after the blastocyst implants
hCG is made only in the second trimester
hCG is made by the mother's pituitary gland
hCG is broken down by the corpus luteum
e: hCG is secreted by the trophoblast once the blastocyst implants, about a week after fertilization.
At 3 days the embryo is still a small cleavage-stage ball of cells drifting toward the uterus, so no hCG has been made yet.

q: In deuterostomes such as humans, the blastopore that forms during gastrulation becomes the:
e: Deuterostome means 'second mouth': the blastopore becomes the anus and the mouth forms later at the other end.
In protostomes (such as most invertebrates), the blastopore becomes the mouth.

q: Which extraembryonic membrane forms a fluid-filled sac that cushions the embryo?
e: The amnion encloses the embryo in amniotic fluid, which absorbs shocks and prevents drying.
The chorion helps form the placenta, and the allantois contributes to the umbilical blood vessels.

q: An infant has severe constipation because one segment of the colon lacks the nerve cells normally found in its wall. Failed migration of which embryonic cells best explains this?
e: The enteric nervous system (the gut's own neurons) is built from neural crest cells that migrate along the gut.
If they fail to reach the end of the colon, that segment cannot push stool along (Hirschsprung disease).

q: A solid ball of cells formed by early cleavage divisions is called a:
e: Zygote → morula (solid ball) → blastula/blastocyst (hollow) → gastrula (three germ layers).

q: Webbing between fingers disappears during development through:
e: Controlled cell death sculpts structures like fingers and toes.

q: In a lab, blocking a signal from the notochord prevents the neural tube from forming. This supports which idea?
o: Induction: ectoderm needs the notochord's signal to form neural tissue
Apoptosis: the notochord's signal kills ectoderm that isn't neural
Gastrulation: the notochord's signal forms the three germ layers
Endoderm origin: the neural tube develops from endoderm cells
e: Removing the inducer removes the response.
That's the classic test for induction.

q: A mutant fruit fly grows legs on its head where its antennae should be. A mutation in which kind of gene is most likely?
o: A gene for neural crest migration
e: Homeotic genes tell each body segment what structures to build.
When one is expressed in the wrong segment, a normal structure forms in the wrong place, such as legs instead of antennae.

q: Hox genes in an embryo mainly control:
o: The identity of body segments along the head-to-tail axis
The left–right asymmetry of the heart and gut
The timing of cell divisions in the early cleavage stage
The differentiation of germ cells into eggs or sperm
e: Hox genes encode transcription factors that tell segments what to become.
Mutations can put structures in the wrong place (for example, legs instead of antennae in fruit flies).

q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF) help the fetus get oxygen from the mother?
o: HbF binds O₂ more tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds O₂ less tightly than adult hemoglobin
HbF binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than adult hemoglobin
HbF has more heme groups per molecule than HbA
e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its O₂ curve is left-shifted.
O₂ moves from maternal hemoglobin to fetal hemoglobin across the placenta.

q: Embryonic stem cells taken from the inner cell mass are pluripotent. Which cells can they NOT normally give rise to?
e: Pluripotent cells can form all three germ layers, so neurons, heart muscle and liver are all possible.
By the blastocyst stage, inner cell mass cells are already committed away from the trophoblast lineage, which forms the fetal part of the placenta, so they do not normally make trophoblast.
t: Totipotent = embryo + placenta. Pluripotent = embryo only.

q: Ependymal cells line the brain's ventricles. What do they help produce?
e: Ependymal cells, especially in the choroid plexus, help make and circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
CSF cushions the brain and spinal cord.

q: Organophosphate poisoning blocks acetylcholinesterase everywhere. Which symptoms are expected?
o: Excess salivation, sweating, small pupils and muscle twitching
Dry mouth, dilated pupils, flushed skin and urinary retention
Rapid heart rate, bronchodilation, dilated pupils and dry skin
Flaccid paralysis with dry skin and no glandular secretions
e: ACh builds up at parasympathetic (muscarinic) and neuromuscular (nicotinic) synapses.
Parasympathetic overdrive plus muscle twitching, then paralysis.

q: A neuron is placed in a solution with half the normal extracellular Na⁺. How will its action potentials most likely change?
o: The peak will be lower (less positive)
The peak will be higher (more positive)
The resting potential will drop to −90 mV
e: The peak approaches the Na⁺ equilibrium potential, which depends on the Na⁺ gradient.
Halving [Na⁺] outside lowers E<sub>Na</sub> by about 61.5 × log 2 ≈ 18 mV, so the overshoot is smaller.
The resting potential barely changes, because the resting membrane is mainly permeable to K⁺.

q: A person steps on a tack with the right foot. The right leg pulls away while the left leg straightens to bear the body's weight. Which statement is correct?
o: Spinal interneurons link the pain input to both legs
The brain must register the pain before either leg moves
A single synapse links the pain receptor to both legs
The left leg's flexor muscles contract along with the right
e: This withdrawal + crossed-extensor reflex is polysynaptic: interneurons in the spinal cord excite right flexors and left extensors.
It happens before the pain is consciously felt, and the left leg's EXTENSORS contract.

q: Which receptor type converts light into nerve signals?
e: Photoreceptors contain light-sensitive pigments (opsins with retinal).

q: A sensory neuron carries a signal from a touch receptor. Through which part of the spinal cord does it enter?
e: Sensory (afferent) fibers enter through the dorsal root.
Motor (efferent) fibers leave through the ventral root.
t: 'SAME DAVE': Sensory Afferent, Motor Efferent; Dorsal Afferent, Ventral Efferent.

q: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart:
e: The vagus nerve releases ACh at the SA node, slowing it down.

q: Two subthreshold signals arrive at the same synapse in quick succession and together reach threshold. This is:
e: Temporal summation: repeated inputs from one source, close in time.
Spatial summation: inputs from several sources at once.

q: Which brain structure is most important for forming new long-term explicit memories?
e: Damage to the hippocampus causes anterograde amnesia: trouble forming new memories.

q: GABA binding to its receptor usually makes the postsynaptic neuron:
e: GABA opens Cl⁻ channels; Cl⁻ entering hyperpolarizes the cell.
GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain.

q: Which brainstem region controls breathing and heart rate?
e: The medulla contains centers for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

q: Local anesthetics block pain without making a patient unconscious. Based on how they act, where do they work?
o: On voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in local nerve fibers, blocking conduction
On GABA receptors in the brain, dampening conscious awareness of pain
On voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in muscle, preventing contraction
On opioid receptors in the spinal cord, inhibiting pain transmission
e: They stop action potentials from traveling in nerves near the injection site.
Pain signals never reach the brain.

q: Right after a person loses about 1 L of blood, which hormonal changes help restore blood volume and pressure?
o: ADH and aldosterone rise, while ANP falls
ADH and aldosterone fall, while ANP rises
ADH rises, while aldosterone and ANP fall
ADH falls, while aldosterone and ANP rise
e: Low pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, which boosts ADH release; low kidney perfusion releases renin → angiotensin II → aldosterone.
The atria are stretched less, so ANP (which promotes Na⁺ and water loss) falls.

q: A pituitary tumor begins secreting excess growth hormone in a 40-year-old man. His hands, feet and jaw slowly enlarge, but he does not grow taller. Why?
o: His growth plates have fused, so long bones can't lengthen
Growth hormone acts only on the bones of the hands and face
Excess growth hormone blocks IGF-1 production by the liver
Adults lack growth hormone receptors on their bone cells
e: Growth hormone, acting largely through IGF-1 from the liver, stimulates bone and soft-tissue growth.
After puberty the epiphyseal plates have fused, so bones can only thicken and soft tissues enlarge (acromegaly); before fusion the same tumor causes gigantism.
t: GH excess before the plates close → gigantism; after → acromegaly.

q: A patient's pituitary tumor secretes excess prolactin. Which symptom is most likely?
o: Milk production and irregular menstrual cycles
Low blood calcium and muscle tetany or cramps
High blood glucose and frequent urination
Rapid heart rate, weight loss and heat intolerance
e: Prolactin stimulates milk production.
High prolactin also suppresses GnRH, disrupting the cycle.

q: How does the posterior pituitary differ from the anterior pituitary?
o: It releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons
It makes its own hormones when releasing hormones arrive
It is glandular tissue that secretes only steroid hormones
It gets hypothalamic signals only through portal blood
e: The posterior pituitary is neural tissue: axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons.
ADH and oxytocin are made in hypothalamic cell bodies, shipped down the axons, and released into the blood on nerve signals.

q: A patient with Graves' disease has antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. Which lab pattern is expected?
e: The antibodies stimulate the thyroid directly, raising T₄.
High T₄ then suppresses pituitary TSH by negative feedback.

q: Why is cortisol given as an anti-inflammatory drug?
o: It suppresses the immune and inflammatory responses
It increases white blood cell activity
e: Glucocorticoids reduce production of inflammatory molecules like prostaglandins and cytokines.

q: Peptide hormones like insulin act by:
o: Binding cell-surface receptors and triggering second messengers
Diffusing into the nucleus and binding DNA directly
Crossing the membrane and binding cytoplasmic receptors
Binding intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors
e: Peptides are water-soluble and can't cross the lipid bilayer, so they use surface receptors.

q: Calcitonin and PTH work as antagonists. If blood calcium is too high, which response is expected?
e: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium (bone deposition).
PTH raises it, so it would be reduced.

q: Which hormone does the posterior pituitary release?
e: The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH, made in the hypothalamus.
The others come from the anterior pituitary.

q: A bodybuilder injects large doses of testosterone for months. What happens to his own LH secretion and his sperm production?
o: LH falls and sperm production drops
LH rises and sperm production increases
LH falls but sperm production increases
LH rises but sperm production drops
e: Excess androgen feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering GnRH, LH and FSH.
Spermatogenesis needs FSH and high testosterone made inside the testes, so the testes shrink and sperm counts fall.

q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
e: Contractions trigger more oxytocin, which strengthens contractions, until birth ends the loop.

q: A patient has low ACTH and low cortisol. Where is the problem most likely located?
e: If the adrenal gland were the problem, ACTH would be HIGH (no feedback).
Both low means the signal from above is missing.

q: Most CO₂ is carried in the blood as:
o: CO₂ bound to iron in hemoglobin
e: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
About 70% of CO₂ travels this way.

q: What happens to intrapulmonary pressure during normal inspiration?
o: It rises well above atmospheric pressure
It stays exactly above atmospheric pressure
e: Thoracic expansion decreases alveolar pressure and draws air inward.

q: Exercising muscle releases CO₂ and heat. How does this help O₂ delivery?
o: It shifts the O₂–hemoglobin curve right, so more O₂ is unloaded
It shifts the curve left, so hemoglobin holds O₂ more tightly
It raises hemoglobin's O₂ affinity, so more O₂ is loaded in muscle
It dissolves more O₂ in plasma, bypassing hemoglobin
e: The Bohr effect: CO₂, H⁺, heat and 2,3-BPG all lower hemoglobin's O₂ affinity.

q: Mucus and cilia in the airways:
o: Trap and sweep particles up and out of the airways
Exchange O₂ and CO₂ across the bronchial wall
Produce surfactant that keeps the bronchi open
Absorb water to keep the airway lining dry
e: This 'mucociliary escalator' clears debris; smoking damages it.

q: A patient with COPD has chronically high CO₂. Why might giving too much O₂ be risky?
o: Extra O₂ worsens V/Q matching and lowers Hb's CO₂ binding, raising CO₂
Extra O₂ causes metabolic alkalosis by lowering blood H⁺
Extra O₂ blocks hemoglobin's heme sites like carbon monoxide
Extra O₂ causes excess surfactant to flood the alveoli
e: Giving high-flow O₂ to some COPD patients can raise CO₂ further.
Current evidence points mainly to worse ventilation–perfusion matching (O₂ reverses protective vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated lung) and the Haldane effect (oxygenated Hb carries less CO₂).
The older 'loss of hypoxic drive' explanation plays a smaller role. Clinicians target a moderate O₂ saturation (about 88–92%).

q: Inhaled air is warmed and saturated with water vapor (47 mmHg) in the trachea. At a total pressure of 760 mmHg and 21% O₂, what is the P(O₂) of this humidified air?
e: Water vapor takes up 47 mmHg, leaving 760 − 47 = 713 mmHg for the other gases.
P(O₂) = 0.21 × 713 ≈ 150 mmHg. (160 mmHg is dry air; about 100 mmHg is found later, in the alveoli.)

q: Why is oxygen delivery to tissues in severe anemia low even when P(O₂) in arterial blood is normal?
o: There's less hemoglobin to carry O₂
The lungs can't take in O₂
e: Most O₂ in blood is carried by hemoglobin.
With little hemoglobin, total O₂ content drops even if saturation and P(O₂) are normal.

q: Why does gas exchange occur so efficiently across the alveolar wall?
o: Its thin wall and huge surface area allow rapid diffusion
Active transport pumps move O₂ into the capillary blood
Its thick wall stores O₂ for steady release into blood
Air pressure forces O₂ into the blood by bulk flow
e: Fick's law: diffusion rises with surface area and falls with wall thickness.

q: What is the main function of pulmonary surfactant?
o: Trap inhaled particles so cilia can sweep them out
Lower surface tension so alveoli don't collapse
Carry O₂ across the alveolar-capillary membrane
Keep the pleural layers lubricated during breathing
e: A thin layer of water lines each alveolus, creating surface tension.
Surfactant (made by type II cells) lowers that surface tension.
This keeps alveoli open and makes breathing easier. Premature infants often lack enough of it.
t: This links biology to physics (4B): surface tension in a small sphere tends to collapse it.

q: In systemic capillaries, HCO₃⁻ formed inside red blood cells moves out into the plasma. Which ion moves in to balance the charge?
e: A band 3 exchanger swaps HCO₃⁻ out for Cl⁻ in (the chloride shift), so the cell stays electrically neutral.
The H⁺ made alongside HCO₃⁻ stays inside, buffered by hemoglobin.

q: Which airway is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage?
e: Cartilage rings keep the trachea from collapsing as pressure changes during breathing.
Bronchioles have no cartilage; their smooth muscle controls their diameter.

q: During an asthma attack, a bronchiole's radius shrinks to two-thirds of its normal value. By about what factor does its resistance to airflow increase, according to Poiseuille's law?
e: Resistance is proportional to 1/r⁴.
With r reduced to 2/3, resistance rises by (3/2)⁴ = 81/16 ≈ 5.1 times.
t: Resistance depends on r⁴: small changes in airway radius have huge effects.

q: Urine leaves each kidney and travels to the bladder through the:
e: Each kidney has one ureter that carries urine down to the bladder.
The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
t: Ureters: two (one per kidney). Urethra: one (out of the body).

q: Constricting the afferent arteriole would cause GFR to:
e: Less blood enters the glomerulus, lowering glomerular pressure and filtration.
Constricting the efferent arteriole would raise GFR.

q: The descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to ___, while the thick ascending limb actively pumps out ___.
e: Descending: water leaves into the salty medulla.
Ascending: impermeable to water but pumps out salt.

q: Where is most of the filtered glucose reabsorbed?
e: The proximal tubule reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids and most Na⁺ and water.

q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by:
o: Constricting arterioles and triggering aldosterone release
Dilating arterioles and triggering aldosterone release
Constricting arterioles and blocking ADH and thirst
Increasing Na⁺ excretion and lowering blood volume
e: It also stimulates thirst and ADH release.

q: A drug blocks the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb. What happens?
o: Less concentrated urine and more urine volume
More concentrated urine and less urine volume
No change, since collecting ducts compensate
Less Na⁺ in the urine and lower urine volume
e: Loop diuretics (like furosemide) weaken the medullary salt gradient, so less water is reabsorbed.

q: Loop and thiazide diuretics block Na⁺ reabsorption before the collecting duct, and patients often develop low blood K⁺. Why?
o: More Na⁺ and fluid reach the collecting duct, which boosts K⁺ secretion
The diuretics pump K⁺ directly from the blood into the urine
Less fluid reaches the collecting duct, so K⁺ becomes trapped in the urine
The diuretics block K⁺ absorption from the small intestine
e: Extra Na⁺ reaching the collecting duct is reabsorbed there in exchange for K⁺ secretion.
Higher flow and the volume loss (which raises aldosterone) both increase K⁺ loss in the urine.

q: Renal plasma flow is 600 mL min⁻¹ and GFR is 120 mL min⁻¹. What fraction of the plasma reaching the glomeruli is filtered?
e: Filtration fraction = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow.
= 120 ÷ 600 = 0.20 = 20%; the other 80% leaves through the efferent arteriole.

q: Why does drinking alcohol increase urination?
e: Less ADH → fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct → more dilute urine.

q: Which region of the kidney contains the glomeruli and the convoluted tubules?
e: Glomeruli, Bowman's capsules and the proximal and distal convoluted tubules all sit in the outer cortex.
The medulla holds the loops of Henle and collecting ducts; the pelvis collects urine.

q: When blood pressure drops, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole more than the afferent arteriole. How does this help the kidney?
o: It keeps glomerular pressure up so GFR is maintained
It lowers glomerular pressure so less fluid is filtered
It increases blood flow into the vasa recta
It stops filtration completely to save water
e: Narrowing the outflow vessel (efferent) backs blood up in the glomerulus.
Higher glomerular hydrostatic pressure helps keep GFR near normal even though less blood is arriving.
t: Squeeze the exit (efferent) and pressure rises upstream; squeeze the entrance (afferent) and it falls.

q: Which hormone is made by the kidney and stimulates red blood cell production?
e: Low O₂ in the kidney triggers EPO release.

q: When a person stands up quickly, blood pools in the legs and blood pressure briefly drops. How do baroreceptors respond?
o: They fire less, increasing sympathetic drive to the heart and vessels
They fire more, increasing vagal output to slow the heart and dilate vessels
They fire less, increasing parasympathetic output to the heart
They fire more, increasing sympathetic drive to the heart and vessels
e: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense stretch.
Less stretch → less firing → the brain boosts sympathetic activity.

q: A patient with polycythemia has a hematocrit of 65%. How does this affect the heart's workload?
o: Thicker blood raises resistance, so the heart works harder
More red cells lower resistance, so the heart works less
Higher O₂ content lets the heart beat much more slowly
Thicker blood lowers blood pressure, easing the heart
e: More red cells make blood more viscous.
Resistance rises with viscosity, so the heart must generate more pressure to keep the same flow.
t: Poiseuille: resistance rises with viscosity, so more red cells is not always better.

q: Why can't cardiac muscle be driven into a sustained tetanic contraction like skeletal muscle?
o: Its long plateau phase keeps it refractory
It lacks the troponin needed to bind Ca²⁺
Its cells are not joined by gap junctions
It stores too little Ca²⁺ to contract for long
e: L-type Ca²⁺ channels hold the cardiac action potential in a long plateau (about 250 ms).
The refractory period lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so a new beat cannot start until relaxation begins; the heart can refill between beats.

q: Which heart chamber pumps blood to the lungs?
e: Right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs.

q: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What are its stroke volume and ejection fraction?
e: SV = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL.
t: EF uses EDV in the denominator, not ESV.

q: Pressure in the leg veins is very low. What mainly helps return blood from the legs to the heart?
o: Vein valves plus squeezing by skeletal muscles
Strong rhythmic contraction of the thick vein walls
Capillaries actively pumping blood into the veins
Lymph vessels emptying red cells into the veins
e: Contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins, and one-way valves let blood move only toward the heart.
Breathing also helps: falling chest pressure during inspiration draws blood into the thoracic veins.

q: Which ABO blood type's plasma can be given to a patient of any ABO type?
o: Type AB, since it has no anti-A or anti-B
Type O, since its red cells lack A and B
Type A, since it has only anti-B antibodies
Type B, since it has only anti-A antibodies
e: Plasma carries the antibodies; the danger is donor antibodies attacking the recipient's red cells.
Type AB people make neither anti-A nor anti-B, so their plasma is safe for any recipient. Type O plasma has both antibodies.
t: Red cells: O is the universal donor. Plasma: AB is the universal donor. It's flipped.

q: Platelets help stop bleeding by:
o: Forming a plug and helping start the clotting cascade
Making antibodies that neutralize microbes at the wound
Engulfing bacteria that enter through the wound
Breaking down fibrin so the wound edges can seal
e: Platelets stick to damaged vessel walls, and fibrin threads then strengthen the plug.

q: A patient's aortic valve becomes stiff and narrowed (aortic stenosis). Over years, which change in the heart is most likely?
o: The left ventricular wall thickens to push harder
The right ventricular wall thins from lower demand
The left ventricular wall thins from lower demand
The left atrium shrinks as less blood enters it
e: A narrow valve means the left ventricle must produce much higher pressure to eject blood.
Chronic pressure overload makes cardiac muscle cells grow larger, thickening the wall (concentric hypertrophy).
t: Pressure overload thickens the wall; volume overload enlarges the chamber.

q: Mean arterial pressure is 100 mmHg and cardiac output is 5 L min⁻¹. What is total peripheral resistance?
e: MAP = CO × TPR, so TPR = MAP ÷ CO
100 ÷ 5 = 20 mmHg·min L⁻¹

q: Most systemic organs are supplied by arteries arranged in parallel rather than in series. What is a key advantage?
o: Each organ gets fresh arterial blood and its own flow control
Blood passes each organ in turn, so all of its O₂ gets used up
Total resistance is higher, so blood pressure stays steadier
The heart can pump less blood per minute to supply the body
e: In parallel, every organ receives arterial blood straight from the aorta, not blood already used by another organ.
Each organ's arterioles can change its own flow, and parallel paths also lower total resistance.

q: Why does the AV node delay the electrical signal briefly?
o: So the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
So the SA node can recharge before firing the next impulse
So the ventricles contract before the atria to prevent backflow
So the ventricles can repolarize, producing the T wave
e: The delay coordinates the timing of atrial and ventricular contraction.

q: Oral rehydration solution contains both glucose and salt. Why does adding glucose help a dehydrated patient with diarrhea absorb water?
o: SGLT1 co-transports Na⁺ with glucose, and water follows by osmosis
Glucose binds water in the lumen, blocking its loss in stool
Glucose kills the bacteria that are causing the diarrhea
Glucose triggers insulin, which drives water into intestinal cells
e: Na⁺–glucose co-transport still works in many diarrheal illnesses.
The absorbed solutes pull water into the body.

q: A pancreatic tumor secretes huge amounts of gastrin. Which finding is most likely?
o: Excess stomach acid causing ulcers in the stomach and duodenum
Very little stomach acid and poor protein digestion
Constipation caused by an excess of bicarbonate
Unusually high absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
e: Gastrin drives parietal cells to secrete HCl.
Constant high gastrin means constant high acid, which overwhelms the mucus and bicarbonate defenses and causes ulcers.

q: An infant has a thickened pyloric sphincter and vomits forcefully after every feeding. The vomit contains stomach contents but no bile. Blood tests show a high pH and high HCO₃⁻. What explains the acid–base change?
o: Loss of stomach HCl leaves extra bicarbonate in the blood
Swallowed air causes the infant to retain extra CO₂
Vomiting removes pancreatic bicarbonate from the body
The kidneys stop excreting bicarbonate after feeding
e: Each H⁺ that parietal cells secrete into the stomach leaves an HCO₃⁻ in the blood.
Normally that H⁺ is later neutralized in the duodenum; when it is vomited instead, the extra HCO₃⁻ remains, causing metabolic alkalosis.
No bile in the vomit fits a blockage before the duodenum.

q: Where does most absorption of nutrients take place?
e: The small intestine has villi and microvilli, giving a huge surface area.
Most digestion products (sugars, amino acids, fats) are absorbed there.
The large intestine mainly absorbs water and electrolytes.
t: Duodenum = mostly digestion; jejunum and ileum = mostly absorption.

q: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and returned to the liver. The drug cholestyramine binds bile salts in the gut so they're excreted. Why does this lower blood cholesterol?
o: The liver uses more cholesterol to replace the lost bile salts
Bound bile salts carry blood cholesterol directly into the gut
The drug blocks the liver from making new bile salts
Losing bile salts makes the gut absorb more dietary fat
e: Bile salts are made from cholesterol in the liver.
When the recycled bile salts are lost in the stool, the liver converts more cholesterol into new bile salts and pulls more LDL from the blood.

q: Na⁺ cotransporters in the apical membrane carry glucose and amino acids into intestinal cells. Why does this absorption also depend on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase in the basolateral membrane?
o: The pump keeps cell Na⁺ low, maintaining the gradient that drives cotransport
The pump moves glucose directly across the apical membrane into the cell
The pump digests disaccharides into monosaccharides at the brush border
The pump releases ATP into the lumen to power the cotransporters
e: Cotransporters use the 'downhill' flow of Na⁺ into the cell to drag glucose or amino acids 'uphill'.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase constantly pumps that Na⁺ back out; without it, cell Na⁺ would rise and the gradient would vanish.
t: Secondary active transport always has a primary pump working somewhere else.

q: The stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori makes large amounts of the enzyme urease. How does this help it survive in the stomach?
o: Urease makes ammonia, which neutralizes acid around it
Urease digests the mucus that protects the stomach
Urease blocks parietal cells from making intrinsic factor
Urease converts pepsinogen into inactive fragments
e: Urease splits urea into NH₃ and CO₂.
Ammonia is a base, so it neutralizes H⁺ and creates a less acidic pocket around the bacterium.

q: Why are pancreatic enzymes released as inactive zymogens?
o: To prevent them from digesting the pancreas itself
Because the liver must activate them
Because they work only in the stomach
e: Premature activation causes pancreatitis.

q: A patient with celiac disease has damaged villi in the small intestine. Which problem is expected?
o: Faster protein digestion in the mouth
e: Gluten triggers an immune attack on the intestinal lining, flattening villi and reducing surface area.

q: Secretin is released when acidic chyme enters the duodenum. What does it trigger?
o: The pancreas releases bicarbonate to neutralize the acid
Parietal cells in the stomach release more HCl
The gallbladder contracts to release stored bile
The liver stops making bile until the duodenal acid clears
e: Bicarbonate raises pH so pancreatic enzymes can work.

q: Which digestive enzyme begins significant starch digestion in the mouth?
e: Salivary amylase begins hydrolysis of starch glycosidic linkages.

q: Which structural features give the small intestine its huge absorptive surface?
e: Each level of folding multiplies the surface area.

q: Why do organ transplant patients take immunosuppressant drugs?
o: To keep T cells from attacking foreign MHC molecules on the donor organ
To boost antibody production against infections after surgery
To prevent blood clots from forming in the new organ's vessels
To keep the donor organ's own cells from dividing uncontrollably
e: Donor cells display different MHC (HLA) proteins.
Recipient T cells recognize them as foreign and attack.

q: The innate immune system:
e: Innate: skin, phagocytes, inflammation, complement.
Adaptive: B and T cells, specific and with memory.

q: Where do B lymphocytes mature in humans?
e: B cells are made and mature in the bone marrow; T cells are made there but mature in the thymus.
Spleen and lymph nodes are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet antigen.
t: B for Bone marrow, T for Thymus.

q: After strep throat, a child develops heart valve damage because antibodies against a strep protein also bind heart tissue. This is an example of:
o: Immunodeficiency from too few B cells
e: The strep protein resembles a heart protein, so antibodies made against the microbe cross-react with self.
This is how rheumatic fever damages heart valves.

q: Which cells produce antibodies?
e: Activated B cells become plasma cells that secrete large amounts of antibody.

q: In chronic granulomatous disease, phagocytes lack NADPH oxidase, the enzyme that makes superoxide. A patient's neutrophils engulf bacteria normally. What happens next?
o: Many bacteria survive, since no oxidative burst occurs
The bacteria are killed but can never be digested
The neutrophils can no longer leave the blood vessels
The bacteria escape before they can be engulfed
e: Superoxide and the reactive oxygen species made from it (the oxidative burst) are a main way phagocytes kill engulfed microbes.
Without it, bacteria survive inside phagocytes, causing recurrent infections and clusters of immune cells called granulomas.

q: Inflammation causes redness and warmth at an injury site mainly because:
o: Histamine and other signals dilate blood vessels
Red blood cells multiply rapidly at the injury site
Damaged skin cells generate heat through metabolism
Histamine constricts vessels, trapping warm blood
e: Vasodilation brings more blood; increased permeability lets fluid and white cells enter.

q: Where do T cells mature?
e: T cells are made in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus.
B cells mature in the bone marrow.

q: As HIV destroys CD4⁺ helper T cells, why do both antibody and cytotoxic T cell responses weaken?
o: Helper T cells give signals B and CD8⁺ cells need
HIV also infects and kills most B cells and CD8⁺ cells
Helper T cells make the antibodies that CD8⁺ cells use
CD4⁺ cells are the precursors of B cells and CD8⁺ cells
e: Helper T cells release cytokines and give contact signals that B cells need to make class-switched antibodies.
They also help activate and sustain CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells, so losing them weakens both arms.

q: Helper T cells (CD4⁺) recognize antigen presented on:
e: MHC II is found on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells).
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognize MHC I, found on all nucleated cells.
t: Rule of 8: CD4 × MHC II = 8; CD8 × MHC I = 8.

q: In type 1 diabetes, immune cells destroy pancreatic β cells. What kind of disorder is this?
e: The immune system attacks the body's own cells, failing self-tolerance.

q: Which antibody class is the first made in a new infection?
e: IgM is a large pentamer made early.
IgG follows and dominates later responses and memory.

q: In a resting skeletal muscle fiber, what prevents myosin heads from binding to actin?
o: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
Troponin is bound tightly to the myosin heads
Titin holds the thick filaments away from actin
Calmodulin keeps all the myosin heads in a locked state
e: Tropomyosin strands lie along the thin filament, blocking myosin-binding sites.
When Ca²⁺ binds troponin, troponin pulls tropomyosin aside and cross-bridges can form.

q: Which muscle type is voluntary and striated?
e: Skeletal: striated and voluntary. Cardiac: striated but involuntary. Smooth: non-striated and involuntary.

q: Rigor mortis (stiffening after death) occurs because:
o: No ATP is left to detach myosin from actin
No Ca²⁺ is left to expose actin's binding sites
Actin filaments dissolve, locking the sarcomere
Motor neurons keep firing for hours after death
e: Without ATP, cross-bridges stay locked.

q: Torn knee cartilage heals much more slowly than a broken bone. Why?
o: Cartilage is made mostly of calcium phosphate
Cartilage is constantly broken down by osteoclasts
e: Cartilage is avascular, so nutrients and repair cells reach it only slowly by diffusion.
Bone has a rich blood supply that brings cells and nutrients for repair.

q: What is the basic contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber?
e: Sarcomeres are arranged end to end, from Z-line to Z-line.

q: A sprained ankle is a stretch or tear of the dense connective tissue that holds the bones of the joint together. This tissue is:
e: Ligaments connect bone to bone at joints.
Tendons attach muscle to bone; articular cartilage covers bone ends inside the joint.

q: Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle cannot be driven into tetanus by rapid stimulation. Why?
o: Its refractory period lasts nearly as long as each contraction
It has no sarcoplasmic reticulum to store any Ca²⁺
It lacks troponin, so it can't be activated quickly
Its fibers are not electrically connected to each other
e: The cardiac action potential has a long plateau, so the cell can't fire again until it has nearly relaxed.
This prevents summation and makes sure the heart relaxes and refills between beats.

q: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by some anesthetics that cause uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release in skeletal muscle. Why does body temperature rise so dangerously?
o: Constant contraction and Ca²⁺ pumping burn huge amounts of ATP, releasing heat
The anesthetic shuts down sweat glands, so body heat can't escape
Released Ca²⁺ resets the hypothalamic set point to a much higher temperature
Skin vessels constrict, trapping metabolic heat in the body core
e: Muscles burn ATP rapidly to contract and to pump Ca²⁺ back.
Much of that energy is released as heat.

q: Bones are connected to muscles by:
e: Tendons: muscle to bone. Ligaments: bone to bone.

q: Why do long bones in children grow in length but adult bones do not?
o: Children's growth plates are still active cartilage; adults' have fused
Adults have no osteoblasts, so new bone matrix can't be laid down
Children's bones lack calcium, so they lengthen under mechanical load
Adults completely stop secreting growth hormone after puberty
e: Cartilage at the growth plates divides and is replaced by bone.
After puberty, the plates close (ossify).

q: During muscle contraction, what happens to the sarcomere?
o: The H zone and I band shorten; the A band stays the same
The A band shortens; the I band stays the same
The thick filaments shorten; the H zone stays the same
The Z-lines move apart; the H zone and A band lengthen
e: Filaments slide past each other; they don't shorten themselves (sliding filament model).

q: Which type of muscle forms the walls of blood vessels and the digestive tract?
e: Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated.
It lines hollow organs such as blood vessels, the gut, the bladder and the uterus.

q: Based on the hormone graph, on about which day does ovulation occur?
o: Day 14, right after the LH surge
e: The LH surge triggers ovulation about a day later.

e: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open at threshold, causing rapid depolarization.

q: Two unaffected parents have both an affected son and an affected daughter (shown). What is the most likely mode of inheritance?
e: Unaffected parents with affected children → recessive.
An affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive.
