q: In Gibson and Walk's visual cliff studies, most crawling infants (about 6–14 months old) would not cross onto the glass over the 'deep' side, even when their mothers called. Why can't this result alone prove that depth perception is innate?
o: The infants had months of visual experience before testing
The infants could feel the glass, so vision was irrelevant
The mothers' calls made the infants too anxious to move
Too few infants were tested to support any conclusion
e: Infants can't be tested until they can crawl, and by then they have had months to learn about depth.
So the study shows depth perception is present by crawling age, not that it was there at birth.

q: When you look directly at a word on a page, its image falls on the fovea. Why is vision sharpest there?
o: It is densely packed with cones that resolve fine detail
It has the highest density of rods in the retina
It is where the optic nerve exits the eye
It contains the most hair cells of any region
e: The fovea is the central pit of the retina, packed with cones and nearly free of rods.
Each foveal cone connects to few downstream cells, which preserves fine detail (high acuity).

q: Kinesthesia (proprioception) is the sense of:
e: Receptors in muscles, tendons and joints tell the brain where the body parts are.

q: A 100 Hz tone makes auditory nerve fibers fire about 100 times per second, matching the sound wave. This observation supports which theory of pitch?
e: Frequency theory: the rate of neural firing matches the sound's frequency, which works well for low pitches.
Place theory (pitch coded by WHERE the basilar membrane vibrates most) better explains high pitches.
t: Low pitch → frequency (firing rate); high pitch → place.

q: On a slide, 12 dots are arranged in three tight clusters of four, and viewers report seeing 'three groups.' Which Gestalt principle explains this?
e: The Gestalt principle of proximity says we group elements that are close together.
All the dots look alike, so similarity is not the basis for grouping here; spacing is.

q: In a hearing study using identical faint tones, Group 1 earns $1 for every hit, while Group 2 loses $1 for every false alarm. Group 1 has a 90% hit rate and 40% false-alarm rate; Group 2 has 60% and 10%. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The payoffs shifted the response criterion, not hearing sensitivity
Group 1 has better hearing sensitivity than Group 2 does
Group 2 has a lower absolute threshold for tones than Group 1
The money changed how loud the tones physically were
e: Group 1's payoff rewards saying 'yes' (liberal criterion); Group 2's punishes it (conservative criterion).
Both hits and false alarms moved together, the signature of a criterion shift.
Converting to z-scores gives d′ ≈ 1.5 for BOTH groups, so their sensitivity is the same.
t: Payoffs and instructions move the criterion; they don't change the ears.

q: The Müller-Lyer illusion makes two equal lines look different in length. Researchers found the illusion is stronger in people raised in 'carpentered' environments with many right angles. What does this support?
o: Perception is shaped partly by experience and culture
Perception of length is innate and the same across cultures
People in carpentered settings have more accurate depth vision
The illusion arises from differences in retinal structure
e: The cross-cultural difference suggests learned depth cues influence how we see the lines.

q: Hubel and Wiesel kept one eye of newborn kittens closed for the first few months. When it was reopened, few visual cortex neurons responded to that eye, and the kittens behaved as if blind in it. Closing one eye in adult cats had little effect. This shows that:
o: Visual development depends on input during a critical period
The retina of the closed eye was permanently destroyed
Visual cortex connections are fixed at birth regardless of input
Depth perception is learned through reinforcement
e: Early in life, cortical connections are shaped by experience: the open eye's inputs took over cortical neurons.
Because adults were barely affected, the window for this kind of plasticity is limited: a critical period.

q: After carbon monoxide poisoning damaged her ventral visual stream, patient D.F. could not say whether a slot was vertical or horizontal, yet she rotated a card correctly to post it through the slot. What does this show?
o: Vision for action can work without conscious object perception
Her dorsal stream was destroyed while her ventral stream survived
She had lost all input to her primary visual cortex
Her deficit was in moving her hands, not in vision
e: The ventral ('what') stream supports conscious recognition of shape and orientation; the dorsal ('how') stream guides action.
D.F.'s intact dorsal stream let her act on orientation she could not consciously report.

q: Each eye has a 'blind spot' where no image is detected. Why?
o: The optic nerve leaves there, so it has no photoreceptors
The retina there contains only rods and no cones at all
The lens cannot focus light onto that region
Ganglion cells there absorb all incoming light
e: Ganglion cell axons gather at the optic disc and exit the eye as the optic nerve.
No rods or cones sit at the optic disc, so light landing there is not detected. The brain fills in the gap.

q: The absolute threshold is the:
o: Minimum stimulus intensity that can be detected 50% of the time
Smallest detectable difference between two stimuli
Strongest stimulus a sense can detect
Point where a sense stops working
e: The difference threshold is the just-noticeable difference (JND).

q: Looking out the side window of a moving train, a passenger sees nearby fence posts race past while distant mountains seem to drift slowly. This depth cue is:
e: In motion parallax, close objects seem to move faster across your view than far objects as you move.
It is a monocular cue; retinal disparity and convergence need both eyes.

q: A child bitten by one dog becomes afraid of all dogs. This is:
e: The response spreads to stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.

q: Participants study a 20-word list. When recall is tested after a 30-second distraction task, which effect is most likely to disappear?
e: The recency effect (remembering the last items) depends on short-term memory.
A distraction task pushes those last items out of short-term memory.
The primacy effect remains because early items were rehearsed into long-term memory.
t: Primacy = long-term memory (rehearsal). Recency = short-term memory (still 'in the buffer').

q: A patient can't form new long-term memories after surgery but remembers childhood well. This is:
e: Anterograde: trouble forming new memories after the event.
Retrograde: losing memories from before the event.

q: Positive punishment is best illustrated by:
o: Getting a speeding ticket after driving too fast
Losing phone privileges for breaking curfew
Taking aspirin to remove a headache
e: Positive = something added; punishment = behavior decreases.
Losing phone privileges is negative punishment (something removed).

q: In Watson and Rayner's 'Little Albert' study, a steel bar was struck loudly behind an infant whenever he reached for a white rat. Before any pairing, the infant's crying at the loud noise was the:
e: The noise naturally caused crying without learning, so the noise is the US and the crying it causes is the UR.
After pairing, the rat became the CS and crying at the rat became the CR.
t: Ask: did this need to be learned? No → 'unconditioned.'

q: Rats drank sweet water while each lick also triggered a flash of light and a click. Then one group was made ill by X-ray exposure, and another received foot shocks. Later, the ill rats avoided the sweet taste but not the light and click, while the shocked rats avoided the light and click but not the taste. What does this show?
o: Animals are biologically prepared to link certain cues to certain outcomes
Any stimulus can be paired equally well with any consequence at all
Taste aversions need many separate pairings before they appear
Rats cannot detect lights and sounds while they are drinking
e: If all pairings were equal, each group would avoid both the taste and the light-and-click.
Instead, taste was linked to illness and light-and-click to pain, so evolution has prepared some associations (Garcia and Koelling's finding).
t: Taste goes with nausea; sights and sounds go with pain.

q: A patient with migraines learns that taking medication at the first sign of a visual aura prevents the headache from developing at all. Her medication-taking is best described as:
e: Escape learning ends an aversive stimulus that is already present; avoidance learning prevents it from starting.
The aura acts as a warning signal, and acting on it avoids the headache. Both are forms of negative reinforcement.

q: Shaping is:
o: Reinforcing successive approximations of a desired behavior
Reinforcing a behavior only after a fixed number of responses
Pairing a neutral stimulus with one that triggers a reflex
Learning a behavior by observing and imitating a model
e: Each small step closer to the goal is rewarded.

q: Remembering the details of your own high school graduation ceremony is an example of:
e: Episodic memory stores personal experiences tied to a specific time and place.
Semantic memory stores general facts (for example, knowing what a graduation is) without the personal context.

q: A dog salivates to a bell, but not to a buzzer, after learning that only the bell predicts food. Later the dog salivates to a light that was repeatedly paired with the bell (never with food). Which phenomenon explains the light?
e: The bell (an established CS) acts like a US to condition a new stimulus, the light.

q: After a concussion, a football player cannot remember the 30 minutes before the hit, but his memories from the previous week and from childhood are intact. What does this pattern suggest?
o: His most recent memories had not yet been fully consolidated
He has anterograde amnesia from hippocampal removal
His older memories are held in sensory memory
His older memories are held in short-term memory
e: Losing memories from before an injury is retrograde amnesia.
Recent memories are lost first because consolidation into stable long-term storage takes time; older memories are more resistant.

q: After living through an earthquake, a woman now startles strongly at minor noises, such as a door closing, that never bothered her before. This is:
e: Sensitization is an increased response to stimuli after exposure to a strong or threatening stimulus.
Like habituation, it is non-associative learning, but it moves responding in the opposite direction.

q: As people age from 30 to 70, which pattern of intelligence is typical?
o: Crystallized intelligence holds steady; fluid intelligence declines
Fluid intelligence holds steady; crystallized intelligence declines
Both fluid and crystallized intelligence rise steadily
Both fluid and crystallized intelligence drop sharply
e: Crystallized intelligence (knowledge, vocabulary) is maintained or even grows into late adulthood.
Fluid intelligence (solving new problems quickly) peaks in early adulthood and then declines.
t: Crystallized = what you know; fluid = how fast you figure out the new.

q: In Piaget's three-mountain task, a 4-year-old is asked what a doll on the far side of a mountain model can see, and she describes her own view. This reflects:
o: Missing object permanence in the sensorimotor stage
Failed conservation in the formal operational stage
Abstract reasoning in the concrete operational stage
e: Preoperational children (about ages 2–7) have trouble taking another person's point of view.
Describing her own view as the doll's shows egocentrism.

q: A patient after a stroke speaks slowly in short, effortful phrases but understands what others say. Which brain area was most likely damaged?
e: Broca's area (frontal lobe) is involved in speech production.
Damage causes non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia, with comprehension mostly spared.
Wernicke's aphasia is the opposite: fluent speech that makes little sense, with poor comprehension.
t: Broca's = Broken speech. Wernicke's = Wordy but makes no sense.

q: Focusing on one conversation in a crowded room demonstrates:
e: Selective attention prioritizes a particular input amid competitors.

q: A 14-year-old says, 'If gravity were twice as strong, basketball players couldn't dunk.' Reasoning systematically about such hypothetical situations is characteristic of Piaget's:
e: The formal operational stage (from about age 12) brings abstract and hypothetical reasoning.
Concrete operational children (about 7–11) reason logically, but mainly about real, concrete objects.

q: According to Piaget, a child who understands that pouring water into a taller glass doesn't change its amount has reached the:
e: Conservation develops around ages 7–11.

q: A patient speaks fluently but uses made-up words and has great difficulty understanding speech. Which language area is most likely damaged?
e: Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
Damage to the arcuate fasciculus alone causes trouble repeating (conduction aphasia).

q: According to the activation-synthesis hypothesis, dreams are:
o: The brain's attempt to interpret random neural activity in REM
Disguised expressions of unconscious wishes and conflicts
A process for consolidating memories from the previous day
Mental rehearsal of threats to prepare for waking life
e: Freud's theory, by contrast, sees dreams as disguised wishes.

q: The difference between the words 'bat' and 'pat' comes from a change in a single:
e: A phoneme is the smallest unit of sound that can change a word's meaning (/b/ vs /p/).
A morpheme is the smallest unit of MEANING, such as the '-s' in 'bats.'

q: A volunteer sits quietly with her eyes closed, awake and relaxed. Which EEG waves will most likely dominate?
e: Alpha waves appear during calm, relaxed wakefulness, especially with the eyes closed.
Beta waves mark alert activity, theta waves light sleep (N1) and delta waves deep sleep (N3).

q: Viewers who are counting basketball passes in a video often fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. This is:
e: When attention is focused on one task, people can miss a clearly visible, unexpected object (Simons and Chabris's study).
Change blindness is failing to notice that something in a scene has CHANGED, for example between two views.

q: An emergency physician instantly 'recognizes' a patient's chest pain as heartburn because he looks like many heartburn patients she has seen, and she misses a heart attack. A checklist that makes doctors list alternative diagnoses reduces such errors. In dual-process terms, the checklist works by:
o: Engaging slow, deliberate System 2 to check fast System 1
Speeding up fast, intuitive System 1 judgments
Replacing slow, deliberate reasoning with a quick heuristic
e: System 1 is fast, automatic and heuristic-based; here it relied on representativeness.
The checklist forces effortful System 2 reasoning, which can catch System 1 errors.

q: Endorphins are natural chemicals that:
o: Reduce pain and produce pleasant feelings
Increase alertness and raise heart rate
Regulate the sleep–wake cycle at night
e: Endorphins act on the same opioid receptors as morphine.

q: In a 1950s study by Olds and Milner, rats with electrodes in certain brain areas (such as the septal region) pressed a lever over and over, sometimes thousands of times per hour, to receive brief electrical stimulation. This was early evidence for:
o: Brain circuits that reinforce behavior (reward pathways)
Brain areas that produce pain when stimulated
Spinal reflexes that operate without the brain
Motor areas that trigger involuntary, reflexive lever presses
e: Animals work hard only for things that are reinforcing, so stimulating these areas acted like a reward.
Later work linked this reward system to dopamine pathways such as the mesolimbic pathway to the nucleus accumbens.

q: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant disorder that causes jerky involuntary movements (chorea) and later cognitive decline. It mainly involves degeneration of the:
o: Hippocampus and the medial temporal lobe
e: The basal ganglia help select and start movements while suppressing unwanted ones.
In Huntington's disease, striatal neurons (caudate and putamen) die, so unwanted movements break through. Parkinson's disease also involves basal ganglia circuits but causes too little movement.
t: Parkinson's = too little movement; Huntington's = too much. Both point to the basal ganglia.

q: Adoption studies are useful in behavioral genetics because they:
o: Separate genes (from biological parents) from environment (from adoptive parents)
Show that the shared rearing environment is the main source of traits
Hold genes constant by studying only adopted identical twin pairs
Remove all environmental effects so that genetic effects can be measured directly
e: Comparing adopted children to both sets of parents helps tease apart nature and nurture.

q: An identical-twin study finds that if one twin has a trait, the other has it 50% of the time; for fraternal twins, it's 15%. What does this suggest?
o: Genes contribute substantially, but environment also matters
The trait is entirely genetic, since identical twins share DNA
Shared family environment fully explains the twin difference
Fraternal twins share more genes, so environment dominates
e: Identical twins share nearly all DNA, so higher concordance points to a genetic role.
Since it's not 100%, environment also plays a part.

q: Researchers apply transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over a volunteer's left motor cortex, and her right thumb twitches. What key advantage does TMS have over fMRI for studying brain function?
o: It alters brain activity directly, so it can test causation
It measures blood flow more precisely than fMRI
It records single neurons directly through the intact skull
It gives detailed images of brain structure
e: fMRI shows which areas are active during a task, which is correlational.
TMS briefly excites or disrupts a cortical area; if behavior changes, that area plays a causal role.

q: Monkeys whose temporal lobes (including both amygdalae) were removed became unusually tame, approached snakes without fear and mouthed objects. Later studies limiting damage to the amygdala reproduced the loss of fear. These findings best support a role for the amygdala in:
o: Evaluating threats and producing fear responses
Relaying visual signals onward to the occipital lobe
e: This pattern is called Klüver–Bucy syndrome.
When the amygdala is lost, animals no longer react to normally threatening stimuli, so the amygdala is needed to detect threats and generate fear.

q: Patients recovering from dental surgery were given a placebo they were told was a painkiller, and many reported less pain. In patients also given naloxone, an opioid-receptor blocker, the placebo's pain relief was much smaller. What does this suggest?
o: Placebo pain relief partly works by releasing endorphins
The placebo itself contained an opioid-like chemical
Naloxone increases pain by damaging pain receptors
Placebo effects are imagined and have no biological basis
e: Naloxone blocks opioid receptors, including those used by the body's own endorphins.
If blocking these receptors weakens the placebo effect, the placebo must have triggered endorphin release, a real biological effect.

q: A split-brain patient sees a word only in the LEFT visual field. Why can't they say the word out loud?
o: The image reaches the right hemisphere, but speech is mainly left-lateralized
The image reaches the left hemisphere, but speech is mainly right-lateralized
Cutting the corpus callosum blocks signals from the eyes to the cortex
The image reaches both hemispheres, but neither can link it to memory
e: Left visual field → right hemisphere.
With the corpus callosum cut, the information can't reach the left hemisphere's language areas.
They can often still pick the object with their left hand.

q: Brain scans of experienced London taxi drivers, who memorize the city's complex street layout, showed larger posterior hippocampi than in controls, and size increased with years on the job. This best supports:
o: Experience-driven plasticity in a region used for spatial memory
Hippocampal size is fixed by genes before adulthood
The hippocampus controls the motor skills of driving
Spatial memory is stored mainly in the cerebellum
e: The hippocampus is important for spatial navigation and memory.
Because size grew with years of driving, the finding suggests that heavy use can reshape brain structure (neuroplasticity), although the study is correlational.

q: A nurse strokes a newborn's cheek, and the baby turns its head toward the touch and opens its mouth. Which reflex is this?
e: The rooting reflex helps a newborn find the nipple: touch on the cheek → head turns toward it.
Like most primitive reflexes, it fades during the first months of life as the cortex matures.

q: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a single-gene disorder that causes intellectual disability if untreated, yet children who follow a low-phenylalanine diet from birth develop normally. What does this best show?
o: A genetic condition's outcome can still depend on environment
PKU cannot actually be a heritable genetic disorder
The diet repairs the DNA sequence of the PKU gene
Intellectual ability is not influenced by genes at all
e: PKU is clearly inherited, but its harmful effects appear only when phenylalanine builds up from the diet.
Changing the environment (diet) changes the outcome without changing the genes: a gene–environment interaction.
t: 'Genetic' does not mean 'unchangeable.'

q: Psychologists commonly describe an emotion as having which three components?
e: An emotion includes a physiological component (bodily arousal), a behavioral component (expressions and actions) and a cognitive component (the subjective feeling and appraisal).
Alarm, resistance and exhaustion are the stages of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, not parts of an emotion.

q: A runner chooses between two equally appealing races scheduled on the same day. This is which type of conflict?
e: Two desirable options: approach–approach.
Two undesirable options: avoidance–avoidance.

q: Self-determination theory says people need three things for healthy motivation. Which set is correct?
e: Meeting these needs supports intrinsic motivation and well-being.

q: After gastric bypass surgery, many patients report feeling much less hungry, and their blood levels of ghrelin fall. Which interpretation is best supported?
o: Less ghrelin from the bypassed stomach may contribute to reduced hunger
Lower ghrelin proves that patients' leptin levels must have risen
The surgery eliminated the hypothalamus's role in feeding
Hunger is controlled only by learned habits, not hormones
e: Ghrelin is a hunger hormone released mainly by the stomach.
When most of the stomach is bypassed, ghrelin drops, which fits with reduced hunger; the data are correlational, so it may be one factor among several.
t: Ghrelin makes you 'grumble' (hungry); leptin makes you 'lean' (full).

q: Smiling when you are not happy can slightly improve your mood. This supports the:
e: Facial expressions may feed back to influence emotional experience.

q: According to the Yerkes–Dodson law, performance on a moderately difficult task is best when arousal is:
e: The Yerkes–Dodson law describes an inverted-U curve.
Too little arousal leads to boredom; too much leads to anxiety.
Moderate arousal gives the best performance (very easy tasks peak a bit higher, very hard tasks a bit lower).
t: A little test anxiety can help. A lot hurts.

q: Research on hunger finds that damage to the lateral hypothalamus in animals leads to a loss of interest in food, while damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus leads to overeating. What does this suggest?
o: The hypothalamus contains areas that both start and stop eating
Hunger signals come mainly from the stomach, not the brain
The lateral hypothalamus signals fullness and stops eating
The hypothalamus controls thirst, while hunger is set elsewhere
e: Lateral hypothalamus: 'hunger center'. Ventromedial: 'satiety center' (a simplified model).

q: Which coping strategy focuses on changing the stressful situation itself?
e: Example: making a study plan to handle exam stress.

q: On her first skydive, a woman feels terror during the jump and mild relief afterward. After 100 jumps, she feels little fear during the jump but intense exhilaration afterward. Which theory explains this shift?
e: Solomon's opponent-process theory says a strong emotional state triggers an opposing state that follows it.
With repetition, the first state weakens while the opposing after-state grows stronger: fear fades and exhilaration builds.
t: The same theory helps explain drug tolerance and withdrawal: the high shrinks while the opposing low grows.

q: In Lazarus's appraisal model, secondary appraisal is:
o: Judging whether you have the resources to cope with a stressor
Judging whether a situation is threatening or harmless
Reassessing a stressor after an initial coping attempt
The body's alarm reaction during the first stage of stress
e: Primary appraisal: Is this a threat? Secondary appraisal: Can I handle it?

q: According to the James–Lange theory, emotion occurs when:
o: We perceive our body's physical reaction to a stimulus
Body reaction and emotion happen at the same time
We label arousal with a cognitive explanation
The amygdala releases an emotion directly
e: 'I'm afraid because I'm trembling.'

q: After a frightening car accident, a mother calls her sister and gathers her children close rather than fighting or fleeing. Shelley Taylor proposed this pattern, linked to oxytocin release, as a stress response called:
e: Taylor's tend-and-befriend model says stress can lead people to protect offspring (tend) and seek social support (befriend).
Oxytocin is thought to promote this bonding response; it was described as more common in women.

q: In the DSM-5-TR, post-traumatic stress disorder is classified in which category?
e: Since DSM-5, PTSD has been placed with trauma- and stressor-related disorders, which require exposure to a traumatic or stressful event.
Acute stress disorder and adjustment disorders are in the same category.
t: PTSD is no longer listed as an anxiety disorder; the MCAT uses current DSM-5-TR categories.

q: Dogs first exposed to shocks they could not escape later failed to escape shocks even when they could easily jump a barrier. Dogs never exposed to inescapable shock learned to escape quickly. How is this finding applied to human depression?
o: Learned helplessness: experiences of no control can lead to passivity and hopelessness
Classical conditioning: the barrier became a conditioned stimulus for pleasure and calm
Drive reduction: the dogs' hunger drive was stronger than their drive to avoid pain
Habituation: repeated shocks made the dogs stop noticing the pain of later shocks
e: Seligman and Maier showed that uncontrollable bad events can teach animals that their actions do not matter.
Seligman proposed that similar learned helplessness contributes to depression, which features passivity and hopelessness.

q: After a frightening argument, a patient suddenly cannot move her right arm. Neurological testing finds no damage, and the symptom does not fit any known neurological disease. DSM-5-TR calls this:
e: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) involves motor or sensory symptoms that are incompatible with recognized neurological conditions.
In factitious disorder, symptoms are deliberately faked; here they are not intentionally produced.

q: Generalized anxiety disorder involves:
o: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things
Intense fear of one specific object or situation
Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks and fear of more
Intrusive memories and avoidance after a trauma
e: Symptoms last at least six months.

q: Fourteen months after her husband died, a 60-year-old woman still feels intense longing for him nearly every day, feels part of herself has died, and cannot return to work or social activities. She has no prior psychiatric history and does not meet criteria for a major depressive episode. Which DSM-5-TR diagnosis fits best?
e: Prolonged grief disorder, added in DSM-5-TR, requires at least 12 months since the death (for adults) with intense yearning or preoccupation and impairment.

She has no flashbacks or trauma-related avoidance (PTSD). Her symptoms center on yearning for the person she lost rather than general low mood lasting 2 years or more (persistent depressive disorder). Adjustment disorder is not diagnosed when the symptoms meet criteria for prolonged grief disorder.
t: Normal grief can be intense; the disorder requires impairing symptoms that last at least a year in adults.

q: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes:
o: Too much dopamine activity in certain brain pathways
Too little dopamine activity throughout the brain
Too little serotonin activity in mood-related pathways
Too much GABA activity in the prefrontal cortex
e: Antipsychotics that block dopamine D₂ receptors reduce positive symptoms.

q: Somatic symptom disorder involves:
o: Excessive worry about physical symptoms that disrupts daily life
Intentionally faking physical symptoms for external gain
Neurological symptoms like paralysis with no medical cause
Persistent fear of having a serious illness despite few or no symptoms
e: The symptoms are real to the person; faking for gain is malingering.

q: A person feels persistent fear that is out of proportion to a specific harmless object. This is most consistent with:
e: Specific phobias involve excessive fear or anxiety associated with particular objects or situations.

q: For more than 2 years, an adult has had many periods of mild highs and mild lows. None meet the full criteria for a hypomanic or major depressive episode. The best diagnosis is:
e: Cyclothymic disorder involves at least 2 years (1 year in youth) of numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never reach full episode criteria.
Bipolar II requires a full hypomanic and a full major depressive episode.

q: A medication blocks dopamine receptors and reduces a patient's hallucinations, but the patient develops tremors and stiffness. Why?
o: Blocking dopamine in the basal ganglia causes Parkinson-like effects
Blocking dopamine in the cerebellum causes tremor and poor balance
Excess serotonin from the drug causes muscle rigidity and tremor
Blocking acetylcholine at muscles causes stiffness and tremor
e: Dopamine also controls movement in the nigrostriatal pathway.

q: The biopsychosocial model explains disorders as resulting from:
o: Biological, psychological and social factors together
Biological factors, such as genes and brain chemistry
Unresolved unconscious conflicts from early childhood
Learned behaviors shaped by reinforcement history
e: This model is now the standard approach.

q: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) in adults requires depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least:
e: Persistent depressive disorder is a long-lasting depression: at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents).
Two weeks is the minimum for a major depressive episode.

q: Cooley's 'looking-glass self' says our self-concept is shaped by:
o: How we imagine others see us
How we compare ourselves to others
e: We use others' reactions as a mirror.

q: Blaming your poor exam score on the professor's unfair questions, when you didn't study, is an example of:
e: Rationalization: giving reasonable-sounding excuses for unacceptable behavior.

q: According to E. Tory Higgins's self-discrepancy theory, a student who feels she falls short of what her parents believe she OUGHT to be is most likely to feel:
e: A gap between the actual self and the ought self (duties, obligations) leads to agitation-related emotions like anxiety and guilt.
A gap between the actual self and the ideal self (hopes, wishes) leads to dejection-related emotions like sadness.
t: Ought → anxious; Ideal → down. Don't swap them.

q: Carl Jung proposed that all humans share inherited images and themes, such as the 'hero' or the 'wise old man,' stored in the:
e: Jung split the unconscious into a personal unconscious and a collective unconscious shared by all people.
The shared images in the collective unconscious are called archetypes.

q: A clinician shows a client ambiguous inkblots and asks what they look like, believing the answers reveal hidden conflicts. This projective test (the Rorschach) comes from which perspective?
e: Projective tests assume people project unconscious feelings onto ambiguous stimuli.
Revealing unconscious conflict is the goal of the psychodynamic approach.

q: A therapist notices a client accusing others of being dishonest while the client is often dishonest. Which defense mechanism fits best?
e: Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings or traits to others.

q: Bandura's concept of reciprocal determinism says behavior results from interactions among:
o: Unconscious drives of the id, ego and superego
e: Each factor affects the others.

q: A child playing on a baseball team understands what the pitcher, catcher and outfielders are each expected to do and how they fit together. According to George Herbert Mead, the child has reached which stage?
o: Game stage, taking the role of the generalized other
Play stage, taking the role of one other at a time
Looking-glass stage, imagining how others judge him
e: In Mead's play stage, children take on one role at a time (like 'doctor').
In the game stage, they understand the attitudes and expectations of many roles at once, the generalized other.

q: According to Erikson, the main psychosocial task of adolescence is:
e: Erikson described 8 stages, each with a central conflict.
Adolescence (about 12–18) centers on forming a stable sense of identity.
Intimacy vs. isolation comes next, in young adulthood.
t: Know the stage for each age group, especially adolescence and young adulthood.

q: Self-efficacy is:
o: Your belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task
Your overall sense of your own worth as a person
Your belief that outcomes depend on your own actions
Your actual skill level at completing a specific task
e: Bandura: higher self-efficacy → more persistence.

q: A college sophomore has tried biology, music and business classes and is actively talking with mentors, but has not yet chosen a path. In Marcia's model, which identity status is she in?
e: Marcia's statuses depend on exploration (crisis) and commitment.
She is exploring but not yet committed, which is moratorium.
t: Moratorium = exploring now; achievement = explored, then committed.

q: Eysenck proposed a biological basis for introversion. According to his theory, why do introverts tend to avoid loud parties?
o: They have higher baseline cortical arousal, so extra stimulation is unpleasant
They have lower baseline cortical arousal, so they need more stimulation
They lack the dopamine receptors needed to feel any pleasure socially
They were punished for socializing, so the behavior was extinguished
e: Eysenck linked extraversion to the brain's reticular activating system.
Introverts already sit at a higher arousal level, so added stimulation pushes them past their comfort point; extraverts seek stimulation to raise low arousal.

q: Differential association theory proposes that people learn deviance from:
o: Interacting with others who engage in deviant behavior
Being labeled as deviant by authority figures
Lacking legitimate means to achieve social goals
Inheriting traits that increase impulsive behavior
e: Sutherland's theory emphasizes learning through social interaction.

q: An attitude has which three components (the ABC model)?
e: Feelings, actions and thoughts about something.

q: When a student talks loudly during a lecture, nearby classmates glare and shush him. In sociology, this reaction is an example of:
e: Sanctions are rewards (positive) or punishments (negative) for following or breaking norms.
Glaring and shushing are unofficial (informal) and disapproving (negative). A fine or expulsion would be formal.

q: A smoker who knows smoking causes cancer tells himself, "My grandfather smoked and lived to 95." This is an attempt to reduce:
e: Cognitive dissonance is discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs and behaviors.
Smoking conflicts with knowing that smoking is dangerous.
He reduces the conflict by adding a belief that minimizes the danger.
t: People reduce dissonance by changing the behavior OR changing the belief. Changing the belief is usually easier.

q: A health class shows teens weak versions of tobacco ad arguments and then helps them refute each one. Later, the teens resist real tobacco ads better than classmates who did not get this training. This is:
e: McGuire's inoculation theory says exposure to weakened attacks, plus practice countering them, builds resistance to later persuasion.
It works like a vaccine, preparing 'defenses' before the real attack.

q: In a study, people who were told that a famous expert supported a claim agreed more, even when the argument was weak. Which persuasion factor is at work?
e: Credibility can persuade without careful analysis.

q: A patient hides his HIV diagnosis from coworkers because he fears it would cause them to see him as discredited and less acceptable. Erving Goffman called this kind of devalued attribute a:
e: Goffman defined stigma as an attribute that deeply discredits a person and spoils their social identity.
Fear of stigma can keep people from disclosing conditions or seeking care.

q: During early childhood, which agent of socialization usually has the greatest influence?
e: The family is the primary agent of socialization: children first learn language, norms and values at home.
Peers, schools and media become more important later in childhood and adolescence.

q: A clinic volunteer first asks a donor to fund a $10,000 equipment purchase. After the donor refuses, she asks for a $100 donation instead, and the donor agrees. Which technique is this?
e: Door-in-the-face starts with a large request that will likely be refused, followed by a smaller, more reasonable one.
The second request seems like a concession, so people feel pressure to reciprocate by agreeing.
t: Foot-in-the-door goes small → big; door-in-the-face goes big → small.

q: According to the elaboration likelihood model, the central route to persuasion involves:
o: Careful thinking about the strength of the arguments
Cues like the speaker's attractiveness or fame
Emotional appeals and catchy, memorable slogans
The sheer number of arguments offered, not their quality
e: Central route changes tend to last longer.

q: Merton's strain theory explains deviance as arising when:
o: People lack legitimate ways to reach goals their society values
People are labeled deviant and come to accept that identity
People learn deviant values from close friends and family
People's bonds to family and community are weak
e: Example: pursuing wealth through crime when legal routes are blocked.

q: An experienced surgeon performs a routine procedure faster when students are watching. This illustrates:
e: Social facilitation: the presence of others improves performance on simple or well-practiced tasks.
It can hurt performance on new or difficult tasks.
Social loafing is putting in LESS effort when working in a group.
t: Well-practiced task + audience = better. New task + audience = worse.

q: A landlord refuses to rent to applicants of one religion, even though city laws and policies forbid it. This is an example of:
e: Individual discrimination is unfair treatment by one person against members of a group.
Institutional discrimination is built into the rules of organizations; here the rules forbid it.

q: Older adults scored lower on a memory test when told it measured age-related memory decline than when told it measured general learning. The best explanation is:
e: Reminding people of a negative stereotype about their group (here, aging and memory) can hurt their performance.
The test was the same; only the framing changed.

q: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when:
o: Expectations lead to behavior that makes those expectations come true
People notice only evidence that confirms their expectations
People believe they had predicted an outcome after learning what happened
Fear of confirming a stereotype lowers a person's performance
e: Example: teachers who expect more from students may help them achieve more.

q: Participants were falsely told they were very good at telling real suicide notes from fake ones. Even after learning the feedback was made up, they still believed they had above-average skill. This is:
e: Belief perseverance is holding onto a belief after its basis has been discredited.
People build explanations for a belief, and those explanations outlast the original evidence.

q: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that:
o: Bad things happen to good people
e: It can lead to blaming victims.

q: A hiring manager unknowingly rates resumes with typically male names more favorably than identical resumes with typically female names. This shows:
e: Implicit biases can influence decisions without awareness.

q: A doctor sticks with an initial diagnosis even after new test results point elsewhere. Which biases are most likely at work?
o: The halo effect and social loafing
e: Anchoring: relying too heavily on the first piece of information.
Confirmation bias: favoring evidence that supports it.

q: During a recession, many residents blame a small immigrant community for job losses that were actually caused by factory automation. This best illustrates:
e: Scapegoating is blaming a less powerful group for problems it did not cause.
Frustration is redirected onto a convenient, vulnerable target.

q: Attribution theory studies how people:
e: We explain behavior by disposition (person) or situation.

q: The Implicit Association Test measures:
o: How quickly people pair concepts, to detect automatic associations
How strongly people endorse prejudiced statements on a survey
Physiological arousal when people view members of other groups
How accurately people recall the faces of other groups
e: Its ability to predict individual behavior is debated.

q: Institutional discrimination is:
o: Unfair treatment built into the policies of organizations or society
Unfair treatment by one prejudiced individual toward another person
Negative attitudes that members of one group hold about another
Oversimplified, generalized beliefs about the traits of a social group
e: It can exist even without individual prejudice.

q: A coworker says a nurse snapped at a patient "because she's just a rude person." This explanation is a:
e: A dispositional attribution explains behavior by a person's traits or character.
A situational attribution would point to outside factors, like a 14-hour shift.

q: Goffman's dramaturgical approach compares social life to:
o: A theater performance with front and back stages
A marketplace where people exchange costs and rewards
A machine whose parts keep the whole system stable
A contest between groups over scarce resources
e: Front stage: how we act for an audience. Back stage: how we act in private.

q: A master status is:
o: The status that most shapes how others see a person
The status a person holds with the highest prestige
A status assigned at birth, such as race or sex
A status a person earns through their own effort
e: Example: being a doctor or having a visible disability may dominate how others react.

q: A securely attached infant typically:
o: Is upset when the caregiver leaves and comforted when they return
Shows little distress when the caregiver leaves or returns
Is very upset when the caregiver leaves and hard to soothe after
Acts confused, approaching and avoiding the caregiver at once
e: The caregiver serves as a secure base for exploring.

q: Vampire bats that fail to feed often receive regurgitated blood from roostmates, including unrelated bats that shared with them before. Unrelated bats that never share are less likely to get help. This best supports:
e: Reciprocal altruism (Trivers) is helping non-relatives who are likely to return the favor later.
Help here tracks past sharing, not genetic relatedness, so kin selection does not explain it.
t: Kin selection follows genes; reciprocal altruism follows past favors.

q: In the Strange Situation, an infant shows little distress when her mother leaves and turns away from her when she returns. This infant is best classified as:
e: Avoidant infants show little distress at separation and ignore or avoid the caregiver at reunion.
Ambivalent infants are very distressed and are hard to comfort, often seeking and resisting contact at once.
t: Avoidant = 'I don't need you'; ambivalent = 'Don't leave, but I'm still mad.'

q: A nurse feels torn because her job requires both caring for patients and enforcing strict hospital rules that frustrate them. This is:
e: Tension within one role.

q: A doctor acts calm and professional with patients but shares frustrations with colleagues in the break room. In Goffman's terms, the break room is the:
e: Back stage: where people relax their performance.

q: A hockey player trips an opponent only to stop a scoring chance, not out of anger. This is best described as:
e: Instrumental aggression is harm used as a means to another goal (here, stopping a goal).
Hostile aggression is driven by anger, with harm as the goal itself.
t: Ask what the harm is FOR: the goal itself (hostile) or a means to something else (instrumental).

q: A medical resident feels torn because her duties as a doctor conflict with her duties as a parent. This is:
e: Role conflict: tension between the demands of two DIFFERENT roles (doctor vs. parent).
Role strain: tension within ONE role (for example, too many demands as a doctor).
Here there are two roles, so it is role conflict.
t: One role = strain. Two roles = conflict.

q: In a study, roommates who were randomly assigned became friends more often than people living farther apart. Which factor does this best illustrate?
e: Random assignment rules out choosing friends based on similarity.

q: Kin selection theory explains why people are more likely to help relatives than strangers. What is the evolutionary logic?
o: Helping relatives helps pass on shared genes
Relatives are more likely to repay the help later
Helping relatives raises the helper's social status
People learn to help relatives through reinforcement
e: Inclusive fitness counts genes passed on through relatives.

q: In a hawk–dove model, a population settles at a stable mix of aggressive and peaceful individuals that no rare new strategy can outperform. Game theorists call this mix:
e: John Maynard Smith defined an evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) as one that cannot be invaded by a rare alternative.
In the hawk–dove game, the ESS can be a stable mixture of fighting and backing down.

q: A country's population is aging quickly because of low fertility and longer life expectancy. Which policy challenge is most likely?
o: Funding healthcare and pensions for a larger elderly population
Building more schools for a growing number of children
Reducing high infant mortality in a young population
Controlling rapid population growth caused by persistently high fertility
e: Fewer workers support more retirees.

q: Factors that drive people away from their home country, such as war or poverty, are called:
e: Pull factors attract people to a new place, such as jobs.

q: In Country Y, death rates are already low. Over 30 years, girls' schooling rises, families move to cities and contraception becomes common, while the birth rate falls from 35 to 18 per 1,000. Which demographic transition stage is Country Y moving through?
o: Stage 3: falling birth rates and slowing growth
Stage 1: high birth rates and high death rates
Stage 2: high birth rates and falling death rates
Stage 4: low, stable birth and death rates
e: Stage 3 begins once death rates are low and birth rates start falling, driven by education, urbanization and contraception.
Growth slows but is still positive while births exceed deaths.

q: A commune rejects private property, money and the wider society's focus on career success, and lives by opposing values. Sociologists call this group a:
e: A counterculture actively opposes key values and norms of the larger society.
A subculture has distinct practices (like medical-student slang) but does not reject mainstream values.

q: A hospital's stated purpose is to treat patients, but it also becomes a place where neighborhood residents form friendships. The friendships are a:
e: Manifest functions are intended and recognized.
Latent functions are unintended consequences.
Friendship-building is an unintended benefit, so it's a latent function.
t: Manifest = meant. Latent = 'later noticed'.

q: A sociologist studies why women physicians are paid less than men in the same specialty and how unpaid caregiving at home shapes their careers. Which perspective is she most likely using?
e: Feminist theory examines gender inequality in power, pay and opportunity, including unpaid domestic labor.
Functionalism focuses on stability; symbolic interactionism on everyday meanings.

q: Functionalism views society as:
o: A system of parts that work together to maintain stability
A struggle between groups over power and resources
A product of meanings created in everyday interactions
The result of individuals weighing costs and benefits
e: Associated with Durkheim and Parsons.

q: In a community, nearly everyone marries a partner from their own religious and ethnic group. This marriage pattern is called:
e: Endogamy is marrying within one's own social group.
Exogamy is marrying outside one's group (endo = within, exo = outside).

q: Assimilation is the process by which:
o: A minority group adopts the culture of the dominant group
A minority group keeps its own culture alongside others
Groups blend equally to form a new, shared culture
A dominant group forcibly removes a minority group
e: Multiculturalism: groups keep distinct cultures.

q: Rational choice theory says people:
o: Weigh costs and benefits before acting
e: Social exchange theory applies this idea to relationships.

q: A country in stage 2 of the demographic transition has a crude birth rate of 40 per 1,000 and a crude death rate of 15 per 1,000 per year, with no migration. About how long will its population take to double?
e: Rate of natural increase = (40 − 15) ÷ 1,000 = 25 per 1,000 = 2.5% per year.
Rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ 2.5 = 28 years.
t: Subtract death rate from birth rate before using the rule of 70.

q: Symbolic interactionism focuses on:
o: How people create meaning through everyday interactions
How large institutions keep society stable over time
How economic classes compete for power and resources
How biological drives shape human social behavior
e: Associated with Mead and Blumer.

q: In a caste system, social position is:
e: Class systems allow more mobility.

q: A chronic condition has a stable incidence of 4 new cases per 1,000 people per year, and patients live with it for an average of 5 years. What is the approximate prevalence?
e: In a steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration.
4 per 1,000 per year × 5 years = 20 per 1,000.
t: Longer duration means more existing cases, even at the same incidence.

q: Social reproduction refers to:
o: The passing of social class status from one generation to the next
The movement of children into a higher class than their parents
The process by which people learn their society's norms
The replacement of a population through births over time
e: Cultural and economic capital help maintain class across generations.

q: Two neighborhoods in the same city differ in life expectancy by 10 years. Which explanation fits best with sociological research?
o: Differences in income, housing, environment and access to care
Genetic differences between the residents of each neighborhood
Differences in personal health choices unrelated to resources
Random variation in deaths across small neighborhood populations
e: Place-based social determinants strongly shape health.

q: In the U.S., the health of Black women tends to worsen earlier in adulthood than that of white women. Arline Geronimus' 'weathering' hypothesis attributes this mainly to:
o: Cumulative stress from social and economic disadvantage
Lower use of prenatal care, and nothing else
e: Weathering is the early health decline caused by repeated exposure to racism, economic hardship and other stressors.
Chronic stress wears down body systems over time (allostatic load).

q: Social capital refers to:
o: The benefits that come from social networks and relationships
The financial assets, like money and property, a person owns
The education, tastes and skills that signal social class
The prestige attached to a person's occupation
e: Who you know can open doors to jobs and resources.

q: Relative poverty means:
o: Having much less than others in the same society
Lacking the resources needed for basic survival
Living below a fixed, government-set income line
Being poor for a short time due to job loss
e: Absolute poverty is lacking the basics needed to survive.

q: A school places students into 'advanced' and 'basic' tracks early. Low-income students are overrepresented in basic tracks, get less experienced teachers and rarely move up. A conflict theorist would argue that tracking:
o: Sorts students fairly by their true ability alone
Promotes upward mobility for most poor students
Has no lasting effect on students' later lives
e: Conflict theorists see tracking as a way schools pass advantage and disadvantage from parents to children.
This is an example of social reproduction.

q: Oscar Lewis's 'culture of poverty' idea claims poverty persists because poor communities develop values such as fatalism that pass to children. A structural critic would most likely respond that:
o: A lack of jobs, schools and services keeps people poor
Poverty is mostly caused by genetic differences
Values passed from parents fully explain poverty
Most poor families rise out of poverty in one generation
e: Structural explanations stress conditions such as job loss, segregation and underfunded schools.
Critics argue the 'culture of poverty' blames the poor for problems created by social structure.

q: Which situation best illustrates a 'food desert'?
o: A low-income area with no nearby supermarket, only convenience stores
A rural farming area with many orchards and roadside stands
A dense city district with several supermarkets and markets
A wealthy suburb with weekly farmers' markets and several specialty grocers
e: Limited access to affordable healthy food contributes to diet-related disease.

q: Two equally skilled new researchers publish similar papers, but the one trained by a famous scientist receives far more citations, grants and invitations, and the gap keeps widening. Robert Merton called this:
e: Merton named this cumulative advantage after the biblical line that those who have will be given more.
Early advantages snowball, so inequality grows over a career or a life course.

q: The Davis–Moore thesis, a functionalist view of stratification, argues that inequality exists because:
o: Higher rewards draw talented people into vital, demanding roles
Ruling classes use their wealth to keep workers powerless
Inequality is passed down through families' cultural capital
People are randomly assigned to social classes at birth
e: Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore argued that some positions matter more and need scarce talent and long training.
Unequal pay and prestige motivate people to fill them; critics note many rewards reflect power, not importance.

q: In the classical conditioning graph, the response returns partway (the segment labeled ?) after a rest period following extinction. What is this called?
e: The response reappears after a pause, showing extinction suppressed it rather than erasing it.

q: According to the hierarchy shown, a person who has just lost their home and has no food would focus mainly on which level?
e: Maslow proposed that basic needs (food, water, shelter) generally come first.
t: Later research shows people often pursue several levels at once; the order is a tendency, not a strict rule.

q: The graph shows recall by list position right after studying. Why are the first words recalled well?
o: They were rehearsed more and reached long-term memory
They were still in sensory memory
They were shown in a larger font
e: This is the primacy effect.
The last items are recalled well because they're still in short-term memory (recency).

e: Points fall tightly along a downward line: strong negative correlation.
Correlation still doesn't show that sleep causes anxiety changes.
